explain: Meeting agreed availability levels is availability management's purpose — design and operation together. Incident management is the trap: it restores service after failures (contributing to availability) but doesn't own the target; capacity owns performance, not availability.

q: A team provisions triple the servers it needs 'just in case', wasting budget. Capacity and performance management would instead:
options: Provision even more headroom for safety
Ignore cost and focus only on speed
Balance performance, demand, and cost — enough capacity without waste
Let incidents reveal the real capacity needs
explain: The practice satisfies current and future demand cost-effectively — over-provisioning fails the cost test as surely as under-provisioning fails the performance test. The 'safety' trap and managing-by-incident are the failure modes.

q: A deployment plan schedules moving components to live environments outside business hours and aligns with the change schedule. This planning is part of:
options: Release management
Deployment management
Incident management
Service validation and testing
explain: Planning and executing the movement of components to live environments is deployment management. Release management is the trap: release decides when features become usable; deployment gets the components into place.

q: IT asset management compares installed software against purchased entitlements. This primarily helps the organization:
options: Restore incidents faster
Authorize changes
Categorize problems
Control costs and manage license compliance risk
explain: Entitlement-versus-installation reconciliation is about cost control and compliance — core IT asset management value. The other options borrow purposes from unrelated practices; none of them track license entitlements.

q: The CAB reviews a proposed database upgrade; the impact analysis, listing affected services, was built from the CMDB. The practice that supplied this information is:
options: Service configuration management
Change enablement
Release management
Monitoring and event management
explain: Configuration management provides the reliable CI data that impact analysis depends on. Change enablement is the trap: it uses the analysis to authorize, but the data itself comes from configuration management.

q: A team makes small monthly tweaks to its incident categorization based on analyst feedback. This is:
options: Not real improvement — improvements must be large projects
A formal project by definition
Continual improvement — ongoing small improvements count
Exclusively change enablement's work
explain: Continual improvement covers ongoing incremental gains, not just big initiatives — small feedback-driven tweaks are its bread and butter. Equating improvement with projects is the trap; authorizing changes is a different practice's job.

q: The service desk resolves a common 'printer offline' issue in minutes using a pre-defined documented procedure. This is an example of:
options: A workaround
Problem management
A standard change
An incident model
explain: Incident models are pre-defined procedures for handling known incident types efficiently. A workaround is the trap: it bypasses the cause of an incident, while a model is the agreed handling procedure; a standard change is a change type, not a handling procedure.

q: Two known errors await permanent fixes, but resources allow only one this quarter. Problem management should prioritize:
options: The easiest fix to clear the backlog faster
The one posing the greater risk — weighing impact and likelihood of recurrence
The oldest record regardless of impact
Whichever the loudest stakeholder demands
explain: Problems are prioritized by the risk they pose (impact and likelihood), not by age or ease. The efficiency trap picks the quick win; the politics trap serves the loudest voice — prioritization must serve the business.

q: An organization lets team leads authorize low-risk, well-understood changes without convening the full CAB. This is acceptable because:
options: The change authority can be a person or a group — it doesn't always have to be the CAB
CABs are optional in ITIL 4
Low-risk changes need no authorization at all
Team leads replace the change enablement practice
explain: ITIL defines the change authority as whoever is authorized — an individual, the change manager, the CAB, or an emergency CAB — scaled to the change's risk. Authorization is still required, just proportionate; the authorizer is not the practice itself.

q: Users bypass the service desk and call engineers directly, causing duplicated effort and untracked work. Re-establishing the desk as the single point of contact fixes this by:
options: Banning users from contacting engineers
Hiring more engineers to take direct calls
Capturing all demand in one place for consistent handling and tracking
Automating every user interaction
explain: The single point of contact captures demand for incidents and service requests so work is consistently handled and visible. The enforcement trap bans contact; the value is in coordinated capture, not in forbidding it.

q: A customer SLA promises 99.9% availability; the internal network team commits to supporting targets through an internal agreement. That internal agreement is an:
options: SLA
External contract
Underpinning change record
Operational level agreement (OLA)
explain: OLAs are agreements between internal provider teams that underpin SLAs; contracts are with external suppliers. The trap is calling it an SLA: SLAs face the customer, OLAs face inward.

q: A monitoring tool logs 'backup completed successfully' each night and no action is taken. This is an:
options: Warning event
Informational event
Exception event
Incident
explain: Informational events need no action — they simply record a change of state. A warning would signal an approaching threshold; an exception would indicate abnormal operation requiring response; an incident requires an unplanned interruption or quality reduction.

q: An employee requests access to a shared finance folder; nothing is broken or degraded. The service desk should handle this as a:
options: Service request — a pre-defined, normal part of service delivery
Incident
Problem
Emergency change
explain: No interruption or quality reduction means no incident — this is a normal, pre-defined service action. Logging everything as an incident is the trap; a routine fulfillment is not an urgent change.

q: During a major incident, the incident manager escalates to senior leadership to authorize emergency spending on vendor support. This is:
options: Functional escalation
A workaround
Hierarchical escalation — seeking greater authority or resources
Problem escalation
explain: Hierarchical escalation moves up authority levels for decisions and resources; functional escalation moves across to different expertise. The scenario is about authority to spend, not about needing new skills — that distinction is the exam trap.

q: A known error has a reliable workaround, but the permanent fix is scheduled for next quarter. The known error record should:
options: Be closed now that a workaround exists
Be deleted to keep the database clean
Be converted into an incident
Remain open until the permanent resolution is implemented
explain: A known error stays open under error control until the permanent fix is applied — the workaround only manages impact. Closing on the workaround is the trap of mistaking impact reduction for resolution.

q: Before authorizing a core switch replacement, the CAB reviews the risk assessment, backout plan, and expected benefits. This assessment exists to:
options: Delay every change as long as possible
Maximize successful changes by ensuring risks are understood and balanced against benefits
Assign blame if the change fails
Generate incidents for the service desk
explain: Change enablement balances speed with risk: assess, authorize, schedule. The bureaucracy trap treats assessment as delay — it actually enables safe speed; the blame trap confuses governance with fault-finding.

q: A service desk analyst asks a caller how many colleagues are affected and whether a business deadline is at risk. This helps the analyst:
options: Assess impact and urgency to prioritize the incident correctly
Authorize a change to fix the issue
Diagnose the root cause
Close the ticket faster
explain: Impact times urgency equals priority — the desk needs business context to set it. The authority trap assumes desks authorize changes (they don't); root-cause diagnosis belongs to problem management.

q: A provider sets SLA targets unilaterally, reports 100% achievement, yet customers remain unhappy. The root mistake is:
options: Measuring service performance at all
Not involving the CAB in target-setting
Targets must be business-based and agreed with the customer — not imposed
Using OLAs instead of SLAs
explain: Service level management aligns targets with business needs through customer agreement — imposed targets produce the 'watermelon SLA', green outside and red inside. The CAB trap is misplaced: the CAB authorizes changes, it doesn't set service targets.

q: Monitoring raises exception events for the same failing service three nights running; each triggers an incident resolved by reboot. The BEST next step is:
options: Keep rebooting — the incidents are being resolved
Disable the monitoring alerts to reduce noise
Raise a standard change for the reboots
Open a problem record to investigate the recurring cause
explain: Recurring incidents signal an unresolved cause — problem management's trigger. Keep rebooting is the trap of confusing restoration with resolution; each reboot treats the symptom while the cause keeps returning.

q: A self-service portal lists 'new laptop', 'software install', and 'access request', each with a description and expected fulfillment time. This published list is part of the:
options: Change schedule
Service catalogue
Known error database
Configuration management database
explain: The service catalogue publishes the services — including requestable ones — available to consumers. The change schedule is the trap: it lists planned changes, not requestable services; the known error database holds problems with documented causes.

q: The service desk's purpose includes capturing demand for:
options: Incident resolution and service requests
Changes and problems
Releases and deployments
Improvements and risks
explain: The desk is the single point of contact capturing demand for incident resolution and service requests. The trap lists changes and problems: those have their own practices — the desk may log them, but its purpose centers on incidents and requests.

q: A zero-day vulnerability is being actively exploited; a fix is deployed within hours after a rapid emergency CAB review. This shows:
options: Emergency changes skip authorization entirely
Emergency changes are just standard changes done quickly
Emergency changes are still assessed and authorized — on an accelerated path
CABs are unnecessary in modern organizations
explain: Emergency means urgent, not uncontrolled — assessment and authorization still happen, just faster, often via an emergency CAB. Skipping authorization is the dangerous trap; standard changes are pre-authorized routine work, a different concept from urgency.

q: After a major incident is resolved, the review finds the underlying cause is unknown and likely to recur. The appropriate next step is:
options: Close all records — the service is restored
Immediately implement an emergency change
Update the SLA targets
Open a problem record to investigate the cause
explain: Restoration isn't resolution: an unknown, recurring cause belongs in problem management. Closing everything is the trap of treating incident closure as the end; changing things without understanding the cause risks making it worse.

q: A provider uses one SLA with company-wide targets, underpinned by service-specific targets in the same structure. This layered approach is a:
options: Customer-based SLA
Multi-level SLA
Service-based SLA
Operational level agreement
explain: Multi-level SLAs combine corporate, customer, and service levels in one structure. The service-based trap describes one service for all customers — the scenario describes layers, not a single-service view.

q: During a major incident, the service desk sends users regular updates on progress and expected resolution. This communication role reflects the desk as:
options: The single point of contact keeping users informed
The change authority
Problem management
The emergency CAB
explain: Users need one trusted source of updates during major incidents — the desk's single-point-of-contact role. Problem management investigates causes and the CAB authorizes changes; neither owns user communication.

q: A faulty storage controller causes repeated outages. The team reboots to restore service, investigates the controller, then replaces it under authorization. This shows:
options: Practices work best in isolation
Only incident management matters in outages
Practices collaborate across the value chain — restore, diagnose, then fix under control
Problem management restores service
explain: Incident management restores, problem management diagnoses, change enablement authorizes the fix — the value chain in action. The silo trap treats practices as separate fiefdoms; real service management integrates them.

q: A new ITSM tool fails because staff were never trained and roles were left unclear — the technology itself worked fine. The neglected dimension is:
options: Information and technology
Partners and suppliers
Value streams and processes
Organizations and people
explain: Skills, roles, culture, and structure are the organizations and people dimension — the tool was fine; the people side wasn't. The trap blames technology; every practice touches all four dimensions, and neglecting any one sinks the initiative.

q: Analysts resolve incidents faster because the knowledge base holds accurate known-error articles. This knowledge belongs to the:
options: Organizations and people dimension
Information and technology dimension
Partners and suppliers dimension
Governance component
explain: Information, knowledge, and technology form one dimension — the knowledge base is information managed with technology. The trap classifies it under people because people use it, but the dimension classifies the asset itself.

q: An organization keeps service design in-house but outsources 24/7 monitoring to a specialist firm. This sourcing decision belongs to the:
options: Partners and suppliers dimension
Information and technology dimension
Value streams and processes dimension
Governance component
explain: Decisions about external relationships, contracts, and what to source where are the partners and suppliers dimension. The governance trap misplaces it: governance directs the organization, but sourcing strategy is classified under this dimension.

q: A team maps every step from 'user requests a laptop' to 'laptop delivered and working', uncovering three handoff delays. This end-to-end workflow view is the:
options: Organization chart
Technology stack
Value streams and processes dimension
Supplier contract
explain: The dimension concerns how work flows across the organization to create value — the end-to-end steps, not the org chart or the tools. Those are the traps: structure and technology support the flow, they aren't the flow.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the ITIL service value system?
options: Guiding principles
Governance
Continual improvement
Service requests
explain: The SVS components are guiding principles, governance, the service value chain, practices, and continual improvement. Service requests are handled within practices — operational items, not system components.

q: Senior leaders define the organization's service vision, policies, and improvement direction for the coming year. This is the value chain activity:
options: Engage
Plan
Obtain/build
Deliver and support
explain: Plan creates shared understanding of vision, current status, and improvement direction. Engage is the trap: it covers stakeholder interaction and relationships, while this scenario is leadership setting direction.

q: Before launch, a team verifies that a new service meets stakeholder expectations for quality, cost, and time to market. This is:
options: Design and transition
Obtain/build
Deliver and support
Improve
explain: Design and transition ensures products and services meet expectations for quality, costs, and time to market. Obtain/build is the trap: it acquires the components; this scenario validates the design against expectations.

q: Day-to-day service operation, user support, and incident handling fall mainly under the value chain activity:
options: Plan
Design and transition
Deliver and support
Obtain/build
explain: Deliver and support covers ongoing delivery and support of services to users. Design and transition is the trap: it prepares services for operation, while this scenario is the operation itself.

q: Purchasing servers and developing in-house software for a new service are part of the value chain activity:
options: Engage
Plan
Deliver and support
Obtain/build
explain: Obtain/build ensures service components are available when and where needed — including purchasing and in-house development. Deliver and support is the trap: delivery uses the components; obtaining them is this activity's job.

q: An improvement team agrees the service desk should answer 90% of calls within 30 seconds, up from 60% today. Setting this measurable target is the continual improvement model step:
options: Where are we now?
Where do we want to be?
How do we get there?
Did we get there?
explain: Defining the desired future state with measurable targets is 'Where do we want to be?' — it follows the current-state assessment and precedes the plan. Mixing up the assessment, target, and plan steps is the standard trap.

q: Three months later, the team measures call-answer performance against the 90% target to check progress. This assessment is the step:
options: Did we get there?
What is the vision?
Take action
How do we get there?
explain: 'Did we get there?' checks results against the targets after action is taken. Take action is the trap: implementation was the earlier phase; this scenario is the post-action assessment.

q: The governing body sets the policy that all changes need risk assessment; managers then implement the change process accordingly. This illustrates:
options: Governance and management are the same thing
Managers perform governance
Governance directs — evaluate, direct, monitor — while management executes within that direction
Guiding principles replace governance
explain: Governance evaluates, directs, and monitors; management plans and executes within the direction set. Equating the two is the classic confusion the exam targets; the policy-versus-implementation split shows the boundary.

q: A surge of customer requests for weekend support hours is, in ITIL 4 terms, an example of:
options: Value
Governance
A practice
Demand — an input to the service value system
explain: Opportunity and demand are the SVS inputs; the system transforms them into value. Value is the trap — it is the output, not the input. Requests for new or changed service are demand.

q: Launching a new service involves engage, plan, design and transition, obtain/build, and deliver and support working together. This combination of activities to achieve an outcome is a:
options: Dimension
Value stream
Practice
Guiding principle
explain: A value stream is the specific combination of value chain activities (plus practices) used to create a particular outcome. Practices is the trap: practices support value streams, but the stream itself is the end-to-end flow of activities.

q: When improving incident management, a team considers staffing, tools, supplier contracts, and workflows. Considering all four dimensions matters because:
options: The dimensions apply to the whole service value system — every practice touches all four
Only incident management uses the dimensions
The dimensions replace the need for practices
Technology is the only dimension that really matters
explain: The four dimensions are relevant to the entire SVS, so any practice improvement must consider all of them — neglecting one sinks the effort. The traps narrow the dimensions to one practice or one dimension.

q: A team runs an improvement using the seven-step sequence: vision, current state, targets, plan, action, assessment, sustaining momentum. They are using:
options: The improve value chain activity
The guiding principles
The continual improvement model
The service value chain
explain: The seven named steps are the continual improvement model — distinct from the improve value chain activity and the continual improvement practice. The exam deliberately tests all three; the step names identify the model.

q: New data-protection regulations force changes to several services. In ITIL 4, such regulations are:
options: Part of the service value chain
A guiding principle
An internal practice
External factors that influence the service value system
explain: The SVS operates within a landscape of external factors — political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental — that shape what the system must do. The value chain is the trap: it is internal, while regulation sits outside it, influencing it.

q: Each service value chain activity:
options: Works in isolation from the others
Takes inputs and transforms them into outputs, contributing to value creation
Applies only to brand-new services
Replaces the need for management practices
explain: Value chain activities are interconnected input-to-output transformations — engage's stakeholder needs become plan's inputs, and so on. The silo trap claims isolation; the chain only creates value because activities feed each other.

q: A team lead sets direction for how her team prioritizes work and monitors whether they follow it. This shows that governance:
options: Exists at every organizational level, not just the board
Is only for senior executives
Is the same as the service desk function
Replaces day-to-day management
explain: Governance — evaluate, direct, monitor — happens at every level; a team lead directing and monitoring her team is governing. Reserving governance for the board is the trap; directing is not the same as doing the work.

q: The service value system creates value for:
options: Only external customers
Only the service provider
The organization, its customers, and other stakeholders
Only shareholders
explain: The SVS transforms opportunity and demand into value for the organization, its customers, and stakeholders broadly — not just the paying customer or the provider alone.

q: A team proposes 24/7 phone support because customers asked for it. The finance lead warns it would double support costs and strain analysts. Applying 'focus on value', the team should:
options: Weigh the customer outcome against the provider's costs and sustainability — value must work for all stakeholders, including the provider
Approve it, because the customer is always the only stakeholder that matters
Reject it, because any cost increase violates the principle
Approve it only if analysts agree to work longer hours
explain: Focus on value considers every stakeholder in the service relationship — the provider's costs, capacity, and people matter alongside customer outcomes. The customer-only trap ignores the provider as a stakeholder; the cost-increase trap treats the principle as a spending ban rather than a value-versus-cost balance.

q: A customer compares two backup providers. Provider X is cheaper per month, but requires the customer's staff to manage restores and retraining. Applying 'focus on value', the customer should evaluate:
options: Only the monthly subscription price
Only the provider's profit margin
Only the feature list
The total value: outcomes achieved minus the full costs of consumption, including staff effort and retraining
explain: Value is outcomes balanced against the full cost of consumption — price plus imposed costs like staff effort and training. Price-only or feature-only comparisons are the traps; they ignore the costs the service relationship imposes on the consumer.

q: Automating routine ticket triage will not change the customer experience much, but it will sharply reduce after-hours workload and burnout for the service desk team. Under 'focus on value', this improvement is:
options: Invalid, because value only concerns external customers
Worthwhile — the provider's own people are stakeholders, and their experience is part of the value equation
Invalid, because the principle forbids internal improvements
Worthwhile only if customers are told about it
explain: Stakeholders include the provider organization and its people — value is not limited to external customers. The traps wrongly restrict the principle to customer-facing outcomes; sustainable services need value for those who deliver them too.

q: Before launching an initiative to cut incident resolution times, a team first measures its current average resolution time and backlog over the last quarter. This measurement step reflects:
options: Optimize and automate
Progress iteratively with feedback
Keep it simple and practical
Start where you are — assess the current state before deciding what to change
explain: Start where you are means understanding the current state — including honest baseline measurements — before designing the improvement. Skipping the baseline is the trap: without it, the team cannot set realistic targets or prove the improvement worked.

q: Leadership wants to outsource network monitoring to a vendor. Following 'start where you are', the FIRST step is to:
options: Assess the current in-house monitoring capability — what works, what gaps exist — before deciding what to outsource
Sign the vendor contract immediately to show progress
Disband the internal monitoring team
Discard all existing monitoring tools as legacy
explain: The principle says to inventory existing services, processes, and capabilities first; the outsourcing decision should build on that assessment. Jumping to a contract or discarding working capability wastes existing value and may outsource something the team already does well.

q: Two companies merge, each with its own incident process. One process is slow but thorough; the other is fast but loses tickets. Applying 'start where you are', the merged team should:
options: Throw out both processes and buy a new tool
Keep the strengths of each — the speed of one, the thoroughness of the other — and build a combined process
Adopt the slower process because it is more documented
Stop handling incidents until a perfect process is designed
explain: Start where you are means assessing what exists and reusing what works — here, combining the strengths of both processes. Blank-slate replacement discards proven value; freezing work until perfection arrives serves nobody.

q: A team pilots a new change process with one department, collects feedback showing the approval step is confusing, ignores it, and rolls the same process out company-wide — where it fails the same way. The mistake was:
options: Piloting with only one department
Collecting feedback at all
Failing to act on the feedback before scaling — progress iteratively WITH feedback means feedback must shape the next iteration
Rolling out too slowly
explain: Iterative progress only works when feedback actually steers the next iteration; collecting it and ignoring it is the same as not collecting it. The traps blame the pilot size or the act of gathering feedback — the failure was discarding what the feedback revealed.

q: A team plans its portal redesign as a single six-month phase with one feedback review at the end. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the better structure is:
options: One twelve-month phase to be extra thorough
No phases at all — just start building
Shorter time-boxed iterations, each delivering something usable and gathering feedback
Six one-month phases with no feedback between them
explain: The principle calls for smaller, manageable sections executed in a timely manner, with feedback before, during, and after each. Long phases without feedback are big-bang delivery in disguise; phases without feedback between them miss the point entirely.

q: Before building a self-service knowledge base, a team interviews users about what articles they actually need. Seeking this input BEFORE the work starts is an example of:
options: Progress iteratively with feedback — feedback is sought before, during, and after each iteration, not only at the end
Keep it simple and practical
Optimize and automate
Think and work holistically
explain: Feedback 'before' validates direction when change is cheapest — the principle explicitly includes the before-phase. The trap treats feedback as a post-delivery review; by then, building the wrong thing is already expensive.

q: A new expense-reporting service is designed entirely by the finance systems team. At launch, employees find it confusing and refuse to use it. Which principle was neglected?
options: Start where you are
Collaborate and promote visibility — the users, as key stakeholders, should have been involved in the design
Optimize and automate
Keep it simple and practical
explain: The right stakeholders — here, the future users — must be involved at the right time, which includes design. Simplicity is a plausible distractor since the result was confusing, but the described failure is stakeholder exclusion, not step-count.

q: A major service upgrade is underway, but progress is tracked in the project manager's private spreadsheet. Stakeholders keep asking for status and getting different answers. To apply 'collaborate and promote visibility', the team should:
options: Restrict status information to avoid confusion
Send longer status emails once a month
Make progress visible — a shared dashboard or board showing real status to all stakeholders
Stop reporting until the upgrade is finished
explain: Visibility means work and its outcomes are transparent to the right people, enabling genuine collaboration. Hiding information or reporting rarely are the opposite of the principle; inconsistent private tracking is what created the confusion.

q: An integration project reaches go-live before anyone involves the external supplier whose API it depends on — and the API cannot support the required volume. The lesson is:
options: Suppliers should never be involved in projects
APIs are too risky to use
Go-live dates should always slip
Collaborate and promote visibility — suppliers are stakeholders who must be involved at the right time, not discovered at the end
explain: Partners and suppliers are stakeholders in the work; involving them early surfaces constraints while they can still be addressed. The traps reject suppliers or blame the technology — the failure was timing of involvement, not the partnership itself.

q: A team plans to introduce an AI chatbot for first-line support. Thinking holistically, they should consider:
options: How it affects people (training, roles), technology (integration), partners (vendor support), and processes (escalation paths) — all four dimensions together
Only the chatbot's purchase price
Only the technology, since it is a technology project
Only the support team's opinion
explain: Think and work holistically means considering how all parts work together — no initiative succeeds on technology alone. The single-factor traps are classic sub-optimization: each ignores dimensions whose neglect sinks the project.

q: Developers automate deployments so code reaches production in minutes, but support documentation and training lag weeks behind, leaving the service desk unable to help users. This shows a failure to:
options: Automate faster
Think and work holistically — the end-to-end service includes documentation, training, and support, not just deployment speed
Hire more developers
Slow down all automation
explain: Local optimization of one step damaged the whole service — holistic thinking considers the full value stream from code to supported user. Automating faster or hiring more developers deepens the imbalance; the fix is seeing the whole system.

q: Procurement buys the cheapest laptops available, saving 20% upfront — but the service desk spends twice as much time supporting their failures. This is a failure to:
options: Negotiate harder with the vendor
Buy even cheaper laptops
Think and work holistically — the purchase decision ignored its downstream impact on support costs and user productivity
Centralize all procurement decisions
explain: One team's saving became another team's cost — the total cost of ownership view is holistic thinking. The traps optimize the purchase price further or reshuffle who decides, without addressing the fragmented, non-holistic decision.

q: A change request form has 25 mandatory fields, but the CAB only ever reads five of them. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Add ten more fields for completeness
Make all fields optional so nothing is ever captured
Require a separate form for each field
Trim the form to the fields that actually achieve the objective — the minimum needed for a good decision
explain: Simplicity means the fewest steps and least effort to achieve the objective; fields nobody uses are non-value-adding complexity. Removing everything swings too far — the principle trims waste, it doesn't abolish the information needed for decisions.

q: A team needs to track improvement ideas. One faction wants a full enterprise PPM suite; the current need is a shared list with owners and dates. 'Keep it simple and practical' favors:
options: Starting with the simplest workable solution — the shared list — and only adding sophistication if a real need emerges
Buying the enterprise suite immediately for future-proofing
Building a custom application from scratch
Tracking ideas on paper sticky notes forever
explain: Practical means choosing the simplest solution that achieves the objective, growing complexity only with demonstrated need. Enterprise-suite-first is the over-engineering trap; the principle resists sophistication for its own sake.

q: A new request type — 'loaner laptop' — needs a fulfillment workflow. Following 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Design a 40-step workflow covering every hypothetical edge case
Start with a simple workflow for the common case, then refine it based on real experience
Refuse to offer the request until the workflow is perfect
Copy another organization's full workflow unchanged
explain: Simple and practical pairs with iterative thinking: start minimal, learn from reality, refine. Exhaustive upfront design is the trap — it burns effort on edge cases that may never occur while delaying the value.

q: A team owns an automation platform but uses only its basic scheduling, while requesting budget for an additional tool. Applying 'optimize and automate', they should FIRST:
options: Buy the new tool — more technology is always better
Abandon automation entirely
Optimize their use of the existing platform's capabilities before adding new technology
Automate the budget approval process
explain: The principle includes using technology to its full capabilities — optimize what you have before expanding the estate. Buying more tools while underusing current ones is the trap of pursuing automation for its own sake rather than for value.

q: A team automates approval of all access requests, including requests for highly sensitive financial systems. A better application of 'optimize and automate' would be:
options: Automating even more, including incident diagnosis
Removing all approvals to maximize speed
Never automating anything involving access
Automating routine low-risk approvals while keeping human judgment for high-risk ones — automate where it adds value
explain: Optimize and automate says to automate only where it adds value — routine work gains speed and consistency, while high-risk decisions still need human judgment. Blanket automation is the trap; the principle is selective, not maximal.

q: A company buys 200 laptops for its staff, taking full ownership of the hardware. It also subscribes to a cloud platform where it uses virtual machines without owning any servers. In ITIL 4 terms, the laptops are ___ and the cloud usage is ___.
options: Goods — ownership is transferred to the consumer; access to resources — the consumer uses the provider's resources without owning them
Services; products
Both goods, since both cost money
Both services, since both support work
explain: Goods transfer ownership to the consumer; services can provide access to resources the provider continues to own. The traps blur the line: payment alone doesn't make something a good, and anything useful isn't automatically a service.

q: A service desk analyst resets a user's password. Within the provider's service offering, this analyst's activity is an example of a:
options: Service action — work performed by the provider to support the consumer
Good
Product
Configuration item
explain: Service offerings combine goods, access to resources, and service actions — the password reset is an action performed by the provider. It isn't a good (nothing is transferred) or a product (the configured resources behind the service).

q: A provider offers a 'managed laptop service' built from specific laptop models, a standard operating system image, and a support contract. This configured combination of resources is, in ITIL 4, a:
options: Service relationship
Service action
Product — a configuration of resources created by the organization
Value stream
explain: Products are configurations of an organization's resources, designed to offer value; services are offered based on one or more products. The service relationship is the cooperation around it; the value stream is the workflow that delivers it.

q: A provider's monthly report celebrates closing 2,000 tickets, while the customer complains that outages keep disrupting month-end processing. The mismatch is between:
options: Utility and warranty
Cost and risk
Goods and services
Outputs and outcomes — the provider measures what it produced, but the customer judges the result it enables
explain: Outputs are deliverables the provider produces (closed tickets); outcomes are the stakeholder results they enable (undisrupted month-end). Measuring outputs while the consumer experiences outcomes is the classic disconnect — activity is not achievement.

q: Two customers use the same project management service. One calls it invaluable; the other calls it overpriced. ITIL 4 explains this by defining value as:
options: The perceived benefits, usefulness, and importance of something — subjective to each stakeholder
Fixed by the provider's price list
Identical for every consumer of a service
Determined solely by the number of features
explain: Value is inherently subjective — perceived benefits, usefulness, and importance as judged by each stakeholder. Fixed-price or feature-count definitions are the traps; the same service legitimately delivers different value to different consumers.

q: During SLA negotiations, the party that defines the service requirements and takes responsibility for the outcomes of consuming the service is the:
options: User
Customer
Sponsor
Supplier
explain: The customer defines requirements and owns consumption outcomes — including in SLA discussions. Users consume day to day, the sponsor authorizes budget, and the supplier is on the provision side, not the consumer side.

q: A board member approves the budget for a new ITSM platform but is not involved in defining its requirements. This board member is acting as the:
options: User
Customer
Sponsor — the role that authorizes the budget for service consumption
Service provider
explain: Authorizing the budget is the sponsor's defining role — distinct from the customer, who defines requirements. The trap merges the two because one person can hold both roles, but the budget-authorization act is sponsorship.

q: When a service fails, the people who raise incidents through the service desk and feel the impact directly are acting in the role of:
options: Sponsors
Customers
Change authorities
Users — the people who use the service
explain: Users are the day-to-day consumers who experience the service directly and report issues. Customers define requirements, sponsors fund consumption — the exam repeatedly tests this three-way split.

q: Moving email to the cloud means the company must hire cloud-integration specialists it never needed before. In the value equation, these new staffing needs are:
options: Costs imposed on the consumer by the service relationship
Costs removed from the consumer
Provider profits
Risks transferred to the provider
explain: Services remove some consumer costs while imposing others — new skill requirements are imposed costs that belong in the value calculation. The trap counts only removed costs, painting an unrealistically rosy value picture.

q: A company adopts managed backup and decommissions its tape library, eliminating hardware maintenance and off-site storage fees. These eliminated expenses are:
options: Costs imposed on the consumer
Costs removed from the consumer — part of the service's value proposition
Risks retained by the consumer
The provider's operating costs
explain: Removing the consumer's need to manage specific costs is central to the service definition — the tape costs disappear because the provider now manages them. The trap confuses whose costs they are: removed from the consumer, absorbed by the provider.

q: Outsourcing email to a cloud provider reduces the company's infrastructure risk, but creates a new dependency: if the provider has an outage, the company cannot communicate. This shows that services:
options: Eliminate all consumer risk
Transfer every risk to the provider
Are risk-free by definition
Can introduce new risks even while reducing others
explain: Service relationships redistribute risk — reducing some while potentially introducing others, like vendor dependency. The absolutist traps claim elimination or total transfer; in reality the risk landscape changes shape rather than vanishing.

q: A provider and customer run a joint disaster-recovery exercise each year, each testing their own responsibilities. This BEST illustrates that in a service relationship:
options: Only the provider has continuity responsibilities
The customer has no role in service continuity
Risk management is entirely outsourced
Managing risk is a shared, cooperative activity between provider and consumer
explain: Service relationships are cooperative — both sides hold continuity responsibilities and exercise them together. The traps assign all responsibility to one side; co-creation applies to risk management as much as to value.

q: Before launch, a team runs load tests proving the ordering service handles twice the expected peak traffic. This testing verifies an aspect of:
options: Warranty — assurance the service meets agreed requirements, including capacity
Utility
Output
Cost
explain: Handling peak load is about capacity — assurance of fit for use, which is warranty. The trap is utility: the features may be perfect, but without performance assurance the service isn't fit for use under real conditions.

q: A healthcare service passes all functional tests but fails its security review because patient data is not encrypted. The service lacks:
options: Utility — the functionality is wrong
Warranty — assurance of meeting agreed requirements, including security
An output
A customer
explain: Security is an aspect of warranty (fit for use) — assurance the service meets agreed requirements. The functionality works, so utility is fine; the trap misdiagnoses a warranty gap as missing functionality.

q: A reporting tool is fast, reliable, and secure, but it cannot produce the regulatory report format the finance team is legally required to file. The missing element is:
options: Warranty — the tool is unavailable
Cost — the tool is overpriced
Utility — the functionality is not fit for the purpose
An outcome
explain: Utility is fit for purpose — the right functionality for the need. The tool's warranty is fine (fast, reliable, secure); it simply doesn't do what the consumer needs. The trap blames warranty because the tool 'fails' the team.

q: A cloud provider maintains spare capacity, trains its engineers, and monitors its platform around the clock. These activities are part of:
options: Service consumption
The customer's responsibilities
Service provision — management of the provider's resources and capabilities to deliver the service
Governance
explain: Provision is the provider's side of the relationship: managing its resources and capabilities so the service can be delivered. The trap is consumption — that is the consumer's side, using what the provider makes available.

q: A company buys a self-service analytics platform, but its reports are useless because departments feed it incomplete, inconsistent data. This shows that service consumption:
options: Requires nothing from the consumer
Includes consumer responsibilities — here, providing quality inputs the service depends on
Is the provider's problem to fix unilaterally
Always fails with self-service tools
explain: Consumption is active, not passive — consumers have responsibilities, including the quality of inputs the service needs. The trap treats the consumer as a bystander; co-creation means the consumer's participation shapes the outcome.

q: A retail company's e-commerce team relies on the internal infrastructure team for hosting, with agreed targets and regular reviews. This arrangement is:
options: Not a real service relationship, because both teams work for the same company
A valid internal service relationship — provision and consumption can occur between teams in one organization
Only a reporting line
Impossible without an external contract
explain: Service relationships exist wherever there is provision and consumption — internal teams count fully, with customers, users, and sponsors among them. The external-only trap is one of the exam's favorite misconceptions.

q: A provider builds a clear status page; users actually check it before calling the desk, cutting duplicate incident reports in half. The improved result came from:
options: The provider acting alone
The users acting alone
Value co-creation — the provider's output combined with the consumers' participation produced the outcome
Eliminating the service desk
explain: Neither side could achieve this alone: the provider supplied the status page (output), users changed their behavior (participation), and the outcome emerged from both. The single-actor traps deny co-creation's essential point.

q: A car-wash membership lets a driver get a clean car every week without buying equipment, maintaining it, or worrying about water regulations. This is service-like because it:
options: Transfers ownership of the car wash to the driver
Is inexpensive
Uses advanced technology
Facilitates the outcome the customer wants without the customer managing the associated costs and risks
explain: That is the ITIL 4 service definition in plain clothes: enabling outcomes while the provider manages specific costs and risks. Ownership transfer would make it a good; price and technology are incidental, not defining.

q: A team rolls a major platform upgrade out to one office first, verifies stability for a week, then proceeds office by office. This cautious movement of components to live environments is a:
options: Phased deployment — deployment management moving components to live environments in stages
Release without deployment
Standard change
Big bang release
explain: Deployment management moves components to live environments; doing it in stages is a phased deployment approach that limits blast radius. The traps confuse deployment with release (making features usable) or with change types.

q: A deployment plan is ready, but the team cannot proceed until the change authority reviews the risk assessment. This shows that deployment management:
options: Authorizes its own changes
Works with change enablement — deployment needs authorization before components move to live environments
Replaces change enablement
Only handles software, not hardware
explain: Practices collaborate: deployment management executes the movement to live, but change enablement authorizes the change first. The trap grants deployment its own authorization power — authorization always sits with the change authority.

q: A team tracks which software versions are installed on each server (for support) and separately tracks license entitlements against purchases (for cost and compliance). The FIRST is service configuration management; the SECOND is:
options: IT asset management — managing the asset lifecycle to maximize value and control costs
Problem management
Incident management
Capacity and performance management
explain: This is the key boundary: configuration management tracks CI information for operational decisions, while IT asset management tracks assets through their lifecycle for value, cost, and compliance. Confusing the two is a favorite exam trap — same data, different purposes.

q: IT asset management reports show a server fleet averaging six years old with rising maintenance costs. Leadership uses this to plan a refresh cycle. This shows IT asset management:
options: Only counts assets once a year
Replaces procurement
Authorizes hardware changes
Supports investment decisions with lifecycle cost and age information
explain: IT asset management plans and manages the full lifecycle — its data informs decisions like refresh timing by revealing true cost of ownership. The traps reduce it to counting or grant it authorization powers it doesn't have.

q: A vendor audit threatens penalties because the company cannot prove how many installations of a licensed product exist. Which practice would have prevented this exposure?
options: IT asset management — reconciling installed software against entitlements to control compliance risk
Incident management
Service validation and testing
Availability management
explain: License compliance is an IT asset management responsibility — knowing what is installed versus what is owned. The traps borrow unrelated purposes; none of those practices track license entitlements.

q: A team decides that network switches, firewall rules, and the CMDB's data model itself will be tracked as configuration items, while individual mouse devices will not. This scoping decision is part of:
options: Change authorization
Configuration identification — deciding what is under the control of configuration management
Incident categorization
Capacity planning
explain: Configuration identification defines which components become CIs and at what granularity. The traps misplace the decision: authorization approves changes, categorization classifies incidents — neither scopes what configuration management controls.

q: A provider keeps CI information across several tools — a discovery tool for servers, a separate database for documentation — linked rather than merged into one system. This is acceptable because:
options: Configuration information can be federated across sources — no single CMDB is mandatory
More tools always means better data
ITIL forbids centralized databases
Audits are not required in ITIL 4
explain: ITIL 4 does not mandate a single CMDB; what matters is that accurate, reliable configuration information is available when and where needed, however it is stored. The single-database assumption is the trap — federation is explicitly acceptable.

q: Every change to a configuration item's status — installed, under maintenance, retired — is recorded with a timestamp. This historical record of CI changes is:
options: The change schedule
The incident log
The service catalogue
Status accounting — tracking the current and historical state of configuration items
explain: Status accounting maintains the record of CI states over time, supporting traceability. The change schedule is the trap: it plans future changes, while status accounting records what actually happened to each CI.

q: The improvement register holds 40 ideas, but the team can fund only a few. Under the continual improvement practice, they should prioritize the ideas that:
options: Are cheapest regardless of impact
Came from senior managers only
Best align with the organization's strategic objectives — improvement serves business direction
Are the most technically interesting
explain: Continual improvement aligns practices and services with changing business needs, so ideas should be weighed against strategic objectives, often with business cases. Cost-only, rank-only, or novelty-based selection are the traps — they disconnect improvement from direction.

q: After each sprint, a development team holds a short retrospective asking 'what should we improve next?' and logs one small action. This habit demonstrates:
options: That improvement requires formal projects
A continual improvement culture — everyone participating in ongoing improvement, not just specialists
That retrospectives replace change enablement
That only developers may suggest improvements
explain: The practice embeds improvement in everyone's work — small, regular, and owned by the team doing the work. The formal-project trap reserves improvement for big initiatives; retrospectives feed improvement but don't replace change control.

q: An organization documents which types of releases it uses, who approves them, and the criteria for going live. This documented approach is the:
options: Change schedule
Incident model
Service level agreement
Release policy — defining the organization's approach to releases
explain: Release management works to a release policy that sets the rules: release types, approval, and readiness criteria. The change schedule is the trap — it lists planned changes, not the policy governing releases.

q: A new release fails in production and the team restores the previous version within minutes using a rehearsed procedure. This recovery was possible because release management includes:
options: Hoping releases never fail
Blaming the deployment team
Skipping testing to save time
Planning for backout — remediation options prepared before the release
explain: Release planning includes rollback/backout planning so a failed release can be reversed quickly. The traps are anti-patterns: no plan, blame, or skipped testing — the opposite of controlled release management.

q: A team tests a new portal's features against requirements AND runs load tests to confirm it stays responsive under peak traffic. Testing both aspects reflects that validation covers:
options: Utility and warranty — that the service does the right things and meets agreed requirements for performance and reliability
Only the user interface
Only the provider's costs
Neither — testing is optional in ITIL 4
explain: Service validation and testing ensures new or changed services meet defined requirements — both utility (fit for purpose) and warranty (fit for use, including performance). Testing only features is the trap; warranty requirements need verification too.

q: A defect in the service design is found during a design review, when fixing it costs a day's work. The same defect found after release would have caused outages. This supports the guidance that testing is most effective when done:
options: Only after release, on live users
As early as possible in the service lifecycle
Only by external auditors
Never — testing delays delivery
explain: Finding issues early is dramatically cheaper than finding them in live operation — validation and testing should start as early as possible. Live-user testing is the trap: it turns incidents into test results.

q: Before a new payroll service goes live, the finance team runs its own month-end scenarios and formally confirms the service is acceptable. These stakeholder-defined checks are:
options: Deployment management
Incident management
Acceptance criteria — the defined requirements the service must meet, verified by service validation and testing
A change collision
explain: Acceptance criteria are the stakeholder-defined requirements that validation and testing verifies before release. Deployment is the trap: moving components live comes after this verification, not during it.

q: A payment service is built so that no single component failure can take it down — traffic automatically shifts to surviving components. This design approach supports:
options: Incident management
Problem management
Change enablement
Availability management — designing services to meet agreed availability levels
explain: Eliminating single points of failure through resilient design is availability management ensuring agreed availability. Incident management is the trap: it responds after failure, while availability management designs so failures don't become outages.

q: An SLA promises 99.5% availability 'excluding scheduled maintenance windows'. Excluding planned downtime from the measurement is:
options: Dishonest reporting that ITIL forbids
Standard practice — agreed availability targets typically apply to agreed service hours, with planned maintenance handled separately
A breach of the guiding principles
Only allowed for cloud services
explain: Availability targets are agreed between provider and customer, and commonly exclude scheduled maintenance — what matters is that the basis is defined and agreed. The dishonesty trap ignores that the exclusion is transparent and part of the agreement.

q: Availability reports show a steady rise in brief network outages over six months. Availability management uses this trend to:
options: Hide the trend from the customer
Blame the network team
Feed continual improvement — identifying an availability risk to address before it becomes a major outage
Declare each outage a separate major incident retroactively
explain: Availability management measures and monitors, then turns findings into improvement — a rising trend is an early warning to act on. Hiding data or blaming teams are the traps; the practice is about ensuring levels, which includes proactive improvement.

q: The business plans to open 30 new stores next year, each needing point-of-sale connectivity. Translating this business plan into future network capacity requirements is:
options: Incident management
Service desk planning
Business capacity management — ensuring future business requirements are considered in capacity planning
Problem management
explain: Capacity and performance management looks ahead: business capacity management converts business plans into capacity needs. The traps are reactive practices — capacity planning happens before the demand arrives, not after it causes incidents.

q: A service meets its targets overall, but one database server runs at 95% CPU every afternoon while others sit idle. The distinction between the service's end-to-end performance and the individual component's load reflects:
options: That only component capacity matters
That only service capacity matters
Service capacity versus component capacity — both are managed, since a strained component threatens the whole service
That capacity management is unnecessary
explain: Capacity and performance management addresses service capacity (end-to-end) and component capacity (individual CIs) — a bottlenecked component is a service risk even when overall numbers look fine. The single-level traps miss that both views are needed.

q: An incident ticket for a recurring email outage is linked to an open problem record investigating the mail server crashes. Linking the records helps because:
options: Incident management can apply the problem's workaround and track recurrence, while problem management sees the incident pattern
It closes the incident automatically
It replaces the need for a workaround
It authorizes the permanent fix
explain: Linked records let practices collaborate: incidents get faster handling via known workarounds, and problems gain recurrence data. The traps overstate the link — it doesn't auto-close, replace workarounds, or authorize fixes; authorization stays with change enablement.

q: An incident initially affecting one user is found to be affecting an entire department facing a payroll deadline. The service desk should:
options: Keep the original priority — priorities never change
Reassess impact and urgency and raise the priority accordingly
Close the ticket and open a new one
Wait for the user to complain again
explain: Priority is impact plus urgency, and both can change as an incident unfolds — prioritization is reassessed, not frozen. The never-change trap treats priority as a label; the close-and-reopen trap destroys the incident's history.

q: A user reports the known 'VPN drops every hour' issue. The analyst finds the matching known-error article, applies the documented workaround, and restores the user's connection in minutes — without diagnosing the cause. This is:
options: Poor practice — every incident needs root-cause diagnosis
Problem management
A change
Correct incident management — restore service quickly using available knowledge; diagnosis belongs to problem management
explain: Incident management's purpose is fast restoration, not diagnosis — using known-error knowledge is exactly how it should work. The diagnose-everything trap confuses incident management with problem management, which owns the underlying cause.

q: The SLA states priority-1 incidents must be resolved within 4 hours. These time limits for incident handling come from:
options: The incident manager's personal preference
Agreed service level targets — incident handling timescales are set against SLA commitments
The change schedule
Random assignment by the service desk tool
explain: Handling timescales derive from agreed service level targets — that is what makes them commitments rather than aspirations. The traps invent arbitrary sources; SLM negotiates the targets that incident management then works to.

q: Investigating repeated database slowdowns, an analyst repeatedly asks 'why?' — why did the query slow, why did the index fragment, why did maintenance not run — until reaching the missed maintenance job. This technique is:
options: The '5 whys' — a problem analysis technique for drilling to the root cause
Hierarchical escalation
Event correlation
A post-implementation review
explain: The 5 whys is a classic problem management analysis technique: repeated 'why' questions peel back symptoms to the root cause. Escalation, correlation, and reviews are the traps — different activities from different practices.

q: Each quarter, a team reviews its open known errors, reassesses their business impact, and decides which permanent fixes to fund next. This review activity is part of:
options: Incident management
Error control — managing known errors, including assessing and prioritizing their resolution
Change authorization
Service validation and testing
explain: Error control manages known errors through to resolution, including prioritizing which get permanent fixes. Incident management is the trap: it restores service, while error control governs the known error's journey to a real fix.

q: A permanent fix for a known error is deployed, and monitoring confirms the recurring incidents have stopped. The problem manager should now:
options: Leave the known error open indefinitely
Delete the problem record
Close the known error record — the permanent resolution is implemented and verified
Open a new incident
explain: A known error stays open until the permanent resolution is implemented — and verified. Closing on deployment alone is the trap; verification that the fix actually worked is what completes error control.

q: The known-error database documents a workaround for a printing fault. When the fault recurs, service desk analysts restore users in minutes instead of hours. This shows that problem management supports incident management by:
options: Taking over incident resolution
Authorizing incident escalations
Replacing the service desk
Providing documented workarounds that speed up restoration
explain: Problem management's workarounds and known errors directly accelerate incident restoration — practices collaborating across the value chain. The takeover traps misunderstand the relationship: problem management enables faster restoration, it doesn't absorb incident management.

q: Server patching follows the same documented steps every month: snapshot, patch, verify, with pre-authorization in place. This repeatable sequence is a:
options: Change model — a pre-defined approach for handling a specific type of change
Problem record
Service request
Major incident procedure
explain: Change models define the repeatable steps for handling particular change types efficiently — this is the change equivalent of an incident model. The traps misclassify it as a record, a request, or an incident procedure.

q: A planned firewall upgrade fails halfway, and the team restores the previous configuration using the documented backout procedure. The fact that a backout plan existed shows change enablement requires:
options: Changes to never fail
Blame to be assigned after failures
Remediation planning — preparing how to recover if the change goes wrong
Incidents to be hidden from users
explain: Assessing risk includes planning remediation: authorized changes carry backout plans so failure is recoverable. The never-fail trap denies reality — the practice maximizes successful changes, and planning for failure is part of that.

q: A low-risk, well-understood database index rebuild is authorized by the change manager alone, without convening the full CAB. This is appropriate because:
options: The CAB has been abolished
Low-risk changes need no assessment
The change authority is scaled to the change type and risk — it can be an individual, not always the full CAB
Change managers can override all governance
explain: The change authority varies: person, change manager, CAB, or emergency CAB, matched to the change's risk. The traps either abolish authorization or inflate the change manager's power — authority is proportionate, not absent or absolute.

q: The change schedule shows two teams planning changes to the same payment system in the same window. The change manager asks one team to reschedule. This use of the schedule prevents:
options: All incidents
Problem investigations
Service reviews
Change collisions — conflicting changes that could interfere with each other
explain: The change schedule exists partly to spot and avoid collisions between planned changes. The traps credit it with preventing all incidents or replacing other practices — its job is coordinating changes, not eliminating every risk.

q: A global company staffs service desks in three time zones so users always reach an analyst during their business hours, with tickets handed over between shifts. This is an example of a:
options: Follow-the-sun virtual service desk — distributed locations acting as one logical desk
Local service desk
Centralized service desk in one building
CAB meeting schedule
explain: A virtual service desk unites distributed locations — including follow-the-sun coverage — into a single point of contact. The local/centralized traps describe single-location models; the CAB trap confuses a practice with a meeting.

q: A service desk analyst notices users repeatedly struggling with a confusing approval step and submits an improvement idea to simplify it. This shows the service desk:
options: Should only log tickets
Acts as an entry point feeding other practices — here, continual improvement
Must authorize the change itself
Should hide user feedback from other teams
explain: The desk's frontline position makes it a valuable entry point for improvement ideas, change requests, and other practice inputs — not just a ticket logger. The authorize-itself trap grants powers the desk doesn't have; ideas still flow through proper channels.

q: A service desk proudly reports falling call volumes, but customer satisfaction scores are dropping because complex issues take too long to resolve. The lesson is that desk performance should be judged by:
options: Call volume alone
The number of analysts employed
Outcomes like customer satisfaction and resolution quality — not just activity counts
How quickly tickets are closed regardless of quality
explain: Activity metrics without outcome measures mislead — satisfaction and real resolution are what matter to value. The traps optimize countable activity; 'focus on value' demands measuring what stakeholders actually experience.

q: A company launches a self-service portal that resolves most password and access requests automatically. The service desk's role after this is to:
options: Close down, since self-service replaces it
Handle only complaints
Stop capturing demand
Remain the single point of contact — handling complex issues, exceptions, and anything self-service cannot resolve
explain: Self-service shifts routine work but doesn't remove the need for a single point of contact — complex, sensitive, and exceptional needs still require the desk. The close-down trap mistakes channel shift for practice elimination.

q: A new customer portal is being designed, and service level management is involved from the start to define availability and response targets. This early involvement matters because:
options: SLA targets should be designed in — agreed during design and transition, not bolted on after launch
The CAB cannot function without SLM
Targets can only be measured after five years
Users set targets unilaterally
explain: Service level requirements should be defined as the service is designed so it can actually meet them — retrofitting targets onto a live service invites failure. The traps invent CAB dependencies, absurd timelines, or unilateral target-setting.

q: A provider proposes new SLA targets to a customer, who pushes back: the targets don't reflect month-end processing peaks. The correct next step is to:
options: Impose the targets anyway
Abandon SLAs entirely
Negotiate and agree targets that reflect the customer's business needs
Ask the CAB to set the targets
explain: SLA targets are negotiated and agreed with the customer — imposition produces the 'watermelon SLA' that looks green while the business suffers. The CAB trap misplaces target-setting; the CAB authorizes changes, it doesn't negotiate service levels.

q: Alongside system metrics, a provider surveys users quarterly about whether the service actually helps them do their jobs. This user-experience input helps service level management:
options: Replace all technical metrics
Avoid ever breaching SLAs
Ensure targets and reports reflect business outcomes and user experience, not just easily measured system data
Eliminate the need for service reviews
explain: Service level management must ensure measurement reflects what matters to the business — user experience complements system metrics. The replace-everything trap swings too far; the practice needs both technical and experiential views.

q: The owner of a new payment service works with the monitoring team to define which events matter — failed transactions, latency thresholds — before go-live. Defining monitoring needs with stakeholders is part of:
options: Incident management
Problem management
Change enablement
Monitoring and event management — establishing what to monitor based on stakeholder needs
explain: Monitoring and event management starts by agreeing with stakeholders what should be observed — you can't manage events you never defined. The traps assign the definition to reactive practices; monitoring requirements come first, responses follow.

q: A market shift toward remote work creates demand for secure home-office connectivity. In ITIL 4, this unmet market need entering the service value system is an example of:
options: Opportunity — a possibility to add value for stakeholders, and an input to the service value system
Value
Governance
A practice
explain: Opportunity and demand are the two inputs to the SVS; an unmet market need is an opportunity to create value. Value is the trap — it is the system's output, not its input; governance and practices are internal components.

q: Existing customers repeatedly ask for a mobile app to complement the web portal. In SVS terms, these requests represent:
options: Value
Demand — the need for services, and an input to the service value system
An external factor
A guiding principle
explain: Demand — needs and wants for services — is an SVS input alongside opportunity. Value is the trap: it is what the system produces from demand, not the demand itself.

q: A new onboarding service creates value for new hires (faster productivity), HR (less admin), and IT (fewer manual setups). This illustrates that the service value system creates value for:
options: Only the paying customer
Only the provider's shareholders
The organization, its customers, and other stakeholders — value is multi-directional
Only external parties
explain: The SVS transforms opportunity and demand into value for the organization, its customers, and stakeholders broadly — providers benefit too. The single-beneficiary traps ignore that value flows to everyone in the service relationship.

q: A recession changes customer spending patterns, forcing a provider to adjust its service portfolio. In ITIL 4, the economic climate is:
options: A value chain activity
A guiding principle
A service request
An external factor influencing the service value system
explain: The SVS operates within political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental factors that shape it. The value-chain trap misplaces it: the chain is internal, while economic conditions sit outside, influencing the system.

q: Which of the following is a component of the ITIL service value system?
options: Practices — the sets of organizational resources for performing work, and one of the five SVS components
Incidents
Service requests
Changes
explain: The five SVS components are guiding principles, governance, service value chain, practices, and continual improvement. Incidents, requests, and changes are the traps — operational items handled within practices, not components of the system.

q: When redesigning its change process, a team checks each design decision against 'keep it simple and practical' and 'focus on value'. This shows the guiding principles:
options: Apply only to senior leaders
Guide every part of the service value system — all components and activities
Replace the need for practices
Are optional recommendations
explain: Guiding principles are recommendations that guide an organization in all circumstances, across the whole SVS. The optional trap understates them; the replacement trap overstates them — they guide how components work, they don't replace them.

q: A company replaces its blame culture with blameless post-incident reviews, and incident learning improves sharply. The changed element belongs to the dimension:
options: Information and technology
Partners and suppliers
Organizations and people — culture, roles, skills, and structure
Value streams and processes
explain: Culture is squarely in the organizations and people dimension — and it enabled better learning without any technology change. The technology trap assumes improvement needs tools; here the people dimension was the lever.

q: A provider treats its knowledge base articles, service reports, and monitoring data as managed assets with owners and lifecycles. This treatment of information belongs to the:
options: Organizations and people dimension
Partners and suppliers dimension
Governance component
Information and technology dimension — information, knowledge, and technology
explain: Information and knowledge are assets of the information and technology dimension, managed alongside the technology itself. The people trap classifies them by who uses them; the dimension classifies what they are.

q: A provider uses three suppliers for one service and appoints an integration function to coordinate them so the customer sees a single seamless service. This coordination of multiple suppliers sits in the:
options: Partners and suppliers dimension — managing relationships with external parties involved in service delivery
Information and technology dimension
Value streams and processes dimension
Continual improvement model
explain: Relationships with external suppliers — including integrating multiple suppliers — are the partners and suppliers dimension. The value-stream trap is plausible since coordination is workflow, but the dimension classifies the relationship aspect.

q: Two teams handle the same request type differently, causing inconsistent service. Management defines one standard end-to-end workflow for it. This standardization addresses the:
options: Technology stack
Value streams and processes dimension — how work flows across the organization to create value
Supplier contract
Governance component
explain: The dimension concerns the integrated workflows by which work gets done — standardizing the flow fixes the inconsistency. Technology and contracts are the traps: they support the flow but aren't the flow itself.

q: Before designing a new service, the provider runs workshops with the customer to understand the outcomes they want and their constraints. This stakeholder interaction is the value chain activity:
options: Plan
Obtain/build
Engage — understanding stakeholder needs and building relationships
Deliver and support
explain: Engage provides a good understanding of stakeholder needs and ensures transparency and relationship-building. Plan is the trap: it creates shared understanding of vision and direction, while this scenario is about learning stakeholder needs.

q: Leadership's vision calls for 30% faster incident resolution; the service management team creates the policies, targets, and improvement roadmap to get there. Creating this direction and plan is the value chain activity:
options: Engage
Improve
Obtain/build
Plan — ensuring a shared understanding of the vision, current status, and improvement direction
explain: Plan turns vision into shared direction: policies, targets, and roadmaps. Improve is the trap: it executes improvement across activities, while this scenario is the planning that precedes and guides it.

q: A post-release review finds that rushed testing caused the last two failed releases, and the finding changes how all future releases are tested. This learning applied across the value chain is the activity:
options: Improve — ensuring continual improvement of products, services, and practices across all value chain activities
Engage
Obtain/build
Deliver and support
explain: Improve is its own value chain activity, operating across the entire chain — lessons from one activity improving others. The traps name single activities; the scenario's cross-cutting learning is improve's signature.

q: Before a new service goes live, the team verifies that support staff are trained, monitoring is in place, and operational procedures exist. Confirming the service can actually be operated and supported is part of:
options: Obtain/build
Design and transition — ensuring products and services meet expectations, including readiness for operation
Engage
Plan
