explain: Design and transition ensures services meet expectations for quality, cost, and time to market — including operational readiness, not just technical design. Obtain/build is the trap: it provides the components, while this scenario validates readiness to operate them.

q: A team needs monitoring capability and evaluates building it in-house versus buying a commercial tool, choosing the option that best meets its needs. This build-versus-buy decision is part of:
options: Plan
Deliver and support
Obtain/build — ensuring service components are available when and where needed
Improve
explain: Obtain/build covers acquiring service components — whether purchased or built in-house — so they're available when needed. Deliver and support is the trap: it uses the components, while obtaining them is this activity's job.

q: After go-live, the provider delivers the service to agreed targets, handles user queries, and manages ongoing support. These ongoing delivery and support activities are:
options: Design and transition
Obtain/build
Plan
Deliver and support — ensuring services are delivered and supported according to agreed specifications
explain: Deliver and support covers ongoing service delivery and user support in live operation. Design and transition is the trap: it prepares services for operation, while this scenario is the operation itself.

q: An improvement team resists the urge to jump to solutions and instead documents current resolution times, backlog age, and user complaints. This honest baseline is the continual improvement model step:
options: Where are we now? — assessing the current state before defining targets
What is the vision?
Take action
How do we keep the momentum going?
explain: 'Where are we now?' grounds improvement in reality — without an honest baseline, targets are guesses and progress can't be proven. The vision trap starts with the future; the model insists on understanding the present first.

q: An improvement plan is approved, and the team starts executing it — communicating progress to stakeholders and adjusting the plan as early results come in. This execution phase is the step:
options: What is the vision?
Take action — executing the improvement plan, typically with communication and course correction
Did we get there?
Where are we now?
explain: 'Take action' is doing the improvement work — with stakeholder communication and adjustments along the way. 'Did we get there?' is the trap: assessment comes after action, not during it.

q: Midway through an improvement, new data shows the original current-state assessment missed a major bottleneck. The team revisits 'Where are we now?' before continuing. This is valid because the continual improvement model:
options: Must be followed rigidly in one pass
Is flexible — steps can be revisited as understanding improves
Skips steps that prove difficult
Only applies to large initiatives
explain: The model is not a rigid waterfall — its steps can be revisited when new information emerges. The rigidity trap treats it as one-pass; in practice, improvement is iterative and the model flexes with it.

q: A company's board sets risk policy and delegates its implementation to executives, but the board remains accountable for governance overall. This shows that:
options: Governance can be fully delegated away
Only executives perform governance
Governance is the same as management
The governing body is accountable for governance — evaluate, direct, monitor — even when execution is delegated
explain: Governance means the organization is directed and controlled; the governing body retains accountability for it even while delegating execution to management. The delegation trap confuses handing off work with handing off accountability.

q: A provider delivers a new reporting dashboard on time and under budget, but no customer uses it because it does not answer their business questions. Applying 'focus on value', the lesson is:
options: Value is determined by the cost of delivery — a cheap, on-time delivery is always valuable
Value is created the moment outputs are delivered, regardless of use
Value is determined by the consumer — outputs only create value when they enable the consumer's outcomes
Adding more features would have made the dashboard valuable
explain: Focus on value means the consumer defines value; on-time, under-budget outputs are worthless if nobody uses them to achieve outcomes. The cost trap confuses efficient delivery with value, and the features trap assumes more output equals more value.

q: A company acquires a smaller firm whose service desk resolves incidents quickly using simple spreadsheets. The CIO wants to replace it immediately with the corporate ITSM suite for consistency. Following 'start where you are', the team should FIRST:
options: Assess the current desk's performance and reuse what works, replacing only what is genuinely deficient
Replace it immediately — consistency across the company matters more than current performance
Discard the spreadsheets as non-compliant shadow IT
Freeze all changes until a perfect target-state design is approved
explain: Start where you are means investigating the existing state and reusing what works rather than defaulting to replacement. The consistency trap sacrifices a working service for uniformity, and the freeze trap confuses careful assessment with doing nothing.

q: A team building a self-service portal releases a working prototype to 20 users after three weeks, gathers feedback, and adjusts before expanding. A manager criticizes the prototype as 'unfinished'. The team can BEST defend its approach because:
options: Prototypes should be polished before anyone sees them
Feedback should be collected only after the full rollout
Iteration slows delivery, so big-bang releases are always faster
Progress iteratively with feedback means early, imperfect releases — feedback on small iterations is cheaper and more useful than one big-bang launch
explain: The principle favors small iterations with feedback over waiting for perfection; an 'unfinished' prototype that generates learning is exactly the point. The polish trap turns iteration into mini-waterfalls, and the big-bang trap ignores how expensive late-discovered mistakes are.

q: During major incidents, the network team and the security team each run their own bridge calls, make conflicting changes, and blame each other afterwards. To apply 'collaborate and promote visibility', the BEST fix is to:
options: Automate failover so the teams never need to coordinate
Create a single shared incident workspace with visible status, so both teams coordinate around one picture of the incident
Simplify the change process so fewer incidents occur
Assign each incident to whichever team gets blamed least
explain: Collaborate and promote visibility means working together with transparent information — one shared view ends the conflicting-actions problem. Automation is the wrong-principle trap (optimize and automate doesn't fix a coordination failure), and blame assignment is the opposite of collaboration.

q: To cut costs, a provider moves its service desk to email-only support. Ticket volumes look steady, but customer satisfaction and renewal rates fall because complex issues cannot be resolved well by email. This is a failure to:
options: Keep it simple and practical — email is the simplest channel
Think and work holistically — the change was judged on one metric without considering its effects on the whole service experience and outcomes
Optimize and automate — the provider should have automated email responses
Start where you are — the provider should have kept the old phone system forever
explain: Think and work holistically requires considering how a change affects the whole system — channel, satisfaction, renewals — not one part in isolation. The simplicity trap mistakes 'simple' for 'good regardless of consequences', and the automation trap treats a system problem as a tooling problem.

q: A new service design includes a 14-step approval for standard, low-risk requests, added 'just in case something goes wrong'. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Keep all 14 steps — more control is always safer
Automate all 14 steps so they run faster
Add the steps gradually over several iterations
Remove steps that add no demonstrable value — every control must be justified by the benefit it provides
explain: Keep it simple and practical means eliminating steps that contribute nothing; 'just in case' controls are complexity without value. The safety trap equates more approvals with less risk, and the automation trap speeds up waste instead of removing it.

q: A team automates its incident routing, but the routing rules were never reviewed — so 30% of tickets are now misrouted faster than before. The lesson from 'optimize and automate' is:
options: Optimize the process first — fix the routing rules — then automate; automating a broken process amplifies the problem
Automation is always beneficial, so the misrouting is acceptable
Remove the automation and go back to manual routing permanently
The problem is poor visibility, so build a dashboard instead
explain: Optimize and automate explicitly orders the work: understand and improve the process before automating it. The automation-first trap assumes technology fixes bad process, and the dashboard trap answers the wrong principle (visibility doesn't fix wrong rules).

q: A provider's monthly report highlights 99.9% server uptime, but the customer's complaint is that month-end invoices still cannot be generated on time. Applying 'focus on value', the provider should:
options: Explain that uptime is the only value that matters
Convince the customer to value uptime more highly
Report on outcomes the customer values — such as invoices generated on time — not just internal technical metrics
Add fifty more technical metrics to the report
explain: Focus on value means measuring and communicating what the consumer values — business outcomes, not provider-centric metrics. The uptime trap mistakes a means (availability) for the end (invoices on time), and the more-metrics trap confuses volume of data with relevance.

q: A team adopts a vendor's 'industry best practice' change model verbatim, ignoring that their organization has no CAB and a strong culture of developer autonomy. The rollout fails. Which guiding principle was neglected?
options: Start where you are — the team should have assessed its current reality and adapted the model to it
Keep it simple and practical — the model had too many steps
Optimize and automate — the team should have automated the model first
Think and work holistically — the team should have considered the whole IT industry
explain: Start where you are requires assessing existing capabilities, culture, and constraints before importing an external model. The simplicity trap misdiagnoses a fit problem as a complexity problem, and the holistic trap stretches the principle beyond the organization's own system.

q: A team must migrate 5,000 mailboxes to a new platform. They propose moving one department first, validating, then continuing in waves. A stakeholder demands an all-at-once migration to 'get it over with'. The team should argue that:
options: Big-bang migrations are always faster in practice
The wave approach is better — small iterations limit the blast radius, and each wave's feedback improves the next
Feedback only matters after the final migration
Iterations waste effort, so one wave is enough
explain: Progress iteratively with feedback limits risk per iteration and uses each wave's learning to improve the next. The big-bang trap trades apparent speed for concentrated risk, and the feedback-last trap turns learning into an autopsy.

q: A change manager approves changes through private emails. Teams discover conflicting changes only when services break. The core failure here is a lack of:
options: Automation — approvals should be auto-approved
Simplification — the approval process has too many steps
Speed — approvals should take minutes, not days
Visibility — changes must be visible to all affected parties so they can coordinate and spot conflicts
explain: Collaborate and promote visibility requires that work and its status are transparent to the right people; hidden approvals make conflicts inevitable. The automation and speed traps treat a transparency problem as an efficiency problem.

q: A team shortens backup windows to improve backup success rates, but the new schedule overlaps with the nightly billing run and corrupts reports. This shows the team failed to:
options: Keep it simple and practical — shorter windows are simpler
Optimize and automate — backups should be fully automated
Think and work holistically — the backup schedule is part of a larger system, and changes must consider all affected activities
Progress iteratively — the change should have been smaller
explain: Think and work holistically means no activity exists in isolation; the billing run was part of the same system as the backup window. The simplicity trap judges the change on its own terms, and the iteration trap mistakes a scope-of-thinking failure for a size-of-change failure.

q: A service catalogue entry for 'new laptop' offers 40 configuration options. Users take 25 minutes to complete it and often choose wrong options. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Add a 10-question wizard to guide users through the 40 options
Simplify the offering — provide a few standard bundles covering most needs, since complexity users cannot navigate adds no value
Automate option selection with AI
Train all 2,000 users on the 40 options
explain: Keep it simple and practical favors the minimum viable complexity — standard bundles serve most needs without the confusion tax. The wizard trap adds complexity to manage complexity, and the training trap makes users compensate for bad design.

q: A team manually reviews every access request, including routine low-risk ones, creating a two-week backlog. They want to automate the reviews. Following 'optimize and automate', they should FIRST:
options: Streamline the process — define which requests are low-risk and auto-approvable — then automate; do not automate the backlog as-is
Automate everything immediately, including high-risk reviews
Hire more reviewers to clear the backlog, then automate
Remove all reviews so there is nothing to automate
explain: Optimize before automating: simplify and standardize the decision rules, then let technology execute them. Automating the unstreamlined process just produces a faster backlog, and removing all reviews confuses optimization with abdication.

q: A provider offers free 24/7 phone support on a low-margin service. Support costs erode the provider's margin while customers rarely call. Applying 'focus on value', the provider should recognize that:
options: Customers always deserve 24/7 phone support regardless of cost
The provider must absorb any cost to keep customers happy
Value must balance across stakeholders — the provider's own sustainability counts alongside customer outcomes
All support should be removed immediately
explain: Focus on value considers every stakeholder, including the service provider — value that bankrupts the provider is not sustainable. The absorb-any-cost trap treats the provider as having no stake, and the remove-everything trap swings from one imbalance to another.

q: An organization replacing its ITSM tool first inventories existing integrations and custom reports that teams rely on, so nothing critical is lost in migration. This reflects:
options: Progress iteratively with feedback — the migration is split into phases
Collaborate and promote visibility — the inventory is shared
Think and work holistically — the whole organization is considered
Start where you are — the migration builds on an honest assessment of the current reality instead of assuming a blank slate
explain: Start where you are means inventorying what exists — integrations, reports, dependencies — before designing the future state. The iteration trap confuses assessment with phasing, and the holistic trap is too broad: the point here is grounding the work in the current state.

q: A team sets a two-week timebox to deliver the first usable version of a new request form, planning to improve it in later timeboxes. A stakeholder wants to wait three months for the 'complete' version. The team should explain that:
options: Timeboxed iterations deliver value sooner and incorporate feedback — waiting for completeness delays both value and learning
Completeness must always come before any release
Timeboxes reduce quality, so the stakeholder is right
Feedback can wait until the complete version exists
explain: Progress iteratively with feedback uses timeboxes to deliver early value and learn fast; the 'complete' version is a guess until users touch something real. The completeness trap confuses speculation with quality, and the feedback-last trap postpones learning until it is expensive.

q: A provider and customer disagree about whether SLA targets were met, because each measures with different tools and definitions. To apply 'collaborate and promote visibility', they should:
options: Declare the provider's tools authoritative and end the discussion
Agree on shared, visible measurement definitions and data, so both parties see the same picture
Add more metrics until the disagreement disappears
Automate reporting from both toolsets separately
explain: Collaboration requires a shared, visible basis for discussion — agreed definitions and transparent data. The authority trap replaces collaboration with dictation, and the more-metrics trap adds noise instead of shared understanding.

q: A new SLA target rewards the service desk for fast call handling. Analysts start rushing callers off the phone, and first-time fix rates collapse. Which guiding principle was neglected?
options: Keep it simple and practical — the target was too complex
Optimize and automate — calls should have been automated instead
Start where you are — the baseline was never measured
Think and work holistically — the target optimized one part of the system and damaged the overall outcome
explain: Think and work holistically would have considered how the speed target affects fix quality and the end-to-end service. The simplicity trap misreads a systems-thinking failure as a target-design failure, and the automation trap answers a different principle entirely.

q: A service design review proposes adding real-time translation to an internal tool used by a single monolingual team, 'for completeness'. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Add it — completeness is always worth the effort
Automate the translation so it costs nothing to include
Reject the addition — every feature must be justified by real stakeholder need, not hypothetical completeness
Defer it to a later iteration and add it then
explain: Keep it simple and practical means doing only what is needed — unneeded features are waste, even if cheap to build. The completeness trap confuses 'could' with 'should', and the deferral trap keeps waste on the roadmap instead of removing it.

q: A provider's 'remote worker package' includes a laptop, access to the VPN, and setup assistance from a technician. This illustrates that a service offering can combine:
options: Only intangible actions — goods are never part of a service
Goods, access to resources, and service actions
Goods and warranties, but never direct human actions
Service actions only — anything physical is a product, not a service
explain: A service offering can include goods (the laptop), access to resources (the VPN), and service actions (setup assistance). The distractors reflect the misconception that services must be purely intangible — ITIL 4 explicitly includes goods and resource access in service offerings.

q: A backup service completes backups reliably every night, but it cannot restore individual files — which is what users actually need when they delete a document. In ITIL terms, the service:
options: Lacks both utility and warranty
Has utility but lacks warranty
Is fit for purpose and fit for use
Has warranty but lacks utility — it is fit for use but not fit for purpose
explain: Reliable nightly completion is warranty (fit for use); the inability to restore individual files means it doesn't do what users need — a utility (fit for purpose) gap. The traps invert the two or conflate them into one idea.

q: A department head approves the budget for a new analytics service but is not involved in defining its requirements and does not use it daily. This department head is acting as the:
options: User
Customer
Sponsor
Service provider
explain: The sponsor authorizes the budget for service consumption. The customer defines requirements and owns the outcomes; the user consumes the service day-to-day — neither matches someone who only funds it.

q: Moving to a new ITSM tool requires the customer to retrain 200 staff and rewrite several integrations. In ITIL value analysis, these retraining and integration efforts are:
options: Costs of service consumption borne by the consumer — they must be weighed against the service's benefits
The provider's costs, irrelevant to the customer
Risks, not costs
Outputs of the service
explain: Service consumption imposes costs on the consumer (time, effort, retraining) that count against the service's value. The provider-cost trap ignores the consumer's side of the equation, and the risk trap mislabels certain effort as uncertainty.

q: A company outsources email: it no longer manages spam-filtering infrastructure, but it now depends on the provider's availability — if the provider has an outage, the company cannot communicate. This shows that services:
options: Remove all risk from the consumer
Transfer every risk entirely to the provider
Have no effect on the consumer's risk position
Can remove some risks while introducing new ones — both belong in the value equation
explain: Services shift the risk profile rather than eliminating risk: old risks (spam infrastructure) disappear while new ones (provider dependency) appear. The eliminate-all-risk trap ignores new dependencies, and the full-transfer trap forgets the consumer still suffers when the provider fails.

q: A training course is delivered to 50 staff, but incident resolution times do not improve because staff never apply the techniques. This shows that:
options: Delivering outputs does not guarantee outcomes — outcomes also depend on the consumer's actions
Outputs and outcomes are the same thing
The provider failed to deliver the service
Training can never create value
explain: The course delivery was the output; improved resolution times would be the outcome — which requires the consumer to act. The identity trap collapses outputs into outcomes, and the provider-failure trap blames the wrong party for the consumer's inaction.

q: A provider supplies a collaboration platform; the customer configures it brilliantly and transforms its teams' productivity. This BEST illustrates that:
options: Value was created solely by the provider
Value is co-created — the provider enables it, and the customer realizes it through use
Value was created solely by the customer
The platform has intrinsic value regardless of how it is used
explain: Value co-creation means provider and consumer cooperate: the platform alone created nothing until the customer applied it. The sole-creator traps ignore one side of the relationship, and the intrinsic-value trap forgets that unused capability is not value.

q: A company both provides payroll services to its subsidiaries and consumes network services from an external vendor. This shows that:
options: Provider and consumer roles are fixed permanently
A provider organization can never consume services
An organization can be provider in one service relationship and consumer in another — they are roles, not identities
Service relationships only flow in one direction
explain: Provider and consumer are roles within a specific service relationship; the same organization plays different roles in different relationships. The fixed-role trap treats the labels as permanent identities.

q: A hospital's IT department uses a cloud provider's infrastructure while also running its own service desk for clinicians. In the cloud relationship, the hospital IT department is the:
options: Service consumer — it consumes the cloud provider's service
Service provider — because it runs a service desk
Sponsor — because it pays the cloud bill
User — the only role that matters here
explain: In the cloud service relationship, the IT department consumes the infrastructure service, making it the consumer. The service-desk trap imports a role from a different relationship, and the sponsor trap confuses paying with the consumer role.

q: A provider maintains a secondary data centre and tests failover twice a year, so services survive a site loss. This investment supports:
options: Utility — it adds new functionality
Warranty — specifically continuity, giving confidence the service will remain available when needed
Outputs — the failover tests are the product
The service offering's goods
explain: Continuity is an aspect of warranty (fit for use): assurance the service keeps working under adverse conditions. The utility trap mistakes resilience for functionality, and the outputs trap confuses the supporting activity with what the customer buys.

q: A university's finance office defines the requirements for a new expense system and takes responsibility for the outcomes of using it; 2,000 staff submit expenses through it; the CFO approved the budget. The finance office is the:
options: User
Sponsor
Provider
Customer
explain: The customer defines the requirements and takes responsibility for the outcomes of service consumption. The staff are the users, the CFO is the sponsor — the finance office holds the customer role by defining needs and owning results.

q: A provider grants a customer use of its high-performance computing cluster for weekend batch jobs, without transferring any ownership of the hardware. This is an example of:
options: Goods — the customer receives hardware
Service actions — the provider operates the cluster
Access to resources — a component of a service offering where use is granted without ownership transfer
A service relationship — which is the same as a service offering
explain: Access to resources grants use without ownership — the defining trait here. The goods trap requires ownership transfer, and the relationship trap confuses the offering's components with the relationship itself.

q: A provider delivers a flawless data-migration service, but the customer misses its product launch because it never prepared its staff for the new system. This shows that:
options: The provider failed to deliver value
Outcomes result from both provider outputs and consumer actions — value is co-created, and the consumer's inaction broke the chain
Outputs and outcomes are identical
The customer bears sole responsibility for everything
explain: The provider's outputs were fine; the outcome failed because value co-creation needs the consumer's part too. The provider-failure trap blames flawless delivery, and the sole-responsibility trap swings too far the other way.

q: An online store's checkout works perfectly in testing, but the site goes down every Friday evening during peak sales. The missing element is:
options: Warranty — specifically availability when the service is needed
Utility — the checkout lacks functionality
Service actions — nobody is operating the site
Goods — the store needs more servers as products
explain: The functionality (utility) is fine; the gap is availability at the moment of need — a warranty aspect. The utility trap misdiagnoses an availability failure as missing features.

q: A service includes a contractual commitment that the provider will resolve priority-1 incidents within two hours, giving the customer confidence during outages. This assurance relates to:
options: Utility — it describes what the service does
Goods — it is written into a contract
Outputs — the two-hour target is the product
Warranty — the assurance that service requirements will be met
explain: Warranty is the assurance that a service will meet agreed requirements — fit for use. The utility trap confuses assurance with functionality, and the outputs trap mistakes the promise for the deliverable.

q: A catering company provides daily office lunches — the client gets fed without hiring cooks or managing food-safety compliance. This arrangement is service-like because:
options: Food is a good, and goods are services
It involves a written contract
The client obtains desired outcomes without owning specific costs and risks
The client owns the kitchen equipment
explain: This is the ITIL definition of a service: enabling outcomes without the consumer owning the costs and risks. The contract trap mistakes paperwork for the essence, and the ownership trap describes the opposite of a service.

q: A retail chain defines the requirements for a new point-of-sale service, funds the project, and its cashiers use the system daily. The chain simultaneously acts as:
options: Customer, sponsor, and user — these are roles, not job titles, and one party can hold several at once
Provider — because it funds the project
Only the customer — roles cannot overlap
Only the sponsor — funding is the only role that counts
explain: Customer, sponsor, and user are roles in a service relationship; one organization can hold all three simultaneously. The no-overlap trap treats roles as exclusive, and the funding trap promotes the sponsor role above the others.

q: A customer compares two monitoring services: one cheaper but requiring heavy staff effort, one pricier but fully managed. ITIL advises the customer to consider:
options: Price alone — the cheapest option is always best value
The total value — benefits weighed against the full costs and risks of each option, not price alone
Features alone — the longest feature list wins
The provider's reputation alone
explain: Value means benefits measured against total costs and risks — staff effort is a real cost of the 'cheaper' option. The price trap ignores consumption costs, and the features trap ignores whether features translate into outcomes.

q: A provider delivers a service; the consumer integrates it into its own operations to achieve its business objectives. The consumer's achievement of those objectives is the:
options: Output — the provider's deliverable
Utility — the service's functionality
Service action — the work performed
Outcome — the result the consumer wants, enabled by the provider's outputs
explain: Outcomes are what the consumer achieves using the provider's outputs — value lives in outcomes. The output trap stops at the provider's deliverable, and the utility trap confuses functionality with results.

q: Which statement about value is CORRECT?
options: Value is delivered solely by the provider to a passive consumer
Value equals the price paid for the service
Value is co-created through the service relationship and perceived by the consumer — it is not fixed or identical for everyone
Value is objective and the same for all stakeholders
explain: Value is co-created by provider and consumer together, and perceived subjectively — different stakeholders can value the same service differently. The sole-provider trap denies co-creation, and the price trap equates money with value.

q: A provider classifies its data, restricts access to authorized staff, and ensures records cannot be altered without detection. The practice responsible for this protection of information is:
options: Information security management — protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information
Incident management — restoring service after breaches
Knowledge management — sharing what staff know
Supplier management — controlling vendor access
explain: Information security management protects information the organization needs — the CIA triad. Incident management is the trap for 'after a breach' thinking, and knowledge management is about using knowledge, not protecting it.

q: Experienced analysts hold troubleshooting knowledge in their heads; when they leave, resolution times spike. The practice that addresses this by capturing, sharing, and reusing knowledge across the organization is:
options: Workforce and talent management — hiring skilled replacements
Incident management — resolving tickets faster
Knowledge management — making information and knowledge effective, efficient, and convenient to use
Measurement and reporting — tracking resolution times
explain: Knowledge management is about the knowledge itself — capturing and reusing it so it survives staff turnover. Workforce management is the close trap (it's about people and skills, not the knowledge assets), and measurement only observes the symptom.

q: Teams collect dozens of metrics, but nobody agrees which ones indicate success or how they support decisions. The practice that defines meaningful metrics and turns data into decision-supporting reports is:
options: Continual improvement — acting on the metrics
Measurement and reporting — reducing uncertainty through well-chosen metrics and clear reports
Monitoring and event management — watching infrastructure events
Service level management — reporting SLA achievement
explain: Measurement and reporting exists to support good decision-making by decreasing uncertainty — choosing the right metrics matters more than collecting many. Monitoring is the trap for infrastructure-focused thinking; it watches events, not decision metrics.

q: A provider depends on three vendors; one repeatedly misses response targets, but nobody tracks vendor performance or enforces contracts. The practice for managing supplier relationships, contracts, and performance is:
options: Service level management — managing customer-facing agreements
Relationship management — nurturing stakeholder links generally
Incident management — escalating vendor-caused incidents
Supplier management — ensuring suppliers and their performance are managed appropriately
explain: Supplier management specifically covers supplier relationships, contracts, and performance. Service level management is the close trap — it manages agreements with customers, not suppliers — and relationship management is broader stakeholder nurturing.

q: After a data-centre flood, a provider restores its critical services at a recovery site within the agreed timeframe. The practice ensuring services can be maintained at sufficient levels during a disaster is:
options: Availability management — day-to-day uptime of components
Incident management — restoring normal operation
Change enablement — authorizing the failover
Service continuity management — maintaining service availability and performance in case of disaster
explain: Service continuity management is specifically about disasters — keeping services going at sufficient levels when catastrophe strikes. Availability management is the close trap: it covers normal operations, not disaster scenarios.

q: Before building a new service, the team designs it to meet availability, capacity, continuity, and security requirements — not just functionality. This design work belongs to:
options: Business analysis — defining the requirements
Service design — designing services that are fit for purpose, fit for use, and deliverable
Service validation and testing — checking the built service
Change enablement — authorizing the build
explain: Service design creates services that meet utility AND warranty requirements and can actually be delivered. Business analysis is the trap for the requirements half — design turns requirements into a deliverable service.

q: Stakeholders give conflicting requirements for a new portal. An analyst interviews them, documents the real business needs, and gets sign-off on a single agreed requirements baseline. This is:
options: Business analysis — analysing needs and recommending solutions to meet them
Service design — building the portal
Project management — running the project
Relationship management — keeping stakeholders happy
explain: Business analysis defines business needs and requirements before solutions are designed. Service design is the trap for jumping to the solution; analysis must come first.

q: Leadership must choose between funding a new AI support service, retiring a legacy reporting service, or expanding the portal — with limited budget. The practice guiding these invest/divest decisions across the service lifecycle is:
options: Service financial management — budgeting and charging
Project management — delivering the chosen option
Portfolio management — ensuring the right mix of services within funding and resource constraints
Strategy management — setting the overall direction
explain: Portfolio management decides the mix of services to invest in across their lifecycle. Service financial management is the close trap (it handles money mechanics, not investment choices), and strategy sets direction that portfolio then implements.

q: A provider calculates the full cost of its backup service and sets a chargeback rate per gigabyte, so business units see what they consume. This budgeting, accounting, and charging activity is:
options: Portfolio management — choosing services to fund
Service financial management — ensuring financial resources and investments are used effectively
Supplier management — paying vendors
Measurement and reporting — reporting the costs
explain: Service financial management covers budgeting, accounting, and charging for services. Portfolio management is the trap for investment decisions; financial management handles the money mechanics of chosen services.

q: A provider holds regular strategic reviews with a key customer to understand changing needs and strengthen cooperation at senior levels. This nurturing of stakeholder links is:
options: Relationship management — establishing and nurturing links with stakeholders
Service level management — agreeing targets and reviewing achievement
Supplier management — managing vendors
Business analysis — defining requirements
explain: Relationship management is about the strategic/tactical links with stakeholders. Service level management is the close trap — it handles targets and agreements, while relationship management handles the relationship itself.

q: Before a major migration, the team identifies what could go wrong, assesses likelihood and impact, and defines responses for each threat. This is:
options: Change enablement — authorizing the migration
Problem management — investigating causes
Risk management — understanding and handling risks effectively
Availability management — keeping the service up
explain: Risk management is the dedicated practice for identifying, assessing, and handling risk. Change enablement is the trap — it manages the change itself, while risk management is the broader discipline applied here.

q: A new ITSM tool is technically ready, but staff resist using it and quietly revert to email. The practice addressing the people side of change — buy-in and adoption — is:
options: Change enablement — authorizing and scheduling the technical change
Project management — delivering on schedule
Workforce and talent management — skills and staffing
Organizational change management — managing the human aspects so lasting benefits are achieved
explain: Organizational change management handles the human side: adoption, resistance, and behaviour change. Change enablement is the classic exam trap — it governs the technical change, not people's acceptance of it.

q: The service desk struggles because analysts lack the scripting skills the new automation tools require. HR builds a training and hiring plan to close the gap. This is:
options: Workforce and talent management — ensuring the right people with the right skills in the right roles
Knowledge management — documenting scripting tricks
Organizational change management — persuading analysts to learn
Service desk management — running daily operations
explain: Workforce and talent management covers skills, staffing, and roles. Knowledge management is the trap — it handles knowledge assets, not people's capabilities and hiring.

q: A service introduction is organized with defined phases, milestones, coordinated resources, and a fixed delivery date. The practice ensuring it is successfully delivered is:
options: Continual improvement — improving after delivery
Release management — making features available
Portfolio management — choosing the investment
Project management — ensuring the project is successfully delivered
explain: Project management is the practice for delivering defined endeavours with phases and milestones. Release management is the trap — it handles making features available, not running the project.

q: A team maintains models showing how business services, applications, and infrastructure relate to each other, guiding long-term technology decisions. This is:
options: Service configuration management — tracking individual CIs
Architecture management — understanding the elements of the organization and how they relate
Service design — designing one service
Strategy management — setting business goals
explain: Architecture management provides the structural big picture — elements and their relationships. Service configuration management is the close trap: it tracks CI records, while architecture models how everything fits together.

q: Executives define which markets to serve, how to differentiate from competitors, and where to invest over the next three years. This formulation of goals and resource allocation is:
options: Portfolio management — selecting specific investments
Project management — delivering initiatives
Strategy management — formulating goals and adopting courses of action
Relationship management — engaging stakeholders
explain: Strategy management formulates the organization's goals and the courses of action to achieve them. Portfolio management is the trap — it implements strategy through investment choices rather than setting it.

q: A team provisions, monitors, and maintains the servers, storage, and networks that services run on. This oversight of the technology platform is:
options: Deployment management — moving code to environments
Software development and management — building applications
Service configuration management — tracking CI information
Infrastructure and platform management — overseeing the infrastructure and platforms services depend on
explain: Infrastructure and platform management covers the underlying technology estate. Deployment management is the trap — it moves software to environments rather than overseeing the platforms themselves.

q: An internal team builds and maintains a custom ticketing application, managing its code, functionality, and reliability through its lifecycle. This is:
options: Software development and management — ensuring applications meet stakeholder needs
Deployment management — moving the code to live servers
Release management — making versions available to users
Service design — designing the ticketing service
explain: Software development and management covers building and maintaining applications through their lifecycle. Deployment management is the close trap — it only moves software into environments rather than developing it.

q: Users cannot find available services; offerings are described inconsistently across intranet pages and outdated PDFs. The practice providing a single source of consistent information on services is:
options: Service request management — fulfilling requests
Service level management — agreeing targets
Service catalogue management — a single source of consistent information on services and offerings
Knowledge management — sharing general knowledge
explain: Service catalogue management maintains the authoritative, consistent view of available services. Service request management is the trap — it fulfils requests for services in the catalogue rather than maintaining the catalogue itself.

q: Which of the following is a GENERAL management practice?
options: Incident management
Risk management
Problem management
Change enablement
explain: Risk management is one of the 14 general management practices (adapted from general business domains). Incident, problem, and change enablement are all service management practices — the trap is assuming every familiar practice is 'service management'.

q: A ransomware attack encrypts file servers across three offices. A dedicated team with executive authority coordinates the response and customer communications. This is most likely a:
options: Problem — the root cause needs investigation
Change — systems need to be rebuilt
Service request — users need their files back
Major incident — significant business impact requiring dedicated resources and special handling
explain: A major incident has significant business impact and triggers special procedures with dedicated resources. The problem trap is premature — investigation comes after restoration — and the request trap mistakes an unplanned outage for a normal request.

q: Two incidents arrive at once: one user cannot print (deadline in three days), and the payroll system is down for 400 staff on payday. The service desk should:
options: Handle the printing issue first — it arrived first
Prioritize by impact and urgency — the payroll outage affects far more people with an immediate deadline
Handle whichever is quickest to resolve
Ask the printer user to wait because their issue is less interesting
explain: Priority combines impact (400 staff vs one) with urgency (payday vs three days). First-come-first-served is the trap — priority exists precisely to override arrival order — and quickest-first optimizes analyst convenience over business impact.

q: An analyst logs 'email slow' for what is actually a network-wide outage affecting all services, delaying correct assignment by an hour. This shows that:
options: Accurate categorization and initial diagnosis matter — they drive routing, prioritization, and trend analysis
Categorization is only useful for monthly reports
Priority alone is enough; categories add no value
Incidents should never be categorized
explain: Categorization drives correct routing and reveals patterns; a wrong category sent the outage down the wrong path. The reports-only trap undervalues categorization's operational role, and the priority-only trap ignores that priority without correct category still misroutes.

q: Two problems await analysis: one behind weekly payroll incidents, one behind rare cosmetic glitches. With limited analysts, problem management should:
options: Investigate in first-in-first-out order
Investigate the easier glitch first for a quick win
Prioritize by impact, urgency, and risk — the payroll problem first, since its business consequences dwarf the glitch
Investigate the most recently raised problem first
explain: Problems are prioritized by risk — impact, urgency, and probability — so limited effort targets the biggest business threat. FIFO is the trap for treating all problems as equal, and easiest-first optimizes analyst comfort over business value.

q: A team documents a workaround for recurring crashes but has not found the root cause. This should be recorded as a:
options: Known error — the workaround is documented
Incident — users are still affected
Problem record — the cause is unknown, so it is not yet a known error
Change — the workaround needs authorization
explain: A known error requires BOTH a documented root cause and a workaround; with the cause unknown, it remains a problem record. The known-error trap forgets the root-cause requirement, and the incident trap confuses the investigation record with the outage record.

q: A normal change to the payment system needs authorization, but the CAB cannot convene in time. Organizational policy designates the change manager as backup authority. This is acceptable because:
options: The change authority authorizes changes — it can be a person or a group as defined by policy; the CAB is not mandatory for every change
Only the CAB can ever authorize a change
Urgent changes need no authority at all
The service desk can authorize changes when the CAB is busy
explain: ITIL defines the change authority as whoever policy assigns — CAB, change manager, or others — based on change type and risk. The CAB-only trap treats one common authority as the only authority, and the no-authority trap abandons control entirely.

q: For database upgrades, a team always follows the same pre-defined sequence: risk assessment, backout plan, testing, implementation, review. This repeatable approach is a:
options: Standard change — the upgrades are low-risk
Change model — a repeatable way of handling a particular category of change
Incident model — the upgrades sometimes cause incidents
Problem record — upgrades address problems
explain: A change model is the pre-defined, repeatable approach for a change category. The standard-change trap confuses the model (how) with the change type (what authorization applies), and the incident-model trap borrows the wrong practice's concept.

q: During a complex outage, a service desk analyst explains the situation in plain business language and gives the caller a realistic workaround for their deadline. This demonstrates that the desk needs:
options: Deep technical expertise only — communication is secondary
The fastest possible ticket closure times
To escalate every complex issue immediately
Communication skills and business context — translating technical issues into guidance users can act on
explain: The service desk bridges technology and users: empathy, clear communication, and business understanding matter as much as technical skill. The technical-only trap forgets the desk's human interface role, and the escalate-everything trap abdicates that role.

q: A small company routes all contacts — phone, chat, email — to a single central team that handles every issue type. This is an example of a:
options: Centralized service desk — one team as the single point of contact
Local service desk — desks co-located with users
Virtual service desk — staff in multiple locations acting as one
Follow-the-sun service desk — desks handing over across time zones
explain: Centralized means one location/team handling all contacts. The virtual trap confuses 'single team' with 'distributed team acting as one', and follow-the-sun requires the time-zone handover that isn't described here.

q: The service desk depends on the internal network team under an internal agreement, and on an external ISP under a formal contract. The internal agreement is an ___; the external contract is a ___.
options: SLA; OLA
Underpinning contract; SLA
OLA; underpinning contract (UC)
SLA; underpinning contract (UC)
explain: Internal provider-to-provider agreements are operational level agreements (OLAs); contracts with external suppliers underpinning services are underpinning contracts (UCs). The SLA traps misplace the customer-facing agreement — SLAs are with customers, not internal teams or suppliers.

q: In a quarterly review, the provider and customer examine missed targets, agree improvement actions, and update targets for a new service launching next quarter. This shows service reviews are meant to:
options: Assign blame for every missed target
Drive improvement and keep agreements aligned with evolving business needs — not just report numbers
Justify cancelling the SLA
Report uptime figures to executives
explain: Service reviews use performance information to strengthen the service and keep agreements current. The blame trap turns reviews into tribunals, and the report-only trap misses their forward-looking improvement purpose.

q: At 3 AM, monitoring detects the payment database is unreachable and automatically opens a high-priority incident. This is correct because:
options: All events should open incidents automatically
Monitoring tools should wait for users to report issues first
A problem record should be opened instead
Exception events indicate a failure or breach — they should trigger incident management, which can be automated
explain: Exception events mean something is broken or about to break; the right response is incident management, and automation speeds it. The all-events trap would flood the desk with informational noise, and the wait-for-users trap wastes monitoring's early-warning value.

q: Before a major change, a team records monitoring baselines; after implementation, it compares new performance against those baselines to confirm the change worked. This shows:
options: Monitoring is only useful for detecting incidents
Baselines are only used by capacity management
Changes do not need monitoring data
Monitoring and event management supports other practices — here, validating change outcomes
explain: Monitoring data serves many practices: change enablement uses baselines to verify results. The incidents-only trap narrows monitoring to one consumer, and the capacity-only trap assigns baselines to a single practice.

q: Requests for 'new starter setup' follow a pre-defined workflow: HR form submission, account creation, laptop provisioning, and access grants, with approvals built in. This pre-defined fulfilment workflow is a:
options: Incident model — new starters are incidents
Service request model — a pre-defined way of fulfilling a particular type of request
Change model — setups change the environment
Problem record — setups cause problems
explain: A service request model defines the agreed steps for fulfilling a request type efficiently. The incident-model trap borrows the wrong practice's concept, and the change-model trap confuses fulfilment workflow with change control.

q: Service requests are prioritized using:
options: Agreed practices and business expectations — for example, policies defining which request types get priority
The impact-and-urgency formula used for incidents
The cost of fulfilling the request
Strict first-come-first-served ordering in all cases
explain: Unlike incidents, service requests are prioritized by agreed policies and business expectations, not the impact/urgency matrix. The incident-formula trap imports the wrong practice's method, and the cost trap confuses prioritization with financial management.

q: During a major incident, the service desk sends users updates every 30 minutes — even when there is no new fix to report. This is good practice because:
options: Updates should only go out once the incident is resolved
Communication during incidents wastes analyst time
Regular communication manages expectations and reduces duplicate contacts — even 'no news yet' updates have value
Users prefer silence to honest status updates
explain: Proactive communication keeps users informed, reduces repeat contacts, and maintains trust. The resolved-only trap leaves users in the dark (generating more calls), and the waste-of-time trap undervalues communication as part of incident handling.

q: A team wants to skip risk assessment for a 'small' firewall change to save time. The change manager refuses. This is correct because change enablement exists to:
options: Maximize the number of successful changes by ensuring risks are properly assessed and changes authorized — skipping assessment defeats its purpose
Slow changes down with bureaucracy
Make risk assessment optional for small changes
Let teams self-authorize anything labelled small
explain: Change enablement's purpose is maximizing successful service changes through proper risk assessment and authorization — size labels don't waive that. The bureaucracy trap mistakes control for delay, and the optional-assessment trap guts the practice's core function.

q: One SLA covers the email service for all customers; another SLA covers all services for one key hospital client. These are, respectively:
options: Both multi-level SLAs
Both service-based SLAs
Invalid — all SLAs must use the same structure
A service-based SLA and a customer-based SLA — different structures for different needs
explain: A service-based SLA covers one service for all its customers; a customer-based SLA covers all services for one customer. The identical-structure trap ignores that SLA structures exist precisely to fit different situations.

q: The service desk tracks that 60% of contacts arrive via chat and staff accordingly, while keeping phone available for complex issues. This shows the desk should:
options: Close the phone channel — chat is more popular
Understand demand patterns across channels and resource accordingly, while remaining the single point of contact
Treat every channel identically regardless of demand
Ignore channel data — it does not affect service
explain: The desk stays the single point of contact but staffs intelligently based on how demand actually arrives. The close-the-phone trap abandons users with complex needs, and the identical-treatment trap wastes resources where demand is thin.

q: Monitoring trend data shows memory usage on application servers climbing steadily over several weeks, though no incident has occurred yet. The team raises a problem record to investigate. This shows monitoring supports:
options: Only the detection of active failures
Only capacity management — trends belong there
Proactive problem management — detecting deteriorating conditions before they cause incidents
Incident management exclusively
explain: Monitoring data enables proactive problem management: spotting trends and investigating before users are affected. The active-failures trap limits monitoring to reactive detection, and the capacity-only trap assigns trend analysis to a single practice.

q: A consultant claims the service value system consists of the service value chain, practices, and the four dimensions. This is:
options: Correct — those are the three SVS components
Correct, except that demand is also a component
Wrong — the SVS components are guiding principles, governance, service value chain, practices, and continual improvement; the dimensions are perspectives on the SVS, not components
Wrong — the dimensions replace governance in the SVS
explain: The SVS has five components; the four dimensions are lenses applied to the whole SVS, not components of it. The three-component trap omits guiding principles, governance, and continual improvement — the elements that direct and sustain the system.

q: A market shift creates demand for secure remote access; the provider's service value system turns that demand into a new service delivering value. In SVS terms:
options: Value is the input and demand is the output
Demand is an output of the service value chain
The SVS has no inputs — it generates value spontaneously
Opportunity and demand are the inputs to the SVS; value is its key output
explain: Opportunity and demand enter the SVS; value comes out. The reversed trap flips the flow, and the no-inputs trap treats the SVS as self-generating rather than demand-driven.

q: Each value chain activity — from engage to deliver and support — includes steps to evaluate and enhance its own performance. This reflects that the 'improve' activity:
options: Operates within and across all value chain activities — improvement is embedded everywhere, not a separate phase at the end
Runs only after deliver and support finishes
Belongs exclusively to a dedicated continual improvement team
Replaces the other value chain activities
explain: Improve ensures continual improvement of products, services, and practices across all value chain activities — it is woven through them. The end-phase trap turns improvement into a waterfall stage, and the dedicated-team trap confines it to one group.

q: A provider improves its internal deployment pipeline, cutting its own costs even though customers see no direct change. Within the SVS, this still counts as value creation because:
options: Only customer-facing changes can create value
The SVS creates value for all stakeholders — including the provider organization itself, not only customers
Internal efficiency is never value
Value requires direct customer involvement in every change
explain: The SVS serves customers, users, the provider, and other stakeholders — provider-side gains are genuine value. The customer-only trap denies the provider a stake in its own system, and the involvement trap demands customer participation where none is needed.

q: Two teams merge; differing working cultures and unclear responsibilities cause friction in the new incident process, even though the tools and workflows are sound. The dimension that needs attention is:
options: Organizations and people — culture, roles, responsibilities, and competencies
Value streams and processes — the workflows must be wrong
Partners and suppliers — a vendor must be at fault
Information and technology — the tools must be replaced
explain: Culture, roles, and responsibilities sit in the organizations and people dimension — the tools work, the people side doesn't. The workflow trap blames process for a people problem, and the tooling trap reaches for technology when culture is the issue.

q: Analysts cannot troubleshoot effectively because CMDB data is outdated and monitoring dashboards contradict each other. The failing dimension is:
options: Value streams and processes — the troubleshooting workflow is wrong
Information and technology — the information and knowledge the dimension covers is unreliable
Partners and suppliers — the data vendors are at fault
Organizations and people — the analysts need retraining
explain: The information and technology dimension covers information, knowledge, and technology — here the information itself (CMDB, dashboards) is untrustworthy. The retraining trap blames people for bad data, and the workflow trap misses that no process works on false information.

q: A provider's cloud vendor suffers an outage; the provider has no contractual recourse or fallback because the relationship was never formally managed. The neglected dimension is:
options: Information and technology — the cloud platform failed
Value streams and processes — the failover workflow is missing
Organizations and people — internal staff caused it
Partners and suppliers — supplier relationships, contracts, and risks must be actively managed
explain: The partners and suppliers dimension covers exactly this: managing supplier relationships, agreements, and their risks. The platform trap blames technology for a relationship failure, and the workflow trap looks for a process fix to a contracting gap.

q: A value stream map for onboarding new starters shows that 80% of lead time is waiting between steps, not doing the work. Acting on this insight belongs to the dimension:
options: Organizations and people — hire faster staff
Information and technology — buy workflow software
Value streams and processes — how work flows end-to-end, where waste hides between steps
Partners and suppliers — outsource the onboarding
explain: Value streams and processes is about the end-to-end flow of work — the map revealed waiting waste between steps. The hiring trap throws people at a flow problem, and the software trap buys tools before understanding the flow.

q: A competitor launches a cheaper ITSM suite, and customers start asking why the provider's service costs more. In ITIL 4, this competitive pressure is:
options: An internal political issue
An external factor — part of the environment (like PESTLE forces) that the SVS must consider in planning
A value chain activity
A guiding principle
explain: External factors — political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental — shape the SVS from outside; competition is one of them. The internal trap mislocates a market force, and the activity trap confuses an environmental input with something the provider does.

q: A team has set its improvement targets and now defines the specific actions, owners, and timelines to reach them. In the continual improvement model, this planning step is:
options: What is the vision?
Take action
Did we get there?
How do we get there? — turning targets into an actionable improvement plan
explain: 'How do we get there?' is the planning step between targets and action. The take-action trap jumps to execution before planning, and the did-we-get-there trap assesses results that don't exist yet.

q: Before starting an improvement, a team agrees the effort should support the company's goal of becoming the region's most responsive provider. In the continual improvement model, this is:
options: What is the vision? — aligning the improvement vision with business vision and stakeholder objectives
Where are we now?
How do we get there?
Take action
explain: 'What is the vision?' comes first: improvement direction must serve the business vision and stakeholder objectives. The where-are-we-now trap skips straight to baseline without direction, and the take-action trap starts doing before deciding why.

q: After hitting its targets, a team embeds the new process into staff onboarding and schedules quarterly reviews to prevent backsliding. This is the continual improvement model step:
options: Did we get there?
Take action
How do we keep the momentum going? — sustaining gains and building on them
Where do we want to be?
explain: 'How do we keep the momentum going?' is about sustaining improvements and finding the next one — preventing regression. The did-we-get-there trap confuses assessment (already done) with sustainment, and the take-action trap re-executes instead of embedding.

q: A governing body reviews service performance reports, sets direction on risk appetite, and checks that controls are followed. These evaluate, direct, and monitor activities are:
options: Management — day-to-day execution
The service value chain — transforming inputs to outputs
Continual improvement — enhancing practices
Governance — the means by which an organization is directed and controlled
explain: Governance is evaluate, direct, and monitor — directing and controlling the organization. Management is the trap for execution-level work; governance sits above it, setting direction and overseeing.

q: A provider adopts all seven guiding principles but applies them only to the service desk, ignoring the rest of the organization. This is:
options: Wrong — the guiding principles apply across the entire service value system and organization, not to one practice
Correct — principles work best when scoped narrowly
Acceptable — the principles are optional guidance
Correct — principles replace practices, so one practice is enough
explain: The guiding principles are universal recommendations applying to the whole SVS and everything the organization does. The narrow-scope trap confines enterprise-wide guidance to one team, and the optional trap ignores their foundational role.

q: A single firewall rule change touches engage (user communication), design and transition (planning), obtain/build (implementation), and deliver and support (monitoring). This shows that value chain activities:
options: Must run in strict sequence: plan, then engage, then design and transition, and so on
Combine flexibly — different activities contribute to different value streams, with no fixed order
Cannot overlap on a single change
Always start with obtain/build
explain: Value chain activities combine into value streams in whatever combination the work needs — there is no mandatory sequence. The strict-sequence trap treats the activity list as a waterfall, which ITIL 4 explicitly rejects.

q: A team treats incident, problem, and change management as isolated silos with no handoffs between them. Within the SVS, this is:
options: Correct — practices work best in isolation
Correct — practices replace the value chain
Wrong — practices work together within value streams; handoffs between practices (like incident to problem) are essential
Acceptable — only seven practices matter anyway
explain: In the SVS, practices are resources combined within value streams — incident to problem to change handoffs are core flows. The isolation trap defeats the system's purpose, and the replace-the-chain trap confuses components with the model.

q: A startup designs its first service by considering its people, its data and tools, its vendors, and its workflows — from day one. This is correct because:
options: All four dimensions should be considered for every service from the start — not bolted on later
Dimensions only matter for large enterprises
Technology first, the rest later, is the recommended sequence
Two dimensions are enough for a small company
explain: The four dimensions apply to all services and should be considered together from the beginning. The enterprise-only trap exempts small organizations, and the technology-first trap sequences what should be simultaneous.

q: An improvement achieves its targets. The team documents lessons learned and uses them to launch the next improvement cycle. This is valid because the continual improvement model:
options: Ends permanently once targets are met
Is iterative — completion feeds the next cycle; improvement never truly ends
Treats lessons learned as optional paperwork
Only applies its cycles to failed improvements
explain: The model is a continuous loop — 'how do we keep the momentum going?' feeds new cycles. The ends-at-targets trap treats improvement as a project with a finish line, and the failures-only trap ignores improving on success.

q: Which statement BEST describes the service value system?
options: It is a single process for delivering services
It applies only to IT organizations
Value is created by practices alone, without the other elements
It describes how all the components and activities of the organization work together to facilitate value creation
explain: The SVS is the overarching model showing how guiding principles, governance, the value chain, practices, and continual improvement combine to create value. The single-process trap shrinks a system to a procedure, and the practices-alone trap ignores the other components.

q: A new privacy law affects what customer data the provider may store, which vendors it may use, and how staff handle access requests — touching information and technology, partners and suppliers, and organizations and people. This shows that:
options: Only one dimension is ever affected by external change
Dimensions should ignore external factors
External factors like regulation can affect all four dimensions — dimensions must be considered with their external context
PESTLE analysis replaces the four dimensions
explain: External factors cut across dimensions — a single regulation touched three of them here. The one-dimension trap underestimates external impact, and the replaces trap confuses an analytical input with the dimensional model itself.

q: A provider builds a self-service reporting tool that works exactly as specified. However, customers must spend hours learning it and reformatting its outputs before any report is usable. Applying 'focus on value', what does this show?
options: The tool is a success because it was delivered on specification
Value was not created — the effort the tool imposes on customers outweighs its usefulness to them
The provider should add more features to the tool
Only the provider's effort determines whether value exists
explain: Focus on value judges by outcomes for stakeholders, not delivery against a specification — a tool that costs customers more effort than it saves creates no value. The on-spec trap confuses output with outcome; the more-features trap adds effort without value; the provider-only trap ignores that value is defined by the consumer's perception.

q: A new service manager inherits a service desk with strong morale and effective informal mentoring, but almost no documented procedures. Applying 'start where you are', the manager should FIRST:
options: Replace the whole operating model on day one
Ignore the current state and design the ideal process from a blank slate
Assess and build on the existing strengths — such as the mentoring culture — before deciding what to change
Document everything exactly as it is and forbid any future change
explain: Start where you are means investigating the current state and reusing what works rather than defaulting to rip-and-replace. The day-one-replacement trap discards existing value; the blank-slate trap ignores current strengths; the freeze trap confuses observing the current state with preserving it unchanged.

q: A team must redesign employee onboarding (accounts, laptop, access). Instead of a nine-month project with a single launch, they automate account creation first, gather feedback from new hires, then tackle laptop provisioning. This follows 'progress iteratively with feedback' because:
options: Work is organized into manageable sections, with feedback shaping each subsequent iteration
Big projects always fail
Feedback is only needed after the final launch
Iterations eliminate the need for any planning
explain: The principle calls for organizing work into smaller manageable sections that can be completed in a timely manner, using feedback before, during, and after each iteration. The big-projects-fail trap overstates the claim; the feedback-only-at-end trap inverts the principle; the no-planning trap confuses iteration with improvisation.

q: During a major incident caused by a cloud provider outage, the provider's team troubleshoots internally for two hours without telling the customer anything. Applying 'collaborate and promote visibility', the problem is:
options: The team should have fixed the outage faster
Internal troubleshooting should be banned
The customer was not invited onto the bridge call
Stakeholders were denied the timely information they needed to make their own contingency decisions
explain: The principle requires making information visible so stakeholders can make informed decisions — here the customer could not activate its own contingency plans. The fix-faster trap blames speed instead of visibility; the ban-internal-work trap misreads collaboration; the bridge-invite trap narrows visibility to one mechanism.

q: To hit an aggressive incident-resolution target, a service desk starts closing tickets at first response even when users confirm the issue persists. Reopen rates soar, and problem management never sees the recurring patterns. Which guiding principle is being violated?
options: Keep it simple and practical
Think and work holistically
Optimize and automate
Start where you are
explain: Optimizing one part (resolution time) damaged the whole — hidden recurrences and lost problem data. Think and work holistically requires considering how each element affects the end-to-end service. The keep-it-simple trap mislabels the issue as complexity; the other options name real principles that do not address cross-element impact.

q: A team tracks 45 KPIs for incident management, but nobody can say which ones influence any decision. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Keep only the metrics that inform real decisions and drop the rest
Add more metrics to cover every possible question
Keep all 45 metrics but report them less often
Stop measuring incident management entirely
explain: The principle says to eliminate anything that does not contribute to value — metrics nobody acts on are waste. The more-metrics trap adds complexity without outcome; the report-less-often trap preserves the waste; the stop-measuring trap discards useful measurement along with the useless.

q: A team wants to automate its change-approval workflow, but the current workflow has five approval steps that nobody can justify. Applying 'optimize and automate', the team should FIRST:
options: Automate the workflow exactly as it is
Understand and simplify the workflow, then automate the optimized version
Never automate approvals, because human judgment cannot be replaced
Add extra approval steps to be safe before automating
explain: The principle explicitly says to optimize before automating — automating a wasteful process just produces waste faster. The as-is trap skips optimization; the never-automate trap rejects the principle's second half; the extra-steps trap adds the very complexity the principle removes.

q: A service desk handles tickets strictly first-in-first-out. A payroll outage affecting 500 staff waits behind a routine 'how do I print double-sided?' request. Applying 'focus on value', the desk should:
options: Keep strict FIFO — it is the only fair method
Treat every ticket as equal in value
Let analysts pick whichever tickets they prefer
Prioritize work by its value and business impact, not by arrival order
explain: Focus on value means directing effort where it creates the most value — a payroll outage for 500 staff outweighs a printing question. The fairness trap confuses equal treatment with equal value; the equal-value trap ignores business impact; the analyst-preference trap replaces one arbitrary rule with another.

q: A development team measures its success by story points completed. The business measures success by customer outcomes. The team's velocity rises while customer complaints grow. Applying 'focus on value', the team should:
options: Redefine success around the value delivered to stakeholders, not internal activity metrics
Increase story-point targets to work harder
Stop measuring the team's work
Treat velocity as the only objective measure of value
explain: Focus on value requires mapping work to stakeholder value; story points measure activity, not value. The work-harder trap doubles down on the proxy metric; the stop-measuring trap discards measurement; the velocity-is-value trap confuses output with outcome.

q: A team runs three iterations of a new request workflow, but each iteration simply adds more features — the plan never changes in response to user feedback. This violates 'progress iteratively with feedback' because:
options: Iterations should be as large as possible
Feedback should only come from management
Feedback must actually shape the next iteration; iterating without adapting is just phased delivery
Three iterations are too many
explain: The principle requires seeking and acting on feedback before, during, and after each iteration — unchanged plans mean feedback is decoration. The large-iterations trap inverts the principle; the management-only trap narrows the feedback sources; the too-many trap invents a limit the principle does not set.

q: After a major incident, the technical team sends the executive board a 20-page log extract full of error codes and stack traces. Applying 'collaborate and promote visibility', the team should instead:
options: Send nothing — executives do not need incident details
Provide a business-impact summary the board can understand and act on
Send even more technical detail to be thorough
Wait until the full root-cause analysis is complete before communicating
explain: Visibility means information stakeholders can actually use — communication must fit the audience. The send-nothing trap withholds needed visibility; the more-detail trap confuses volume with clarity; the wait-for-RCA trap delays decisions that need early information.

q: A new change process requires CAB approval for every release, but release management still plans weekly releases and the CAB meets monthly. The two designs now conflict. Which guiding principle was ignored?
options: Optimize and automate
Start where you are
