Progress iteratively with feedback
Think and work holistically
explain: The change process was designed in isolation without considering its impact on release management — holism requires seeing how elements interconnect. The other options name real principles, but none addresses cross-practice impact, which is the failure here.

q: A team designs an incident categorization scheme with 8 levels and 120 categories. Analysts cannot navigate it and pick categories at random, making the data useless. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Simplify to the minimum set of categories needed to achieve the desired outcome
Add training so analysts memorize all 120 categories
Add more categories for finer detail
Let each analyst invent their own categories
explain: The principle favors the minimum steps and complexity needed for the outcome — unusable precision is waste. The training trap preserves the complexity; the more-categories trap deepens it; the invent-your-own trap destroys consistency.

q: A company configures monitoring to auto-close incidents the moment an alert clears — including for the payment system, where a brief alert flap auto-closes the ticket for a genuine outage. Applying 'optimize and automate', the flaw is:
options: Automation should never be used in incident management
Alerts should never be allowed to auto-clear
The team failed to define where human judgment and control must remain — automation removed a necessary check
Monitoring tools cannot be trusted
explain: The principle requires defining what can be automated and where human intervention is needed; full automation without control points is reckless. The never-automate trap rejects automation outright; the never-clear trap misdiagnoses the mechanism; the distrust-tools trap blames the tool instead of the design.

q: An improvement cuts the provider's costs by closing the service desk two hours earlier, but customers in later time zones lose support during their business day. Applying 'focus on value', the assessment missed:
options: The provider's costs do not matter
Service desks should never change their hours
Only the largest customer's value counts
Value for all affected stakeholders — the saving came at the cost of other stakeholders' outcomes
explain: Focus on value weighs every stakeholder; a provider-side saving that damages customer outcomes is not value creation. The costs-don't-matter trap inverts the principle; the never-change trap freezes improvement; the largest-customer trap repeats the single-stakeholder error.

q: A service desk with a 70% first-contact resolution rate is told to adopt another company's 90% target immediately. Applying 'start where you are', the team should FIRST:
options: Understand its own baseline, constraints, and context before judging whether the external target fits
Adopt the 90% target without question — best practice is best practice
Reject targets entirely as demotivating
Copy the other company's entire operating model
explain: Start where you are means grounding decisions in the current state — a target divorced from context is a wish. The adopt-blindly trap imports context-free goals; the reject-targets trap discards improvement; the copy-everything trap ignores organizational differences.

q: A team wants a service catalogue with 200 services documented on day one. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the better approach is:
options: Build all 200 entries before showing anyone
Wait until the catalogue can be perfect
Publish the most-requested services first, gather feedback, then expand
Skip the catalogue — users will find services anyway
explain: Iterative progress delivers usable value early and uses feedback to steer expansion. The build-all-first trap is big-bang thinking; the wait-for-perfect trap delays value; the skip trap abandons the need the catalogue serves.

q: A provider outsources monitoring to a vendor but never shares its incident priorities, so the vendor alerts on everything with equal urgency and the service desk drowns in noise. Applying 'collaborate and promote visibility', the provider should:
options: End the outsourcing contract
Share its priorities and context with the vendor so alerts reflect what matters
Tell the vendor to send fewer alerts, without explanation
Accept the noise as the price of outsourcing
explain: Collaboration extends to suppliers — shared context lets the vendor act on what matters. The end-contract trap avoids the relationship instead of fixing it; the fewer-alerts trap withholds the context needed; the accept-noise trap normalizes the failure.

q: A weekly CAB meeting spends three hours reviewing every change — including standard changes that were already pre-authorized. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the meeting should:
options: Keep reviewing every change — thoroughness is always worth the time
Cancel the CAB entirely
Add more attendees to get through the agenda faster
Remove pre-authorized standard changes from the agenda and focus CAB time on normal changes that need judgment
explain: Practicality means the minimum effort to achieve the objective — re-reviewing pre-authorized changes adds no value. The thoroughness trap defends waste; the cancel trap discards needed governance; the more-attendees trap adds complexity instead of removing it.

q: A new 'smart' ticket form asks users 15 questions to 'intelligently' route their request. Users abandon the form and phone the desk instead. Applying 'optimize and automate', the lesson is:
options: Users should be forced to use the form
Smart forms never work
Technology should make things simpler and more effective for users — automation that adds burden is not optimization
The routing logic needs more questions
explain: Optimization means making something as effective and efficient as practical requires; a form users abandon fails that test. The force-users trap blames the user; the never-work trap rejects the approach; the more-questions trap deepens the burden.

q: A vendor adds a powerful analytics feature to its service, but the feature slows the service so badly that reports now miss their agreed delivery times. What does this illustrate?
options: Utility is more important than warranty
Warranty is more important than utility
Value needs both fit for purpose and fit for use — a utility gain that destroys warranty reduces value
New features always increase value
explain: Utility (fit for purpose) and warranty (fit for use) are both required for value; improving one at the expense of the other can destroy value. The utility-first and warranty-first traps each crown one half of the pair; the features-always trap equates novelty with value.

q: A provider's 'secure email service' includes the mail platform, a mobile app, and an onboarding session where engineers configure each user's client. The onboarding session is an example of:
options: Goods
Access to resources
A service action included in the service offering
Service consumption
explain: A service offering can include goods, access to resources, and service actions — the engineer configuring the client is an action performed by the provider. The goods trap mislabels an activity as a thing; the access trap mislabels it as resource use; the consumption trap assigns the provider's action to the consumer.

q: A logistics company hires a provider to build a tracking portal. The operations director defines what the portal must do and is accountable for the delivery outcomes; drivers use the portal daily; the CFO releases the funds. The operations director is the:
options: Sponsor
Customer
User
Provider
explain: The customer defines the requirements for a service and takes responsibility for the outcomes of service consumption. The sponsor (CFO) authorizes the budget; the users (drivers) use the service; the provider builds it.

q: A company outsources its data center. The provider now manages hardware failures, but the company remains accountable to regulators for protecting customer data. This shows:
options: Outsourcing transfers all risks to the provider
The provider is now the customer
Regulators are part of the service offering
Some risks stay with the consumer — accountability cannot be outsourced even when activities are
explain: Services transfer some risks and costs but impose others; accountability to regulators remains with the consumer. The all-risks-transfer trap overstates what outsourcing moves; the provider-is-customer trap inverts the relationship; the regulators-in-offering trap misplaces an external factor.

q: A provider delivers 50 configured laptops to a customer. The customer's desired result is that new hires are productive on day one. The 50 configured laptops are:
options: Outputs
Outcomes
Utility
Value
explain: Outputs are the tangible or intangible deliverables of an activity; the outcome is the result the stakeholder wants (productive new hires). The outcome trap confuses the deliverable with the result; the utility trap names functionality instead of the deliverable; the value trap jumps to perceived benefit.

q: A provider and customer hold joint quarterly planning sessions to align the service roadmap with the customer's business plans. In ITIL 4, these joint activities are:
options: Service provision
Service consumption
Service offerings
Service relationship management
explain: Service relationship management comprises the joint activities performed by provider and consumer to ensure value co-creation. Provision covers the provider's delivery activities alone; consumption covers the consumer's use alone; offerings describe services, not the joint work.

q: A customer requires that a service be available during business hours, support 1,000 concurrent users, survive a data-center failure, and encrypt data in transit. These requirements describe:
options: Utility
Warranty
A service offering
A value stream
explain: Warranty is the assurance that a service will meet agreed requirements — fit for use — covering availability, capacity, continuity, and security. Utility (fit for purpose) is about functionality; the offering describes the services; the value stream is the steps to deliver them.

q: A provider's 24/7 operations center depends on its monitoring platforms and on its engineers' certified expertise and proven escalation processes. The expertise and processes are:
options: Goods
Outputs
Capabilities
Resources
explain: Capabilities are the abilities of an organization, person, process, or service — expertise and effective processes are classic examples. Resources are the inputs (the platforms); goods and outputs mislabel organizational abilities.

q: To use a provider's analytics service, the customer must supply clean sales data each week and assign staff to review the dashboards. These customer activities are part of:
options: Service provision
Service consumption
Service design
Service validation
explain: Service consumption is the activities the consumer performs to consume services — supplying data and reviewing dashboards are the customer's part. Provision is the provider's delivery work; design and validation are earlier lifecycle activities.

q: A freelance consultant buys her own project-management SaaS subscription, defines what she needs from it, and uses it daily. In this situation she acts as:
options: User only
Customer, user, and sponsor
Sponsor only
Provider
explain: One person can hold multiple roles — she defines requirements and owns outcomes (customer), uses the service (user), and authorizes the budget (sponsor). The user-only and sponsor-only traps each keep one role; the provider trap assigns the wrong side of the relationship.

q: A provider spends heavily to cut a service's response time from two seconds to half a second, but users never notice because their real bottleneck is an internal approval process. What does this illustrate about value?
options: Value is determined by stakeholder perception — improvements that do not affect perceived outcomes create no value
Faster is always more valuable
Providers should never improve performance
User perception is irrelevant to value
explain: Value is the perceived benefits and usefulness as judged by stakeholders; effort the consumer cannot perceive does not create value. The faster-is-better trap equates speed with value; the never-improve trap overcorrects; the perception-is-irrelevant trap contradicts the definition of value.

q: A backup service runs flawlessly every night, but the customer never defines a retention policy or tests a restore. When data loss strikes, recovery fails. What does this show?
options: The provider failed to deliver value
Backup services cannot create value
The customer is the provider
Value is co-created — it requires the consumer's active participation, not just the provider's delivery
explain: Value emerges from the service relationship through both parties' contributions; the consumer's missing participation (no policy, no restore tests) meant no value materialized. The provider-failed trap blames delivery that worked; the cannot-create trap dismisses the service; the customer-is-provider trap mislabels the roles.

q: An email service is fast, secure, and always available, but it cannot send attachments larger than 1MB — which the design team needs every day. The service lacks:
options: Utility
Warranty
A value stream
Service consumption
explain: Utility is fit for purpose — the functionality to meet the need — and the missing attachment capability is a functionality gap. Warranty (fit for use) is fine here; the value-stream and consumption options name unrelated concepts.

q: Each night the provider runs backups, monitors the platform, and applies patches; each morning the customer's staff log in and process orders. The provider's nightly activities are:
options: Service consumption
Service relationship management
Service provision
Service validation
explain: Service provision is the activities the provider performs to provide services. Consumption is the customer's use; relationship management is the joint activity; validation happens before launch.

q: A retailer's desired result is 'customers complete purchases during the holiday peak without delays.' In ITIL 4, this desired result is:
options: An output
An outcome
Utility
A service action
explain: An outcome is a result for a stakeholder enabled by one or more outputs. The output trap names the deliverable instead of the result; utility names functionality; service action names a provider activity.

q: A customer and provider sign a contract, the provider delivers the service, the customer uses it, and they meet monthly to review performance and plan improvements. This end-to-end cooperation is:
options: A service relationship
A service offering
Service provision
A value stream
explain: A service relationship is the cooperation between provider and consumer, encompassing provision, consumption, and joint management. The offering describes the services; provision is only the provider's side; the value stream is the steps to create and deliver.

q: As part of its 'new starter service', a provider supplies pre-configured laptops that become the customer's property. The laptops are:
options: Goods included in the service offering
Service actions
Access to resources
Warranty
explain: Goods are tangible items supplied as part of a service offering — ownership transfers to the consumer. Service actions are provider activities; access to resources implies use without ownership; warranty is assurance of performance.

q: The HR department defines the requirements for the payroll service run by the company's own IT department and funds it from HR's budget. HR is:
options: An external customer
A user
A supplier
An internal customer
explain: An internal customer is part of the same organization as the provider. The external trap misplaces the boundary; the user trap names only those who operate the service; the supplier trap inverts the relationship.

q: A service offers strong functionality, but its price plus the effort required to use it exceed what the customer gains from it. The customer will most likely perceive:
options: High value, because functionality is strong
High warranty
Low or negative value — value weighs perceived benefits against costs and risks
An improved service offering
explain: Value reflects benefits set against the costs and risks the consumer bears; strong functionality alone does not guarantee value. The high-value trap ignores cost; the warranty trap names assurance instead of perceived worth; the offering trap confuses the description with the judgment.

q: A video-conferencing service works well for 50 participants but collapses at 200 — yet the customer's all-hands meetings need 300. The service lacks:
options: Utility
A service catalogue entry
Service consumption
Warranty — it cannot meet the expected performance and capacity
explain: Capacity and performance under load are warranty (fit for use) concerns. Utility covers whether the features exist; the catalogue and consumption options are unrelated to the performance gap.

q: Before go-live, a team installs the new release in a staging environment that mirrors production, to verify the installation steps work. This activity belongs to:
options: Release management
Deployment management
Change enablement
Service validation and testing
explain: Deployment management moves new or changed components to live environments — and also to staging and test environments. The release trap confuses making available for use with the technical move; change enablement authorizes rather than moves; validation tests rather than installs.

q: A company plans next year's laptop purchases, tracks its current devices, and schedules secure disposal of old ones. Managing this full lifecycle is the purpose of:
options: Service configuration management
Capacity and performance management
Change enablement
IT asset management
explain: IT asset management plans and manages the full lifecycle of IT assets to maximize value, control costs, and manage risks. Configuration management tracks configuration information, not lifecycle value; capacity plans performance; change enablement authorizes changes.

q: A team can answer 'which services depend on this server?' in seconds from its CMDB, but it cannot say what the servers cost or when warranties expire. A manager calls this a failure of service configuration management. The manager is:
options: Right — configuration management should track costs and warranties
Right — the CMDB is incomplete without financial data
Mistaken — the CMDB is doing its job; tracking costs and warranties is IT asset management, not configuration management
Mistaken — configuration management is unnecessary
explain: Service configuration management ensures accurate information about the configuration of services and CIs is available when needed — cost and warranty lifecycle tracking belongs to IT asset management. The right-traps confuse the two practices; the unnecessary trap discards configuration management entirely.

q: A service desk analyst suggests better ticket categorization, a developer automates a manual check, and a manager funds a monitoring upgrade. This illustrates that continual improvement:
options: Is everyone's responsibility across the organization
Belongs only to a dedicated improvement team
Applies only to services, not practices
Requires executive approval for every idea
explain: The continual improvement practice applies throughout the organization — everyone who contributes to service value can identify improvements. The dedicated-team trap centralizes what should be distributed; the services-only trap narrows its scope; the approval trap adds bureaucracy the practice does not require.

q: A release manager coordinates new features, documentation, user training, and communications so everything is ready for users on launch day. This coordination is:
options: Deployment management
Change enablement
Service validation and testing
Release management
explain: Release management makes new and changed services and features available for use — including the surrounding components. Deployment moves the components; change enablement authorizes; validation tests against requirements.

q: Before building a new booking service, the team agrees with the customer exactly what 'working correctly' means and designs its tests around that agreement. This reflects service validation and testing because:
options: Testing should start after go-live
Validation confirms that new or changed services meet defined requirements
Only the provider defines requirements
Agreement with customers is unnecessary
explain: The practice ensures services meet defined requirements — agreeing what 'correct' means up front is how validation gets its criteria. The after-go-live trap inverts the lifecycle; the provider-only and unnecessary-agreement traps contradict the stakeholder focus.

q: A team analyzes outage patterns and adds redundant network paths so the ordering service meets its agreed 99.9% availability target. This is:
options: Availability management
Capacity and performance management
Service continuity management
Incident management
explain: Availability management ensures services deliver agreed levels of availability. Capacity addresses performance and demand; continuity addresses disaster recovery; incident management restores service after failure rather than designing availability in.

q: Users complain that the search function is slow at peak times, even though the servers have plenty of spare capacity. This performance concern belongs to:
options: Availability management
Incident management
Capacity and performance management
Problem management
explain: The practice covers performance requirements, not just capacity — slow response with spare capacity is a performance issue. Availability concerns whether the service is up; incident restores; problem investigates causes — but the practice accountable for performance is capacity and performance management.

q: A software vendor makes a new version available for customers to download and install when they are ready, rather than pushing it to them automatically. This is the deployment approach known as:
options: Big bang
Pull
Phased
Continuous delivery
explain: In a pull approach the new version is made available and users pull it when ready, versus push where it is sent out. Big bang deploys everything at once; phased rolls out in stages controlled by the provider; continuous delivery is frequent small deployments.

q: A network scan finds 40 laptops in active use that were never recorded in the asset register. The GREATEST concern for IT asset management is:
options: The laptops work too well
The register looks untidy
Users prefer these laptops
Unmanaged assets carry unknown risks — unpatched software, license gaps, and untracked costs
explain: IT asset management exists to control costs, manage risks, and support decisions — invisible assets defeat all three. The other options trivialize a genuine risk and control gap.

q: Each quarter, a team compares CMDB records against what is actually installed and corrects the mismatches. This activity is:
options: Change enablement
IT asset management
Configuration verification and audit
Service validation and testing
explain: Verification and audit ensure configuration information remains accurate and reliable — a core part of service configuration management. Change enablement authorizes changes; asset management tracks lifecycle value; validation tests new services.

q: A team selects improvement ideas specifically because they support the organization's goal of halving customer onboarding time. This shows continual improvement:
options: Aligned with the organization's vision and strategy
Limited to cost-cutting ideas
Focused only on technology
Independent of business direction
explain: Improvements should align practices and services with changing business needs — the vision sets the direction. The cost-cutting trap narrows improvement to savings; the technology-only trap ignores people and process; the independent trap severs the business link.

q: A new payroll feature is deployed to production but hidden behind a configuration switch until month-end testing completes. The feature is deployed but NOT yet released. This shows:
options: Deployment and release are the same thing
Testing is unnecessary
The feature is available for use
Deployment moves components to live environments; release management makes them available for use
explain: The scenario separates the two practices cleanly — code in production (deployed) but not yet usable (not released). The same-thing trap collapses the distinction; the testing trap and available-for-use trap misread the scenario.

q: Before launch, a team runs penetration tests and failover drills on a new payment service — not just functional checks. This reflects service validation and testing because:
options: Only functionality needs testing
Validation covers warranty aspects such as security and continuity, not just features
Penetration tests replace user acceptance
Failover drills are part of incident management
explain: Validation confirms the service meets its defined requirements, which include warranty aspects like security and continuity. The functionality-only trap narrows testing; the replace-UAT trap overstates one test type; the incident trap misplaces the activity.

q: Servers report 99.99% uptime, yet users face regular lunchtime slowdowns that prevent order entry. For availability management, the lesson is:
options: Availability should be measured from the user's perspective, not just component uptime
Server uptime is the only valid measure
User complaints should be ignored
Slowdowns are not an availability concern
explain: Availability management ensures agreed levels of availability to meet customer and user needs — component uptime that masks user-facing degradation misses the point. The uptime-only trap measures the wrong thing; the ignore-complaints trap dismisses the signal; the not-a-concern trap misclassifies degraded service.

q: Monitoring alerts when CPU exceeds 75% for an hour, triggering a capacity review before users notice any slowdown. This threshold-based action is part of:
options: Incident management
Problem management
Capacity and performance management
Change enablement
explain: Acting on thresholds before performance degrades is proactive capacity and performance management. Incident reacts to interruptions; problem investigates causes; change enablement authorizes changes.

q: Decommissioned data-center servers are wiped and repurposed for the test lab instead of being scrapped. This decision about re-use of assets is supported by:
options: Service configuration management
Change enablement
Capacity and performance management
IT asset management
explain: IT asset management supports decision-making about purchase, re-use, retirement, and decommissioning of assets. Configuration management tracks configuration data; change enablement authorizes changes; capacity plans performance.

q: Each server record includes its owner, warranty expiry date, and installed software versions. In service configuration management, these details are:
options: CI attributes — the information recorded about each configuration item
Change records
Incident categories
Service level targets
explain: Attributes are the data recorded about each CI, making configuration information useful when and where needed. Change records document changes; incident categories classify interruptions; targets belong to SLAs.

q: A team reviews its improvement register monthly, funds the ideas that still align with business goals, and retires those that no longer do. This shows the register is:
options: A dumping ground for every suggestion
Actively managed — ideas are evaluated, prioritized, and retired
Only for management's ideas
Unnecessary once improvements start
explain: The continual improvement register is a working tool — ideas are captured, assessed, prioritized, and removed when obsolete. The dumping-ground trap lets it rot; the management-only trap narrows its sources; the unnecessary trap discards it.

q: Moving code to production requires an authorized change; the technical move itself is planned and executed by the deployment team. The authorization to proceed is governed by:
options: Deployment management
Release management
Change enablement
Service validation and testing
explain: Change enablement authorizes changes after risk assessment; deployment management performs the move. The deployment trap confuses execution with authorization; release makes available for use; validation tests.

q: An incident is escalated to a specialist team, but nobody tracks its progress and the user receives no updates for hours. The missing element is:
options: A faster specialist team
Clear ownership — every incident needs an owner who tracks progress and keeps the user informed
More escalation levels
A major incident procedure
explain: Incident management requires incidents to be owned and tracked through to resolution with user communication. The faster-team trap blames capability; more levels adds bureaucracy; a major incident procedure is for the highest impact class, not the general gap here.

q: A recurring storage fault is traced to a firmware bug that only the hardware vendor can fix. For problem management, this means:
options: The problem record should be closed — vendors are outside problem management
Problem management has failed
Resolving the problem may require involving the supplier — problem management coordinates the resolution, including third parties
The vendor automatically becomes the problem owner
explain: Problem management manages workarounds and known errors through to resolution, which often needs supplier action coordinated by the problem owner. The close-record trap abandons the problem; the failed trap misjudges the situation; the automatic-owner trap invents a handoff that does not happen.

q: A company requires full CAB review for every change, so urgent improvements wait weeks while competitors ship daily. The change enablement flaw is:
options: Failing to balance the need for changes against their risk — excessive control blocks value
Having a CAB at all
Allowing any urgent changes
Reviewing changes too quickly
explain: Change enablement maximizes successful changes by assessing risk proportionately — control must balance speed and stability. The no-CAB trap discards governance; the no-urgent trap blocks responsiveness; the too-quickly trap inverts the facts.

q: A user calls the service desk asking for a new laptop. The analyst logs the request, checks the service catalogue, and triggers the fulfillment workflow. This shows the service desk:
options: Should only handle incidents
Is bypassing the proper process
Cannot use the service catalogue
Captures demand for service requests as well as incident resolution
explain: The service desk's purpose includes capturing demand for both incident resolution and service requests. The incidents-only trap narrows its purpose; the bypassing trap misreads proper handling; the cannot-use trap contradicts catalogue use.

q: An SLA written three years ago still targets 95% availability, although the business now depends on the service far more heavily. Service level management should:
options: Leave the SLA unchanged — stability matters most
Review and update the SLA so targets reflect current business needs
Hide the outdated targets from the customer
Report 95% as achieved and move on
explain: SLM ensures targets stay business-based — as needs evolve, agreements must be reviewed and updated. The unchanged trap preserves irrelevance; the hide trap destroys trust; the report-and-move-on trap measures against a meaningless target.

q: A team monitors server CPU and disk closely, but nothing watches the customer-facing checkout process — so the team learns about outages from social media. The monitoring gap is:
options: Too much monitoring
Monitoring the wrong servers
Monitoring components but not the service from the user's perspective
A lack of incident management
explain: Monitoring and event management should systematically observe services, not just infrastructure components — user-facing visibility is the point. The too-much trap inverts the gap; the wrong-servers trap misses the perspective issue; the incident trap names the response instead of the detection gap.

q: A request for access to the payroll system needs the finance manager's approval before fulfillment; a request for a mouse does not. This shows that service request management:
options: Uses different workflows with appropriate authorizations depending on the request type
Treats every request identically
Should eliminate all approvals
Cannot handle access requests
explain: Service requests are pre-defined with agreed fulfillment procedures, which can include authorization steps matched to risk. The identical-treatment trap ignores request variety; the eliminate-approvals trap removes needed control; the cannot-handle trap contradicts the access-request example.

q: After a major outage, a review finds escalation took 40 minutes because nobody knew who could declare a major incident. The lesson for incident management is:
options: Major incidents cannot be planned for
Escalation should be improvised each time
Reviews are a waste of time
Major incidents need a pre-defined procedure with clear roles and authority
explain: Major incidents get a separate procedure with dedicated resources — roles and authority must be agreed before the crisis. The cannot-plan trap denies preparation; the improvise trap guarantees delay; the reviews-waste trap discards learning.

q: Incident records show the same authentication failure 30 times this month, but each ticket was closed independently with a password reset. The missed step was:
options: Faster password resets
Problem identification — recurring incidents should trigger investigation of the underlying cause
Closing tickets more slowly
Deleting the incident records
explain: Repeated incidents with a common pattern should feed problem management for cause analysis. The faster-resets trap treats symptoms; the slower-closing trap confuses process with purpose; the delete trap destroys the evidence.

q: At 2 AM a critical vulnerability is being actively exploited. The CAB cannot convene, but the emergency change policy names the on-call security lead as change authority. This is valid because:
options: Emergency changes need no authorization
Policies do not apply at night
Emergency changes follow a separate, faster assessment and authorization path defined in advance
The security lead outranks the CAB
explain: Emergency changes are still authorized — through an expedited path with a designated authority, established before the crisis. The no-authorization trap skips governance; the night-exemption trap invents a loophole; the outranks trap misunderstands authority.

q: When hiring service desk analysts, a company prioritizes customer-service skills alongside technical knowledge. The BEST reason is:
options: The service desk shapes the customer's experience of the whole service — empathy and communication are core to its purpose
Technical skills do not matter on a service desk
Customers prefer slow, friendly service to fast resolution
Hiring choices are unrelated to service quality
explain: The desk is the human face of the provider; its purpose of capturing demand depends on effective, empathetic interaction. The tech-doesn't-matter trap discards needed skill; the slow-friendly trap invents a trade-off; the unrelated trap denies the link.

q: A customer wants stricter SLA targets than the provider can meet at the agreed price. Service level management should:
options: Promise the stricter targets to win the deal
Refuse any discussion of targets
Set targets unilaterally
Negotiate realistic, business-based targets that balance ambition with what can be delivered at the agreed cost
explain: SLM sets clear business-based targets and ensures delivery is assessed against them — targets must be achievable, not aspirational fiction. The promise-anything trap guarantees breaches; the refuse trap abandons negotiation; the unilateral trap repeats a classic SLM error.

q: When disk space runs low, the monitoring tool automatically runs a cleanup script and only raises an alert if the cleanup fails. This is an example of:
options: Incident management
Monitoring and event management triggering an automated response
Problem management
Change enablement
explain: Event management can initiate automated responses to defined events — the alert-plus-auto-remediation pattern. Incident begins when human-managed restoration is needed; problem investigates causes; change enablement authorizes changes.

q: Requests for 'new starter setup' always follow the same steps — HR form, account creation, laptop provisioning — so the team documents this sequence as the standard fulfillment path. This documented sequence is:
options: An incident model
A change model
A service request model
A problem record
explain: A service request model is the pre-defined procedure for fulfilling a specific request type. Incident models handle interruptions; change models handle changes; problem records track causes.

q: In one call, a user reports 'the printer is jammed' and asks 'can I get a second monitor?' The analyst should:
options: Log them separately — the jammed printer is an incident, the monitor is a service request — and handle each per its practice
Log both as a single incident
Log both as a single service request
Ignore the monitor request until the printer is fixed
explain: Incidents (unplanned interruptions) and service requests (pre-defined, user-initiated) follow different practices and must not be conflated. The single-incident and single-request traps force one practice onto both; the ignore trap drops legitimate demand.

q: Problem management documents a workaround for a known error but never tells the service desk. Analysts keep troubleshooting the same fault from scratch. The failure is:
options: Documenting the workaround
Having a known error at all
The service desk's fault for not finding it
Not communicating the workaround to those resolving incidents — known-error information must reach the desk
explain: Workarounds reduce incident impact only if the people handling incidents know them — communication is part of managing known errors. The documenting trap blames the right action; the known-error trap blames the record; the desk's-fault trap blames the victim of the communication gap.

q: A change to the email system is scheduled for Saturday. Users learn about it only when email stops working. The change enablement failure is:
options: Scheduling the change on a weekend
Not communicating the change schedule to affected stakeholders in advance
Making any change to email
Using a change schedule at all
explain: The change schedule exists partly to communicate planned changes so stakeholders can prepare — silence defeats its purpose. The weekend trap blames timing; the any-change trap blames the work; the schedule trap blames the tool.

q: A user suggests an improvement to the expense workflow during a service desk call. The analyst logs the suggestion and routes it to change enablement. This shows the service desk:
options: Should reject all suggestions
Can approve changes itself
Acts as an entry point for change requests as well as incidents and service requests
Owns the expense workflow
explain: The desk captures demand broadly — it is a natural entry point for change requests, which it routes rather than authorizes. The reject trap discards input; the approve trap confuses routing with authority; the owns trap misassigns accountability.

q: A provider's SLA targets are written in dense technical terms that the customer's business managers cannot interpret. Service level management should:
options: Rewrite targets in business terms the customer understands — SLAs must be business-based
Keep the technical language — precision matters more than comprehension
Remove the targets entirely
Let the customer guess what they mean
explain: SLM sets clear business-based targets — if the customer cannot understand them, they cannot agree that service meets business needs. The precision trap sacrifices comprehension; the remove trap abandons targets; the guess trap is abdication.

q: An event rule states: 'three failed logins trigger a warning; ten failed logins trigger an exception and open an incident.' This rule defines:
options: An SLA target
A change model
A problem record
How events are classified by significance and what response each classification triggers
explain: Event management relies on defined rules correlating significance with response — informational, warning, and exception events each drive appropriate action. The SLA trap misplaces the agreement; the change-model and problem-record traps name unrelated artifacts.

q: A product team maintains a roadmap showing how the current service portfolio will evolve over the next two years to achieve the agreed service vision. Maintaining this roadmap is mainly the value chain activity:
options: Engage
Plan
Deliver and support
Obtain/build
explain: Plan ensures a shared understanding of the vision, current status, and improvement direction for all four dimensions and all products and services. Engage handles stakeholder interaction; deliver and support runs live services; obtain/build secures components.

q: Each month, a team reviews lessons from every value chain activity and adjusts how work gets done. This continual adjustment is the value chain activity:
options: Plan
Engage
Improve
Design and transition
explain: Improve ensures continual improvement of products, services, and practices across all value chain activities and all four dimensions. Plan sets direction; engage manages stakeholders; design and transition creates new offerings.

q: A team agrees its improvement goal is 'better service'. When asked how it will know it succeeded, nobody can say. The continual improvement model requires:
options: 'Where do we want to be?' — targets must be specific and measurable, or progress cannot be verified
Vague goals, to stay flexible
Skipping measurement to save time
Letting each person define success privately
explain: The model step 'where do we want to be?' sets specific, measurable targets; 'did we get there?' is impossible without them. The vague-goals trap prevents verification; the skip-measurement trap discards the check; the private-definitions trap destroys shared direction.

q: An improvement fails because three teams each assumed a different team owned the new process. Within the four dimensions, this is a failure in:
options: Information and technology
Partners and suppliers
Value streams and processes
Organizations and people — roles, responsibilities, and communication were unclear
explain: The organizations and people dimension covers roles, responsibilities, culture, and communication — the missing ownership sits here. Information and technology covers data and tools; partners covers third parties; value streams covers workflows.

q: Leaders decide which services to retire based on cost and usage data from the service portfolio. This decision-support role of data illustrates the dimension:
options: Organizations and people
Information and technology
Partners and suppliers
Governance
explain: The information and technology dimension includes the information and knowledge needed to manage services — data as a decision input. Organizations and people covers culture and roles; partners covers suppliers; governance is direction and control, not data.

q: A provider holds joint roadmap sessions with its strategic cloud partner, while buying office supplies on price alone. This difference reflects the dimension:
options: Value streams and processes
Information and technology
Partners and suppliers — relationships vary with strategic importance
Organizations and people
explain: The partners and suppliers dimension encompasses the organization's relationships with other organizations involved in designing, developing, deploying, delivering, and supporting services — cooperation deepens with strategic partners. The other dimensions cover workflows, data and tools, and internal people.

q: A value stream for resolving incidents includes steps from engage (user contact), deliver and support (resolution), and improve (lessons learned). This shows that value streams:
options: Combine multiple value chain activities to create and deliver value
Each belong to exactly one value chain activity
Replace the service value chain
Apply only to incident management
explain: A value stream is a series of steps combining value chain activities to create and deliver products and services. The one-activity trap fragments them; the replace trap confuses the model; the incident-only trap narrows their scope.

q: A breakthrough in AI assistants changes what customers expect from service desks. In PESTLE terms, this external factor is:
options: Political
Economic
Social
Technological
explain: PESTLE's technological factor covers innovations that reshape services and expectations. Political covers government action; economic covers markets and spending; social covers demographics and attitudes.

q: A board reviews whether the organization's risk controls are actually working, then adjusts the risk policy accordingly. These activities are:
options: Management, not governance
Governance — evaluating performance and directing policy
Value chain activities
Guiding principles
explain: Governance is the means by which an organization is directed and controlled — the governing body evaluates, directs, and monitors. Management executes within that direction; value chain activities are operational; principles guide behavior.

q: Incident, problem, and change practices are combined into one coordinated flow for handling major outages. Within the SVS, this shows:
options: Practices must never be combined
Only the service value chain creates value
Practices are combined into value streams to facilitate value creation
Major outages need no practices
explain: The SVS works because its components — including practices — combine into value streams rather than operating as silos. The never-combine trap enforces silos; the chain-only trap ignores practices; the no-practices trap abandons method.

q: A team uses the continual improvement model to improve its own improvement process — assessing how it improves, and improving that. This is valid because:
options: The continual improvement model applies to the SVS as a whole and all of its components
The model only applies to services
Improvement processes cannot be improved
The model is only for large organizations
explain: Continual improvement applies across the SVS — to services, practices, and the improvement approach itself. The services-only trap narrows it; the cannot-improve trap is self-contradictory; the large-org trap invents a restriction.

q: A stakeholder suggests the provider offer compliance auditing — a service it does not provide yet — spotting an unmet market need. In SVS terms, this is:
options: Demand
Opportunity
Value
An outcome
explain: Opportunity represents options or possibilities to add value for stakeholders — here, an unmet need the provider could address. Demand is a need or desire for existing products and services; value is the result; outcome is the stakeholder's result.

q: A manufacturing company uses the service value system to improve its equipment-maintenance services. This is appropriate because:
options: The SVS is only for IT organizations
The SVS applies to any organization that delivers services, not just IT
Manufacturing is not a service
The SVS replaces all other management methods
explain: ITIL 4 and the SVS address service management generally — maintenance services are services regardless of industry. The IT-only trap narrows the system; the not-a-service trap misclassifies; the replaces-all trap overstates its role.

q: Change enablement, incident management, and service level management belong to which practice category?
options: General management practices
Technical management practices
Service management practices
Guiding principles
explain: These are service management practices — developed in service management and ITSM contexts. General management practices come from general business domains; technical ones from technology management; guiding principles are not practices.

q: A provider and its cloud vendor hold joint planning sessions and share technology roadmaps. Within the four dimensions, this cooperation belongs to:
options: Partners and suppliers
Information and technology
Organizations and people
Value streams and processes
explain: Joint planning with an external organization is squarely in the partners and suppliers dimension. Information and technology covers data and tools; organizations and people covers internal culture and roles; value streams covers workflows.

q: New regulations require data centers to report carbon emissions, forcing a provider to redesign its infrastructure for efficiency. In PESTLE terms, this driver is primarily:
options: Political
Social
Technological
Environmental
explain: Carbon and sustainability pressures are environmental factors in PESTLE. Political covers government policy mechanisms; social covers attitudes and demographics; technological covers innovation.

q: A provider's practices, value chain activities, and improvement efforts each pull in different directions, optimized locally but conflicting globally. Within the SVS, the problem is:
options: The components are working as a system — this is normal
The SVS components must work together as an integrated system, not as isolated parts
The service value chain should be removed
Practices should never change
explain: The SVS describes how all components and activities work together — local optimization without integration breaks value creation. The normal trap accepts dysfunction; the remove-chain trap discards the operating model; the never-change trap freezes practices.

q: The service value system takes opportunity and demand as inputs. Its output is:
options: More opportunity
Practices
Value — for the organization, its customers, and other stakeholders
The service value chain
explain: The SVS describes how components work together to facilitate value creation — value is the output. Practices and the value chain are components, not outputs; opportunity is an input.

q: A governing body checks that the organization meets its legal obligations while pursuing its service vision. This illustrates governance as:
options: Evaluating and directing — ensuring conformance alongside performance
Day-to-day service operation
A value chain activity
Optional for small providers
explain: The governing body evaluates conformance and directs the organization — governance, not management. The operation trap confuses governance with delivery; the value-chain trap misplaces it; the optional trap invents an exemption.

q: A provider aligns its guiding principles, governance, value chain activities, practices, and improvement efforts so they work together to create value. This integrated whole is:
options: A single process
A service catalogue
A value stream
The service value system
explain: The SVS is precisely this — how all components and activities work together to facilitate value creation through service relationships. The single-process trap shrinks it; the catalogue trap names a list of offerings; the value-stream trap names one series of steps.

q: A provider is considering retiring a little-used reporting feature. Support tickets show almost no one uses it, but removing it would force two long-standing customers to change their workflows. Applying 'focus on value', the team should:
options: Weigh the value for all affected stakeholders — the provider's savings against the disruption to those customers — before deciding
Remove it immediately, since low usage proves it has no value
Keep it forever, because focus on value forbids removing anything a customer uses
Decide based only on the provider's maintenance costs
explain: Focus on value considers value for every stakeholder in the service relationship, not just usage counts or provider costs. Option B tests the trap that low usage equals no value; C tests the misread that the principle forbids removal; D tests provider-only thinking that ignores customer impact.

q: A new CIO wants to replace the incident management process on day one, calling it outdated. Following 'start where you are', her FIRST step should be:
options: Hire consultants to design a replacement immediately
Assess how the current process actually performs and what to keep before deciding what to change
Freeze all incident handling until the new process is designed
Adopt a competitor's process without reviewing the current one
explain: Start where you are means honestly assessing the current state and reusing what works. Options A and D skip assessment entirely (D also copies blindly); C destroys existing value while waiting for perfection.

q: A team wants to automate incident categorization with AI. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the BEST approach is:
options: Automate all categories at once and measure accuracy afterward
Spend six months training the model on historical data before any live use
Pilot it on one ticket category, review accuracy with analysts, improve, then expand to more categories
Deploy it silently and let analysts discover miscategorized tickets themselves
explain: The principle favors small increments with feedback loops so direction can be corrected cheaply. Options A and D go broad immediately — D even hides the change; B is a big-bang approach that delays learning until the end.

q: A company is redesigning its payroll service, which depends on an external payroll vendor's platform. To apply 'collaborate and promote visibility', the project team should:
options: Finish the design internally, then inform the vendor of the changes
Exclude the vendor to keep the project team small
Share only the final rollout date with the vendor
Involve the vendor in design workshops so constraints and capabilities are visible early
explain: Collaboration means working together across boundaries — including suppliers — and making relevant information visible. Options A, B, and C all keep the vendor in the dark, which is exactly how late, expensive integration surprises happen.

q: A proposed change to the login system will alter the authentication flow for users, change what the service desk must support, require new monitoring rules, and affect SLA reporting. The holistic response is to:
options: Assess the change's effects across all of these areas together, since they form one system
Approve the technical change and let each team adapt afterward on its own
Focus only on the technical implementation, as that is the actual change
Split the change into separate independent changes with no coordination
explain: Holistic thinking treats the service as an integrated whole — a change in one part ripples through others. Options B and D fragment the work and invite conflicting adaptations; C ignores that the change's value depends on people, monitoring, and agreements, not just code.

q: An audit of the incident process finds analysts must fill in 18 categorization fields, but reports only ever use 4 of them. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Keep all fields in case they are ever needed
Remove the fields that add no value, keeping only what is actually used
Add guidance text to all 18 fields to make them easier
Require managers to review every field for completeness
explain: The principle says eliminate what does not contribute to value — unused complexity is waste. Option A keeps waste 'just in case'; C and D add effort around waste instead of removing it.

q: Before automating server provisioning, a team standardizes the request data, removes duplicate approvals, and defines clear fulfillment steps. Only then does it build the automation. This illustrates:
options: Automate first, then fix the process around the tool
Automation removes the need to understand the process
Optimize the work before automating it, so the technology amplifies an effective process
Manual processes should never be automated
explain: Optimize and automate explicitly orders the work: simplify and optimize first, then automate. Option A inverts the order and cements waste into code; B treats automation as a substitute for understanding; D rejects automation entirely rather than sequencing it properly.

q: A provider assumes its customers want 24/7 phone support and plans an expensive staffing increase. Applying 'focus on value', the team should FIRST:
options: Hire the staff, since more support always adds value
Ask only the provider's own managers what customers want
Launch the 24/7 line and measure value afterward
Check with customers what they actually value before investing
explain: Value is defined by the consumer, not assumed by the provider — the principle starts from understanding stakeholder needs. Option A assumes more is better; B substitutes internal opinion for customer input; C spends first and validates later, reversing the principle's order.

q: A new service manager inherits a service desk with no formal processes but several highly experienced analysts. Following 'start where you are', she should FIRST:
options: Learn how the analysts actually work today and build improvements on their existing knowledge and routines
Impose a textbook process model immediately, ignoring how the team works today
Send everyone for certification before allowing any changes
Replace the team with new hires trained in the latest methods
explain: Start where you are means assessing and building on existing capabilities — including people's tacit knowledge. Options B and D discard that asset; C delays improvement behind a credential gate instead of starting from the current state.

q: A team must modernize a customer portal used by 40,000 users. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the BEST plan is:
options: Rebuild the entire portal over nine months and switch everyone over in one go
Deliver the new portal in monthly releases, each usable and informed by user feedback on the last
Design everything upfront, then build it exactly as specified with no changes
Release the full new portal to all users immediately and iterate afterward
explain: Iterative progress delivers value in small, feedback-informed increments, limiting the blast radius of wrong assumptions. Options A and C are waterfall plans that learn nothing until the end; D iterates but skips the small-scale learning the principle requires.

q: After a controversial change is approved, rumors spread that favoritism decided it. To apply 'collaborate and promote visibility' going forward, the change authority should:
options: Keep decision rationale confidential to avoid debate
Announce decisions with no explanation to save time
Publish the reasons behind decisions so stakeholders can understand and trust them
Restrict change information to senior managers
explain: Visibility includes making decisions and their reasoning transparent, which builds the trust collaboration needs. Options A, B, and D all reduce transparency — the opposite of the principle.

q: A team upgrading its monitoring platform considers the supplier's API limits, the analysts' skills, the alert-handling workflow, and the tool's cost together. This reflects:
options: Optimize and automate
Start where you are
Keep it simple and practical
Think and work holistically — considering partners, people, processes, and value together
explain: The scenario deliberately spans the four dimensions of service management — a hallmark of holistic thinking. Option A misreads planning as automation; B misreads it as reusing the old tool; C misreads breadth as simplicity.

q: A 30-person company is designing its first change process. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the BEST choice is:
options: A lightweight peer review in the team chat for most changes, with fuller assessment only for risky ones
A full CAB with weekly meetings, formal minutes, and a 20-page request form for every change
The most comprehensive change model available, to be safe
No process at all, to keep things simple
explain: The principle calls for the minimum sufficient approach — enough control for the risk, no more. Options B and C over-engineer for a 30-person company; D confuses simplicity with absence of control.

q: A team wants to automate the scheduling of standard changes but keep CAB assessment for normal changes requiring judgment. This BEST illustrates:
options: Automating everything, including decisions that need human judgment
Using technology for what it does well while preserving human judgment where it is needed
Avoiding automation because some changes need judgment
Optimizing means removing all human involvement
explain: Optimize and automate means using technology to do whatever it is capable of well — routine scheduling — while humans handle judgment calls. Option A automates judgment itself; C and D treat automation and judgment as all-or-nothing.

q: The service desk wants a knowledge tool; the infrastructure team wants monitoring upgrades; the budget covers only one. Applying 'focus on value', the decision should weigh:
options: Which team asked first
Which option is cheapest, regardless of benefit
Which delivers the greatest value to stakeholders relative to its cost and risk
Which project the loudest stakeholder champions
explain: Focus on value directs scarce capacity toward the best value outcomes, weighing benefits against costs and risks. Option A uses arrival order as a proxy for value; B optimizes cost alone; D serves internal politics rather than stakeholders.

q: An organization wants better problem management but cannot hire specialists. Following 'start where you are', it should FIRST:
options: Wait until it can afford to hire before doing anything
Buy an expensive analytics tool to replace the missing expertise
Copy another organization's problem management team structure exactly
Identify existing staff with strong troubleshooting skills and build on the informal diagnostic routines already in place
explain: Start where you are means inventorying existing capabilities — people and their skills included — before deciding what is missing. Options A and B assume the current state has nothing to offer; C copies without assessing fit.

q: A provider is rolling out a new service that depends on its cloud supplier's platform. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the provider should seek feedback:
options: From all relevant stakeholders, including the supplier, before, during, and after each iteration
Only from internal staff, to keep the loop fast
Only after the full rollout, when results are measurable
Only from the supplier, since the platform is theirs
explain: The principle calls for feedback from all stakeholders — suppliers included — at every stage. Options B and D narrow the loop to one party; C delays feedback until it can no longer steer the work.

q: An improvement initiative is underway, but business stakeholders keep asking for status because updates live in the project lead's private notes. The BEST corrective action is to:
options: Tell stakeholders to stop asking and wait for the final report
Make progress visible — for example, a shared dashboard showing milestones, blockers, and next steps
Assign someone to write longer private status reports
Reduce the initiative's scope so there is less to report
explain: Visibility means progress and blockers are transparent to those with a stake in the work. Option A dismisses legitimate stakeholder interest; C keeps the information private; D avoids the visibility problem instead of fixing it.

q: To save money, a provider switches to a cheaper cloud vendor — then discovers the new vendor's API does not expose the events the monitoring platform needs, leaving operations blind. The holistic lesson is:
options: Always choose the cheapest vendor
Technology decisions never affect other dimensions
Consider how a decision in one dimension — here, partners and suppliers — affects the others, such as technology and processes
Monitoring is unnecessary if the vendor is cheap
explain: Holistic thinking examines cross-dimension effects: a sourcing decision broke monitoring and operations. Option A repeats the original mistake; B denies interdependence; D discards monitoring instead of fixing the decision.

q: A change policy requires the same full risk assessment for a trivial documentation update as for a core database migration. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the organization should:
options: Keep the uniform assessment — consistency matters more than proportionality
Exempt all changes from assessment to save time
Add more assessment steps to the documentation update
Scale the assessment to the risk — light changes get a light assessment, significant changes a fuller one
explain: The principle favors controls proportionate to need — practical, not one-size-fits-all. Option A applies heavyweight control where it adds no value; B removes control entirely; C adds waste instead of removing it.

q: A team successfully deploys a new self-service portal on schedule (the output). Six months later, ticket volumes are unchanged because users cannot find the answers they need (the outcome). The ITIL lesson is:
options: Outputs alone do not create value — value comes from achieving the desired outcomes
The deployment was a failure because outputs do not matter
Outcomes are the provider's internal metrics, so the provider decides if value was created
Value is guaranteed whenever a project delivers its outputs on time
explain: ITIL 4 distinguishes outputs (deliverables) from outcomes (results for stakeholders); value arises from outcomes. Option B wrongly dismisses outputs; C misassigns who defines value (the consumer does); D is the classic output-equals-value fallacy.

q: A sales team adopts a new CRM. It supports their entire sales workflow — lead tracking, quotes, and forecasting — exactly as they need. In ITIL terms, the CRM's fit for purpose is its:
options: Warranty
Utility
Outcome
Cost
explain: Utility is 'fit for purpose' — what the service does to meet needs. Option A (warranty) is 'fit for use' — how well it performs, such as availability and security; C is the result enabled; D is unrelated to functionality.

q: A hospital requires its patient-records system to recover within two hours of a data-center failure, with no data loss. This requirement addresses which aspect of warranty?
options: Utility
Capacity
Continuity
Usability testing
explain: Continuity — the service's ability to remain available or recover after adverse events — is a warranty aspect. Option A is functionality, not assurance; B concerns performance under load; D is not an ITIL warranty aspect.

q: A business unit defines the requirements for a new analytics service and will be accountable for the business results of using it. In this service relationship, the business unit acts as the:
options: User
Sponsor
Provider
Customer
explain: The customer defines requirements and takes responsibility for outcomes of service consumption. Option A (user) uses the service day-to-day; B (sponsor) authorizes budgets; C provides the service.

q: A CFO approves the budget for a new ITSM platform. She will not define its requirements or use it daily. Her role in the service relationship is:
options: Sponsor — authorizing the budget for service consumption
Customer — defining the requirements
User — consuming the service
Provider — delivering the service
explain: The sponsor authorizes budgets for consumption without necessarily defining requirements or using the service. Option B defines requirements; C uses the service; D delivers it.

q: Hundreds of support analysts log into the ITSM platform every day to manage tickets, while the IT director signed the contract. The analysts are the:
options: Sponsors
Users
Customers
Providers
explain: Users consume the service day-to-day. Option A authorizes budget (the director may be the sponsor); C defines requirements; D delivers the service.

q: A provider delivers a monitoring platform, but outages only fall after the customer assigns staff to act on alerts and tune thresholds jointly with the provider. This shows:
options: The provider failed, since value should come from the provider alone
Monitoring platforms cannot create value
Value is co-created — both provider and consumer must contribute their part
The customer should have built its own monitoring instead
explain: ITIL 4 holds that providers cannot create value alone; the consumer's participation is essential. Option A reflects the outdated provider-creates-value view; B overgeneralizes; D misses the co-creation point entirely.

q: Moving to managed email removes the cost of running mail servers, but requires integration work and retraining for 500 staff. In ITIL value analysis, the retraining and integration effort represents:
options: Costs removed by the service
Risks removed by the service
Utility of the service
New costs imposed on the consumer as part of consuming the service
explain: Service consumption removes some costs while imposing others, such as training and integration — both sides belong in the value equation. Option A reverses the direction; B confuses costs with risks; C is about functionality, not cost.

q: A company avoids moving to the cloud because of perceived security risks — while running aging on-premises servers with no redundancy and failing disks. From an ITIL risk perspective, the flaw is:
options: Treating the risk of inaction as zero — staying put carries its own risks, which must be weighed against the risks of moving
That on-premises servers have no risks
That cloud risks cannot be managed
That risk assessment should only consider the proposed change
explain: Risk analysis must compare options fairly: the status quo has risks too (hardware failure, no redundancy). Option B is factually wrong; C denies risk management; D excludes the current-state risks from the comparison.

q: A provider combines leased infrastructure, its own automation software, and 24/7 support staff into a single managed hosting offering. In ITIL terms, the provider has:
options: Sold three separate products
Configured products into a service designed to co-create value with the customer
Eliminated the need for any service relationship
Created utility without warranty
explain: Services are built by configuring one or more products — goods, software, resources — into value propositions. Option A misses the integrated offering; C misunderstands that services exist within relationships; D invents a gap not in the scenario.

q: A provider's 'new starter package' bundles a laptop (goods), access to SaaS applications (resources), and setup assistance from a technician (service actions). This bundle is best described as a:
options: Single product
Service relationship
Service offering — goods, access to resources, and service actions composed to address consumer needs
Utility requirement
explain: A service offering comprises goods, access to resources, and service actions addressing consumer needs. Option A ignores the service elements; B names the relationship, not the bundle; D names only the functionality aspect.

q: Adopting a cloud platform exposes a company to possible outages, but also offers the chance to scale rapidly for a major product launch. In ITIL 4, this potential positive effect is:
options: Not a risk, because risks are only negative
A warranty requirement
An outcome
An opportunity — the upside dimension of risk
explain: ITIL 4 defines risk as including both threats and opportunities; the scaling upside is an opportunity. Option A reflects the old negative-only view of risk; B mislabels it as assurance; C names a result, not the uncertain potential.

q: A provider celebrates resolving incidents quickly, but customers remain dissatisfied because they would rather the incidents never happened. This shows:
options: Value is determined by the consumer — the provider's internal metrics do not define it
Fast incident resolution has no value
Customers cannot judge value
The provider should stop measuring resolution times
explain: The consumer defines value; provider-centric metrics can miss what matters (prevention over speed). Option B overcorrects; C denies the consumer's role; D discards a useful metric instead of complementing it.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the three elements a service offering can include?
options: Goods are always physical; software can never be a good

Buying servers transfers ownership (goods); subscribing to SaaS grants use without ownership (access to resources); hiring consultants provides expertise applied to the customer's needs (service actions)
Access to resources and service actions are the same thing
Service actions are only performed by automated tools
explain: Option B correctly maps ownership transfer, access without ownership, and actions performed for the consumer. Option A wrongly excludes software goods; C collapses two distinct elements; D wrongly excludes people.

q: After a payroll service runs, the payroll team completes month-end pay accurately and on time, with no manual corrections. The accurate, on-time pay run is an example of an:
options: Output
Activity
Outcome — a result for a stakeholder enabled by one or more outputs
Utility
explain: The result achieved by the stakeholder (accurate pay) is the outcome; the reports or transactions produced are outputs. Option A names the deliverable, not the result; B names the work; D names functionality.

q: A reporting service has all the features finance needs and is available every morning, but during month-end close it responds so slowly that accountants cannot complete their work. The gap is in:
options: Utility
Service offering
Outcome definition
Warranty — the service is not fit for use under peak load
explain: Warranty covers performance under expected conditions (capacity and performance); the features (utility) are fine. Option A is satisfied here; B and C misdiagnose a performance assurance gap.

q: A startup uses a cloud provider instead of building its own data center, avoiding hardware costs, facilities management, and capacity-planning risks. This BEST matches the ITIL idea that a service:
options: Enables value co-creation by facilitating outcomes the customer wants without the customer owning specific costs and risks
Eliminates all costs and risks for the customer
Is always cheaper than doing the work in-house
Removes the customer's accountability for outcomes
explain: The definition centers on facilitating outcomes without owning specific costs and risks — not all of them. Option B overstates ('all'); C invents a price guarantee; D confuses risk transfer with accountability transfer.

q: A provider delivers a backup service with tested infrastructure, and the customer runs quarterly restore drills using its own data. Recovery confidence comes from:
options: The provider alone
Co-creation — the provider's capability plus the customer's active participation
The backup software's warranty
Avoiding any customer involvement
explain: Real recovery assurance needs both sides' contribution. Option A repeats the provider-only fallacy; C narrows it to a product attribute; D contradicts co-creation directly.

q: A provider automates onboarding so thoroughly that each new customer costs almost nothing to serve, improving the provider's margins while customers get faster setup. This illustrates that:
options: Only the customer gains value from services
Providers should not benefit from service relationships
Value is created for the provider too — efficiency and margin are legitimate provider value
Automation removes the need for a service relationship
explain: Focus on value includes the provider organization as a stakeholder; sustainable margin is provider value. Options A and B deny the provider's stake; D confuses efficiency with relationship removal.

q: A university buys a learning platform. The provost approves the budget, department heads define the teaching requirements, and lecturers use it daily with students. Which mapping is CORRECT?
options: Provost: customer; department heads: users; lecturers: sponsors
Provost: user; department heads: sponsors; lecturers: customers
Provost: provider; department heads: customers; lecturers: users
Provost: sponsor; department heads: customers; lecturers: users
explain: The budget authorizer is the sponsor, requirement-definers are customers, daily consumers are users. Options A, B, and C each misassign at least one role — the classic trap is confusing the budget holder with the customer.

q: The service desk receives 40 separate calls about the same email outage. Instead of 40 independent tickets, the desk links them to one master incident record. This is good incident management because:
options: Linking related reports to a single incident keeps tracking, communication, and resolution effort efficient and consistent
Each caller should get a completely separate investigation
Linked incidents can then be ignored
The service desk should never create master records
explain: Incident management benefits from recognizing patterns: one coordinated record avoids duplicated effort and conflicting updates. Option B multiplies work needlessly; C abandons the work; D rejects a standard coordination technique.

q: A known error's permanent fix requires a database schema change. Problem management should:
options: Apply the schema change directly, since the fix is already identified
Raise a change request so change enablement can assess and authorize the fix, while problem management tracks it as error control
Close the known error as soon as the change is requested
Delete the workaround once the fix is planned
explain: Error control manages known errors through to resolution — fixes go through change enablement for risk assessment, and the error stays open until resolved. Option A bypasses change control; C closes prematurely; D removes the safety net before the fix lands.

q: A CAB has rejected the last six change requests purely because 'all change is risky', and beneficial improvements are piling up. The change enablement failure here is:
options: Assessing risk at all — risk assessment slows change down
Allowing any changes to be proposed
Forgetting that the practice exists to maximize successful changes, balancing risk against the need to make beneficial changes — not to prevent change
Not convening the CAB more often
explain: Change enablement's purpose is maximizing the number of successful service and product changes — it manages risk, not avoids all change. Option A rejects assessment itself; B rejects the demand; D adds bureaucracy to a risk-averse culture.

q: A company treats its service desk as 'the phone room' — investing only in headsets while knowledge tools, training, and escalation paths decay. The flaw in this view is:
options: Headsets are the wrong technology
The service desk should only handle incidents
Phone support is outdated
