q: An improvement initiative set a target of '95% of changes deployed without incidents' with an agreed measurement method. At review time, the team compares actual performance against that target using that method. This assessment is valid because:
options: Targets can be invented at review time
Any available metric will do for the assessment
Improvement success is a matter of opinion
'Did we get there?' must be judged against the objectives and metrics defined in 'where do we want to be?'
explain: The continual improvement model links its steps — assessment uses the targets and measures agreed when defining the desired state. Judging against invented-after-the-fact criteria (or vibes) makes the review meaningless.

q: An improvement initiative hits its targets. To sustain the gains, the team publishes a short case study for other departments, adds the new checks to the team's definition of done, and assigns an owner to review the metrics each month. These actions are the continual improvement model step:
options: 'Take action'
'How do we keep the momentum going?'
'What is the vision?'
'Where are we now?'
explain: Keeping momentum means sustaining gains — embedding changes in daily work, monitoring for backsliding, and spreading learning. Without it, improvements decay as old habits return.

q: A board decides the organization will outsource infrastructure operations (setting direction and risk appetite), while managers select the vendor and run the relationship day-to-day. This illustrates that:
options: Governance and management are the same thing
Governance sets direction through evaluate-direct-monitor; management executes within it
Boards should manage vendors directly
Managers should set the organization's risk appetite
explain: Governance evaluates, directs, and monitors; management plans, builds, and runs. The board's outsourcing decision is direction-setting; vendor management is execution. Confusing the two puts boards in operations and managers in strategy.

q: Demand for a popular training service exceeds the provider's delivery capacity for the next quarter. Within the service value system, the provider should:
options: Accept all demand regardless of capacity
Manage the demand — prioritize, schedule, or expand capacity — since value requires balancing demand with capability
Hide the capacity constraint from customers
Cancel the service entirely
explain: Opportunity and demand are SVS inputs, but value only results when demand is matched to capability — through prioritization, scheduling, or capacity growth. Accepting unlimited demand guarantees broken promises.

q: A new law requires all customer-facing digital services to meet accessibility standards within two years. For an IT service provider, this external driver is, in PESTLE terms, primarily:
options: Technological
Social
Legal
Environmental
explain: Legislation and regulation are Legal factors in PESTLE. While accessibility has social dimensions, a compliance mandate from law is squarely legal — it constrains what services may be offered and how.

q: An aging workforce and a shortage of experienced service management professionals make hiring harder across the industry. In PESTLE terms, this external pressure on a provider's 'organizations and people' dimension is primarily:
options: Social
Technological
Legal
Economic
explain: Demographics, workforce trends, and skills availability are Social factors. They shape the people dimension externally — distinct from economic cycles, technology shifts, or legal mandates.

q: Change enablement, the service desk, and incident management are service management practices. Knowledge management is a general management practice, and deployment management is a technical management practice. This categorization is useful because:
options: It ranks the practices by importance
Each category is managed by a different company
It shows that service management adopts proven capabilities from general management and technology domains
Practices in different categories never work together
explain: The three categories reflect origins — ITIL adopts general management practices (like knowledge, risk, and project management) and technology-focused ones (deployment, infrastructure) alongside service-specific practices. Categories describe nature, not rank, and practices collaborate across them constantly.

q: Resolving a customer-impacting incident involves the provider's service desk, an external network vendor's engineers, and the customer's own IT contact — coordinated as one flow. This shows that value streams:
options: Must stay within a single organization
Are the same as organizational departments
Can span organizational boundaries, following value rather than org charts
Only exist in large enterprises
explain: Value streams are defined by the steps needed to create value — they cross teams, departments, and organizations as needed. Org charts describe reporting; value streams describe how value actually flows.

q: A team improves its incident categorization (deliver and support), which produces better trend data for problem management (improve), which drives changes (design and transition) that reduce future incidents. This chain shows the service value chain is:
options: An interconnected system where each activity's outputs feed others
Six independent steps performed in strict order
Only relevant to large organizations
A replacement for all management practices
explain: The SVC is a flexible operating model, not a linear process — activities interconnect, and improvements ripple across them. Treating activities as isolated steps misses the system's power.

q: The company's vision is 'zero unplanned downtime for payment processing'. The database team defines its improvement initiative around automated failover within 60 seconds, explicitly linked to that vision. In the continual improvement model, this is valid because:
options: Only frontline teams may define vision
Strategic visions cannot guide operational improvements
Vision must always be invented fresh for each initiative
'What is the vision?' can cascade from governance and strategy down to team-level initiatives
explain: Vision exists at multiple levels — organizational strategy cascades into initiative-level visions. Alignment between board direction and team improvements is exactly how the model connects strategy to action.

q: A consultant presents the service value system as a strict step-by-step process: first engage, then plan, then design, with no overlap. The correction is that:
options: The consultant is right — the SVS is a linear process
Engage is optional and can be skipped
Only the improve activity matters
The SVS is a flexible model — activities combine and interact as value streams require, not in fixed sequence
explain: The SVS describes how components and activities work together to create value; the value chain is an operating model, not a waterfall. Activities combine differently per value stream — engage, for instance, runs throughout, not just at the start.

q: A vendor offers to add AI-powered sentiment analysis to the monthly service report at no extra cost. The account team is excited, but no customer has ever asked for sentiment data. Applying 'focus on value', the team should FIRST:
options: Ask customers whether sentiment data would help them make better decisions
Accept the feature immediately because it costs nothing to add
Add it quietly and watch whether anyone mentions it
Reject it because new technology always introduces risk
explain: Focus on value means value is defined by the service consumer, so the team must check whether customers actually want the data. A free feature nobody uses adds no value; assuming excitement internally substitutes the provider's judgment for the customer's.

q: A new service manager inherits an incident process that exists only as shared habits in the team's chat channel, yet most incidents are resolved within target. Following 'start where you are', her FIRST step should be to:
options: Replace the informal habits with a best-practice framework on day one
Observe and document what the team already does well before changing anything
Hire external consultants to design a completely new process
Buy a new ticketing tool to force the team into a formal workflow
explain: Start where you are advises assessing and preserving what already works before discarding it. Replacing a working process on day one destroys existing value; the manager should first understand current performance and keep what is effective.

q: A team rolls out a new request catalogue to the entire company, planning to collect user feedback only after three months of live use. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the flaw in this plan is that:
options: Feedback should be skipped entirely to keep the rollout on schedule
Three months of live use is too short a period to judge anything
Feedback arrives too late to shape the design; it should be gathered during iterative development
Only developers are qualified to give feedback on a catalogue
explain: Progress iteratively with feedback means seeking feedback throughout the work — including before and during — not only after launch. Waiting three months locks in design mistakes; small iterations with early feedback let the team adjust while change is cheap.

q: During a major incident, the database team and the application team each run separate war rooms, apply conflicting fixes, and only compare notes afterwards. To apply 'collaborate and promote visibility', the BEST corrective action is to:
options: Assign blame to whichever team applied the conflicting fix
Let each team keep its own war room but require longer incident reports
Escalate all future incidents to senior management immediately
Run a single shared incident channel with one visible timeline of actions and decisions
explain: Collaborate and promote visibility calls for working together with shared, visible information instead of siloed efforts. A single channel with one timeline gives everyone the same picture; blame, separate rooms, and extra reporting all preserve the silos that caused the conflict.

q: A company automates server provisioning, cutting provisioning time from days to minutes — but the still-manual security review becomes the new bottleneck and releases stall. This BEST illustrates:
options: That automation is only worthwhile for large organizations
That security reviews should be eliminated to keep releases moving
That optimizing one part of a system without considering the whole simply moves the bottleneck
That provisioning was never the real problem in the first place
explain: Think and work holistically warns that a service is a system: improving one component in isolation shifts the constraint elsewhere. The provisioning gain is real, but end-to-end flow only improves when the security review step is considered as part of the same system.

q: Requesting a replacement computer mouse requires manager approval, finance approval, and a written business justification. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Add a risk assessment to make sure the mouse is really needed
Keep the approvals but move them into an automated workflow
Require the justification only for wireless mice
Remove the approvals and justification for low-risk, routine items
explain: Keep it simple and practical means eliminating steps that add no value — controls should be proportionate to risk. Approvals for a low-cost routine item cost more in effort than they protect; automation would only speed up a wasteful process.

q: A team plans to automate its weekly availability report, but each tool defines 'downtime' differently and nobody trusts the current numbers. Following 'optimize and automate', they should FIRST:
options: Agree on consistent data definitions and simplify the reporting process, then automate it
Automate immediately so the bad numbers at least arrive faster
Buy a single expensive tool and hope it resolves the definitions
Stop reporting availability until the definitions are perfect
explain: Optimize and automate requires optimizing the process BEFORE automating it — automating a broken process just produces bad results faster. Agreeing definitions and simplifying first ensures the automation amplifies something trustworthy.

q: A provider wants to fund a carbon-neutral data centre for brand prestige, while its customers' top complaint is slow incident resolution. Applying 'focus on value', the provider should FIRST:
options: Build the green data centre because sustainability benefits everyone
Ask customers how they rank faster resolution against sustainability before committing the budget
Do both initiatives at full scale regardless of cost
Ignore sustainability because customers never mention it
explain: Focus on value means the consumer defines what is valuable, so the provider must learn customers' priorities before spending. Building for prestige assumes the provider knows best; ignoring sustainability entirely assumes the opposite — only the customer's ranking resolves the trade-off.

q: After acquiring a smaller company, the CIO wants to scrap its service desk tool on day one because it is not the corporate standard — even though its first-contact resolution rate is the best in the group. Following 'start where you are', the FIRST step is to:
options: Migrate immediately so reporting is consistent across the group
Run both tools in parallel forever to avoid upsetting anyone
Assess what makes the acquired desk effective and preserve it while planning integration
Replace the acquired desk's staff with corporate-standard trained analysts
explain: Start where you are means measuring and keeping what works instead of discarding it for conformity. The acquired desk's performance is an asset to understand and protect; forced standardization on day one risks destroying the very capability being acquired.

q: A team must replace the company-wide change process. Plan X designs the complete new process over six months, then launches it to everyone at once. Plan Y pilots a simplified process with one department, gathers feedback, refines it, and expands in waves. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the team should choose:
options: Plan X, because a single launch avoids prolonged disruption
Plan X, because pilots waste time that could be spent on the full design
Plan Y, but skip the feedback step to keep the waves on schedule
Plan Y, because iterative delivery with feedback reduces risk and improves adoption
explain: Progress iteratively with feedback favours small, reversible steps that learn from real use over big-bang launches. Plan Y surfaces problems while they are cheap to fix and builds adoption; Plan X bets everything on an untested design.

q: A new self-service portal is designed solely by the infrastructure team. At launch, service desk analysts cannot answer questions about it and users bypass it entirely. The neglected guiding principle is:
options: Focus on value
Collaborate and promote visibility
Optimize and automate
Think and work holistically
explain: Collaborate and promote visibility requires involving the stakeholders who will live with the outcome — the desk and the users — throughout the work. Designing in isolation guaranteed the portal would miss real needs and leave support blind; the other principles were not the primary failure.

q: A provider outsources network monitoring to cut costs, but never considers how the vendor's alerts will reach the service desk or how analysts will escalate back to the vendor. Outages now take longer to resolve. This is a failure to:
options: Think and work holistically
Keep it simple and practical
Focus on value
Progress iteratively with feedback
explain: Think and work holistically demands considering how each part affects the whole end-to-end flow. The outsourcing decision optimized one component while ignoring its interfaces with the desk and escalation paths; the failure is systemic, not a matter of simplicity, value definition, or iteration.

q: A configuration manager insists every configuration item record carry 30 attributes 'for completeness'. Analysts spend more time updating records than using them, and data quality collapses. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the BEST response is to:
options: Hire more analysts so all 30 attributes can be maintained
Automate the collection of all 30 attributes
Capture only the attributes that support real decisions and add value
Delete the configuration records entirely
explain: Keep it simple and practical means doing the minimum that achieves the objective — records exist to support decisions, not for completeness. Trimming to useful attributes restores data quality; more staff or automation would just sustain an over-engineered design.

q: A team automates access approvals — including for privileged production systems — with no human checkpoint. A misconfigured rule then grants excessive access for weeks before anyone notices. The lesson from 'optimize and automate' is:
options: That automation should never be used for access management
That misconfigurations are unavoidable so automation must be abandoned
That every approval step should be automated to remove human error
That human judgment should be kept where risk requires it, so automation maximizes the value of human contribution
explain: Optimize and automate says to automate where it adds value but keep human intervention where it genuinely contributes — high-risk decisions need judgment. The failure was removing oversight entirely, not automation itself; the fix is targeted human checkpoints, not abandoning automation.

q: Internal IT builds an executive dashboard showing 400 metrics. Executives ignore it because they only need five numbers to make their decisions. Applying 'focus on value', IT should:
options: Redesign the dashboard around the decisions executives actually make
Add even more metrics so every possible question is covered
Send the full 400-metric report by email instead
Train executives to appreciate the other 395 metrics
explain: Focus on value means starting from what the consumer needs to achieve — here, five decision-supporting numbers. The 400-metric dashboard served IT's idea of thoroughness, not the executives' decisions; more data or training cannot fix a product aimed at the wrong outcome.

q: A team adopting formal problem management holds five years of incident tickets containing workaround notes. Following 'start where you are', it should:
options: Archive the old tickets and start problem records from a blank slate
Mine the existing tickets for recurring patterns as the starting point for problem records
Delete the workaround notes because they were never formally approved
Wait until a new tool is purchased before doing any problem management
explain: Start where you are means reusing existing capabilities and information rather than starting over. Five years of tickets are a rich source of recurring-failure patterns; discarding them wastes the organization's own history, and a new tool is not a prerequisite.

q: A team plans to redesign all 40 of its service request workflows in one big effort before releasing any of them. Which approach BEST applies 'progress iteratively with feedback'?
options: Redesign all 40 workflows, then launch them together
Launch the redesign without consulting users to save time
Redesign the three highest-volume workflows first, gather feedback, then continue in waves
Cancel the redesign because iteration is too slow
explain: Progress iteratively with feedback favours small steps that learn from real use over big-bang delivery. Starting with the highest-volume workflows delivers value fast and the feedback improves later waves; redesigning all 40 at once bets everything on an untested design.

q: Status updates for a critical upgrade live in the project lead's private notebook, so stakeholders keep bombarding the service desk for news. The BEST corrective action is to:
options: Tell stakeholders to stop asking for updates
Have the service desk invent status updates to satisfy callers
Give every stakeholder the project lead's notebook
Publish a shared, visible status page updated on a fixed cadence
explain: Collaborate and promote visibility requires making work and progress visible to those affected. A shared status page gives everyone the same current picture and stops the desk being an information bottleneck; silencing questions or inventing answers both hide reality.

q: A change to the VPN authentication method is assessed only for the remote-access service — but it also breaks the supplier's support tunnel and the backup replication link. This shows the need to:
options: Consider all affected components and stakeholders, not just the service being changed
Stop making changes to authentication systems
Assess changes faster so assessments do not slow work down
Let suppliers assess their own tunnels independently
explain: Think and work holistically means looking beyond the immediate scope of a change to everything it touches. The assessment failed because it treated the VPN in isolation; considering all dependent components and stakeholders would have caught the tunnel and replication impacts.

q: Service desk analysts manually retype incident details from phone calls into the ticketing tool, causing delays and errors. Following 'optimize and automate', the FIRST step is to:
options: Buy speech-to-text software and deploy it immediately
Simplify and standardize the logging process, then automate the parts that need no judgment
Hire more analysts to share the retyping workload
Stop taking incidents by phone
explain: Optimize and automate insists on optimizing before automating — a messy process automated stays messy, only faster. Simplifying and standardizing first makes the automation reliable; buying software first or adding headcount treats the symptom, and dropping the phone channel ignores user needs.

q: A provider delivers a new analytics platform on schedule (the output), but six months later the sales team's forecasting accuracy is unchanged because nobody altered how they work (the outcome). This BEST shows that:
options: Outputs are irrelevant as long as the provider meets its deadlines
The provider should have delivered the platform faster
Delivering outputs does not guarantee outcomes; value depends on the consumer acting on the service
Outcomes are solely the provider's responsibility
explain: An outcome is a result the stakeholder wants, enabled by outputs but realized through the consumer's own actions. The platform (output) was delivered, yet the outcome failed because the consumer never changed its ways; blaming speed or assigning outcomes solely to the provider misses this shared responsibility.

q: An email archiving service is fast and feature-rich, but restores take 48 hours although the contract promises four. In ITIL terms, the gap is in:
options: Utility, because the service lacks the right features
Value, because the customer never defined what value means
Outcome, because outcomes cannot be measured
Warranty, because the service does not meet its agreed assurance levels
explain: Warranty is the assurance that a service will meet agreed requirements — availability, capacity, continuity, security. The restore-time promise is a warranty commitment that is being breached; utility (fitness for purpose) is fine since the features work, so the shortfall is assurance, not functionality.

q: A backup tool runs reliably and securely, but it cannot restore individual mailboxes — the only restore the legal team ever requests. What is missing?
options: Utility, because the service is not fit for the purpose the consumer needs
Warranty, because the backups complete on schedule
Value, because backups are inherently valueless
Outcome, because the legal team never defined an outcome
explain: Utility is fitness for purpose — what the service does. The tool is dependable (warranty) but lacks the specific function the consumer needs, so it is not fit for purpose; the gap is functionality, not assurance or value definition.

q: A hospital board member authorizes the funding for a new patient-portal service but takes no part in defining its requirements and will not use it. In the service relationship, this board member is the:
options: Customer, because the funding came from the board
Sponsor, because she authorizes the budget for consuming the service
User, because the portal serves the hospital
Provider, because she controls the money
explain: The sponsor authorizes the budget for service consumption. The customer defines requirements and is accountable for outcomes; users consume the service daily. Funding authorization without requirement definition marks the sponsor role.

q: A regional manager defines the requirements for a field-service app and is accountable for the results it delivers; technicians use the app on customer sites daily. The regional manager is acting as the:
options: User, because she cares about the results
Sponsor, because she defined what is needed
Provider, because she is accountable
Customer, because she defines requirements and takes responsibility for the outcomes
explain: The customer defines the requirements for a service and takes responsibility for the outcomes of consuming it. The technicians are the users; the sponsor would be whoever authorized the budget. Accountability for outcomes plus requirement definition marks the customer role.

q: A provider's 'new starter' bundle includes a laptop the customer keeps, access to the corporate VPN, and a technician who configures everything on day one. The technician's setup work is best described as:
options: Goods, because it is part of a bundle
A service action, because it is work the provider performs for the customer
Access to resources, because the customer uses the VPN
Warranty, because setup gives confidence
explain: A service offering can include goods (the laptop, ownership transferred), access to resources (the VPN), and service actions — activities the provider performs. The technician's configuration work is an action, not a transferable good or mere access.

q: Moving to managed desktops removes patching effort, but users must follow a strict software policy and wait days for approved applications. In ITIL value analysis, the waiting and policy burden are:
options: Costs removed by the service
Risks transferred to the provider
Costs imposed on the consumer by using the service
Warranty conditions the provider must meet
explain: Every service removes some costs and risks while imposing others — here, new effort and delay fall on the consumer. Recognizing imposed costs is essential to honest value assessment; they are not removed costs, transferred risks, or warranty terms.

q: A company keeps customer data on an aging server 'to avoid cloud risk', while the server has no backup and its disks are failing. From the ITIL 4 perspective on risk, this decision:
options: May increase overall risk, because risk includes both potential loss and the opportunity foregone by avoiding action
Eliminates risk, because the data stays on company premises
Is correct, because cloud services are always riskier
Transfers the risk to the hardware vendor
explain: ITIL 4 defines risk as a possible event causing harm OR opportunity — it is not only negative, and avoiding action carries its own risks. Keeping the failing server avoids one perceived risk while accepting data-loss risk and forgoing cloud benefits; on-premises location alone eliminates nothing.

q: A provider delivers the same collaboration suite to two customers. One redesigns its meeting culture around it and productivity soars; the other barely logs in. This BEST illustrates that:
options: The provider delivered different levels of utility to each customer
Value is co-created: the provider enables it, but the consumer realizes it through use
The second customer received a defective service
Value is determined entirely by the provider's effort
explain: Value is co-created through the service relationship — the provider creates the potential, and the consumer realizes value by using the service effectively. Identical utility produced different value because the consumers engaged differently; the service was not defective, nor is value the provider's alone to determine.

q: A managed print service includes printers installed at the customer's offices that the customer owns outright, plus a maintenance contract for them. In ITIL terms, the printers are:
options: Service actions, because engineers maintain them
Access to resources, because the customer uses them
Goods, because ownership transfers to the consumer
Warranty, because they assure printing
explain: Goods are the component of a service offering whose ownership transfers to the consumer. The printers become the customer's property, which distinguishes them from service actions (the maintenance work) and resource access (use without ownership).

q: To deliver its backup service, a provider relies on its data-centre halls, backup software licences, and the administrators who run them. In ITIL terms, these halls, licences, and administrators are:
options: Resources the provider uses to deliver its services
Outcomes the customer experiences
Warranty terms promised to customers
Goods sold to the customer
explain: Resources are the means the provider uses to deliver services — facilities, tools, licences, and people's skills. They are inputs to service delivery, not outcomes the customer experiences, warranty promises, or goods transferred to the customer.

q: Two teams take the same project-management training. One calls it transformative; the other calls it a waste of time. ITIL 4 explains this because:
options: The training had different utility for each team
One of the teams is objectively wrong about the training
Value can only be measured in financial terms
Value is perceived differently by different stakeholders
explain: Value is subjective — what counts as valuable depends on each stakeholder's needs and context. Identical utility can yield different perceived value; neither team is 'wrong', and value is not limited to financial measurement.

q: A customer and provider hold quarterly sessions to review demand forecasts and adjust capacity together. This BEST illustrates that a service relationship:
options: Is a one-time transaction completed at contract signing
Involves ongoing cooperation and collaboration between provider and consumer
Exists only between external organizations
Requires the provider to dictate all terms
explain: Service relationships are cooperative — provider and consumer work together over time to co-create value. Joint forecasting sessions are collaboration in action; a relationship is not a single transaction, is not limited to external parties, and does not mean provider dictation.

q: A university wants 'students to enrol in courses online without visiting the registrar's office'. In ITIL 4 terms, this desired result is an:
options: Output, because it describes system behaviour
Utility requirement, because it describes functionality
Outcome, because it is a result the stakeholder wants to achieve
Activity in the service value chain
explain: An outcome is a result for a stakeholder, enabled by one or more outputs. Online enrolment without an office visit is the result the university wants — the portal and its functions are only the outputs enabling it; it is not a value-chain activity itself.

q: A service must support 5,000 concurrent users, recover within one hour of a failure, and encrypt data at rest. These requirements are aspects of:
options: Utility, because they describe what the service does
Outcomes, because they describe business results
Costs, because meeting them is expensive
Warranty, because they assure the service meets agreed requirements for capacity, continuity, and security
explain: Warranty covers assurance that requirements will be met — including capacity and performance, continuity, and security. These are not functionality (utility) or business results (outcomes); they are the 'will it work when needed' promises.

q: A reporting tool must produce tax filings in the exact statutory format the finance team is legally required to submit. This requirement addresses:
options: Utility, because it is about the service being fit for its purpose
Warranty, because tax filing is a legal assurance
Risk, because non-compliance is risky
Cost, because development is expensive
explain: Utility is fitness for purpose — whether the service does what is needed. Producing the statutory format is core functionality; warranty would cover whether it does so reliably and securely, while risk and cost are separate considerations.

q: A hospital's IT department delivers the patient-records service to clinical departments, with internal chargeback and quarterly service reviews. This is an example of:
options: An external service provider relationship
A goods transfer, because chargeback is involved
A sponsorship arrangement
An internal service provider relationship
explain: An internal provider sits within the same organization as its consumers — here, hospital IT serving clinical departments. Chargeback is an internal funding mechanism, not a goods sale; external providers serve separate organizations.

q: A 'free' open-source ITSM tool needs no licence fees, but implementing and maintaining it will occupy two engineers for a year. ITIL advises the organization to:
options: Choose it anyway, because only the licence price counts
Consider the total cost of consumption, not just the price
Reject it, because free tools always cost more
Ignore the engineering effort, because staff are already paid
explain: Value analysis weighs the full costs of consumption — implementation, training, maintenance — against benefits, not just the purchase price. 'Free' software can still be expensive to consume; but that does not mean free tools always cost more — each case needs full costing.

q: A car-leasing company gives drivers a maintained, insured car without them buying, servicing, or insuring it themselves. In ITIL terms, this is service-like because:
options: The customer achieves desired results without owning specific costs and risks
The leasing company owns the cars
Cars are goods, not services
Insurance is a warranty
explain: ITIL defines a service as a means of enabling value co-creation by facilitating outcomes customers want without them managing specific costs and risks. The driver gets mobility while the provider carries ownership costs and risks; who owns the cars is incidental to the definition.

q: A company subscribes to a SaaS analytics platform: it never owns the infrastructure but uses the platform's processing power on demand. The customer's use of the platform is best described as:
options: Goods, because the platform has value
A service action, because the provider runs the platform
Access to resources, because the customer uses provider resources without ownership transfer
An outcome, because analytics are produced
explain: Access to resources is the offering component where the consumer uses the provider's resources without taking ownership. The platform stays the provider's property, distinguishing this from goods (ownership transfers); the analytics produced are outputs, and running the platform is the provider's action.

q: A retailer plans to put a new checkout feature live in all stores on Friday night, coordinating the code deployment, staff briefings, and a rollback plan. The practice responsible for making the new functionality available to users is:
options: Deployment management, because it moves code to production
Release management, because it makes new and changed services available for use
Change enablement, because it authorizes the change
Service configuration management, because it tracks the new version
explain: Release management's purpose is to make new and changed services and features available for use — the coordinated rollout to users. Deployment management only moves components into environments; change enablement authorizes; configuration management tracks. The user-facing availability is release.

q: An engineer copies a tested software build onto the production servers, where it sits behind a feature flag until next week's launch. This activity of moving the component into the production environment is:
options: Deployment management
Release management
Change enablement
Service validation and testing
explain: Deployment management moves new or changed hardware, software, or other components to live environments. Release management would be making it available to users (next week); change enablement authorizes the change. The install itself is deployment.

q: A provider commits to 99.5% availability for its ordering service and designs redundancy and monitoring to meet that target. The practice that ensures the service meets its agreed availability needs is:
options: Capacity and performance management
Service continuity management
Monitoring and event management
Availability management
explain: Availability management ensures services deliver agreed availability to meet customer needs. Capacity handles throughput, continuity handles disaster recovery, and monitoring detects events — but owning the availability target is availability management's purpose.

q: Transaction volumes grow 20% each quarter, and the team models next year's load to add database capacity before the holiday peak. The practice behind this forward-looking resourcing is:
options: Availability management
Service financial management
Capacity and performance management
Deployment management
explain: Capacity and performance management ensures services meet agreed and expected performance, accounting for current and future demand. Availability focuses on uptime targets, finance on costs, deployment on moving components — forecasting demand is capacity's domain.

q: After a flood destroys the primary data centre, a provider fails over to a secondary site using a plan it tests twice a year. The practice that prepared this recovery capability is:
options: Service continuity management
Availability management
Incident management
Problem management
explain: Service continuity management ensures service availability and performance can be maintained at sufficient levels during a disaster, via tested continuity plans. Incident management restores normal operation day-to-day; availability covers agreed uptime, not disaster scenarios; problem management targets root causes.

q: A provider classifies its data, encrypts customer records, and runs access reviews to protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information. This is the purpose of:
options: Risk management
Availability management
Information security management
Service configuration management
explain: Information security management protects the organization by ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and availability of its information assets. Risk management is broader, availability covers service uptime, and configuration management tracks CIs — the CIA triad of information is security's purpose.

q: Before replacing the expense system, analysts map the current reimbursement workflow, interview finance staff, and document what the new service must do. The practice of analyzing business needs to define requirements is:
options: Service catalogue management
Business analysis
Service level management
Strategy management
explain: Business analysis analyzes a business or part of it, defining needs and recommending solutions — here, mapping the workflow and requirements. Catalogue management maintains the service list, SLM manages agreements, strategy sets direction; the requirements work is business analysis.

q: Customers keep requesting a 'password reset service' they cannot find, because the customer-facing list of available services still shows last year's offerings. The practice that should keep this list accurate is:
options: Service portfolio management
Relationship management
Service desk
Service catalogue management
explain: Service catalogue management provides a single source of consistent information on all available services for those who use them. The portfolio manages investment decisions behind the scenes; the desk handles contacts; relationship management handles the customer bond — the visible list is the catalogue.

q: Each year the leadership team decides which services to invest in, which to keep running, and which to retire, based on business strategy. The practice supporting these investment decisions across the full set of services is:
options: Service financial management
Service catalogue management
Service portfolio management
Strategy management
explain: Service portfolio management ensures the organization has the right mix of services — managing the pipeline, catalogue, and retired services as investments. Strategy sets overall direction, finance handles budgets and charging, catalogue is the customer-facing list; the invest/keep/retire decision set is the portfolio.

q: A provider defines a five-year direction: focus on managed security services, exit legacy hosting, and target healthcare customers. The practice of formulating the organization's goals and the course of action to achieve them is:
options: Strategy management
Service portfolio management
Business analysis
Continual improvement
explain: Strategy management formulates the goals of the organization and plans how to achieve them, aligning services with direction. Portfolio management acts on that direction for specific services; business analysis defines requirements; continual improvement refines execution — setting the course is strategy.

q: A architects' team maintains a map of how applications, data, and infrastructure relate, and uses it to plan a three-year technology evolution. The practice of understanding and managing these structural relationships is:
options: Service configuration management
Infrastructure and platform management
Software development and management
Architecture management
explain: Architecture management provides an understanding of all the different elements of an organization and how they relate, enabling effective planning. Configuration management tracks individual CIs, infrastructure management runs the platforms, software development builds applications — the structural blueprint is architecture.

q: A cloud vendor repeatedly misses its contracted response times, so the provider invokes penalty clauses and agrees a joint improvement plan with the vendor. The practice managing this vendor relationship and contract performance is:
options: Relationship management
Supplier management
Service level management
Risk management
explain: Supplier management ensures the organization's suppliers and their performance are managed appropriately, including contracts and value. Relationship management covers the customer bond, SLM covers customer-facing agreements, risk is broader — vendor contract performance is supplier management.

q: After a difficult outage, a provider's service manager starts monthly face-to-face meetings with the customer's operations lead to rebuild trust and align on priorities. The practice focused on establishing and nurturing these stakeholder links is:
options: Relationship management
Supplier management
Service desk
Service level management
explain: Relationship management establishes and nurtures links between the organization and its stakeholders at strategic and tactical levels. The desk handles day-to-day contacts, SLM manages agreements and targets, supplier management faces vendors — the strategic customer bond is relationship management.

q: A provider finds its firewall skills are concentrated in two engineers nearing retirement, so it starts a training and succession programme. The practice ensuring the organization has the right people with the right skills is:
options: Organizational change management
Knowledge management
Workforce and talent management
Service desk
explain: Workforce and talent management ensures the organization has the right people with the appropriate skills and knowledge in the correct roles. Knowledge management handles information availability, org change management handles transitions, and the desk is a function — skills and succession planning is workforce and talent.

q: Analysts solve the same VPN issue repeatedly because the fix is buried in one engineer's head. A new system captures solutions, makes them searchable, and keeps them current. The practice of ensuring the right knowledge reaches the right people is:
options: Service configuration management
Knowledge management
Monitoring and event management
Problem management
explain: Knowledge management maintains a structured approach to ensure information is available where and when needed. Problem management finds root causes, monitoring detects events, configuration tracks CIs — capturing and sharing solutions so others can reuse them is knowledge management.

q: A new ITSM tool launch stalls because staff keep using old workarounds and managers never reinforce the change. The practice that prepares people for change and embeds new ways of working is:
options: Workforce and talent management
Service desk
Project management
Organizational change management
explain: Organizational change management ensures changes are smoothly and successfully implemented and that lasting benefits are achieved by managing the human side. Workforce covers skills and staffing, project management delivers the tool, the desk supports users — adoption and behaviour change is org change management.

q: Executives ignore the 60-page monthly service report but act on a one-page summary of three trends tied to business goals. The practice of designing meaningful metrics and reports that support decisions is:
options: Service level management
Continual improvement
Measurement and reporting
Business analysis
explain: Measurement and reporting supports good decision-making by reducing uncertainty — providing the right measures and reports. SLM manages the agreements themselves, continual improvement acts on findings, business analysis defines requirements; designing decision-useful reporting is measurement and reporting.

q: A provider introduces departmental chargeback so each business unit sees exactly what its service consumption costs, and budgets accordingly. The practice covering budgeting, accounting, and charging for services is:
options: Service financial management
Service portfolio management
Strategy management
Service level management
explain: Service financial management supports the organization's strategies by ensuring finances are managed for services — budgeting, accounting, and charging. Portfolio decides investments, strategy sets direction, SLM manages agreements; the money mechanics of chargeback are service financial management.

q: An audit finds the company pays for 300 software licences while only 180 are installed, and 40 laptops are unaccounted for. The practice that manages the full lifecycle of these assets to maximize value and control cost and risk is:
options: Service configuration management
Service financial management
Procurement management
IT asset management
explain: IT asset management plans and manages the full lifecycle of all IT assets to maximize value, control costs, and manage risks. Configuration management tracks CI relationships for service delivery, finance handles budgets — licence optimization and asset tracking across the lifecycle is IT asset management.

q: A change to a database server unexpectedly breaks the reporting tool, because nobody knew the reporting tool depended on that server. The practice that should have provided accurate information about these dependencies is:
options: Monitoring and event management
Service configuration management
Change enablement
Availability management
explain: Service configuration management ensures accurate and reliable information about configuration items and their relationships is available when needed. Change enablement authorizes the change, monitoring detects events, availability manages uptime — knowing what depends on what is configuration management.

q: Two incidents arrive at once: the CEO's laptop cannot print, and the order-processing system is down for 200 customers. The service desk prioritizes the order system FIRST. This is correct because priority reflects:
options: The seniority of the person reporting the incident
Who shouted the loudest on the phone
The order in which the incidents were logged
Impact and urgency, not the reporter's rank
explain: Incident priority combines impact (extent of effect) with urgency (how quickly resolution is needed). The order system's wide business impact outranks one executive's printer; seniority, loudness, and arrival order are not prioritization criteria.

q: The root cause of a monthly billing failure is identified and a workaround is documented, but the permanent fix is scheduled for next quarter. The problem record is now classified as a:
options: Major incident, because billing is affected
Known error, because the cause is understood and a workaround exists
Service request, because a fix has been requested
Change, because the fix is scheduled
explain: A known error is a problem whose root cause is understood and for which a workaround is documented. It remains a known error until the permanent fix is implemented; the scheduled fix itself will go through change enablement, but the record's state is 'known error'.

q: A low-risk password-policy update has been performed dozens of times, follows a documented procedure, and is pre-authorized. In change enablement, this is a:
options: Standard change
Normal change
Emergency change
Major change
explain: Standard changes are low-risk, pre-authorized changes that follow a documented procedure and are well understood. A normal change needs assessment and authorization each time; an emergency change addresses urgent threats. Routine, repeatable, pre-authorized work is standard.

q: A critical vulnerability is being actively exploited in the company's web servers. The team must patch immediately, without waiting for the next scheduled CAB meeting. This requires a(n):
options: Standard change, because patching is routine
Normal change, because the CAB must still assess it first
Emergency change, assessed and authorized through the emergency change process
Change freeze, because exploited systems should not be touched
explain: Emergency changes resolve urgent situations that cannot wait for the normal schedule, and are assessed by an emergency change authority rather than the full CAB. Treating an active exploit as normal or standard would delay the fix dangerously; freezing changes leaves the vulnerability open.

q: Frustrated users have started calling developers directly, bypassing the support team. Developers are interrupted constantly and users get inconsistent answers. The BEST corrective action is to:
options: Publish the developers' phone numbers more widely so users reach the right expert
Reinforce the service desk as the single point of contact and entry point for users
Hire more developers to handle the direct calls
Close the service desk since users prefer developers
explain: The service desk is the single point of contact and entry point between the provider and users, capturing demand and coordinating resolution. Bypassing it fragments communication and overloads specialists; the fix is restoring the desk's role, not widening the bypass.

q: A user asks for access to a shared project folder — a pre-defined, low-risk request that forms a normal part of service delivery. This should be handled as a:
options: Service request
Incident
Problem
Change
explain: Service requests are pre-defined, user-initiated requests that are a normal part of service delivery. Nothing is broken (not an incident), there is no underlying cause to investigate (not a problem), and routine fulfillment is not a change.

q: A monitoring tool detects a database server's disk at 95% capacity and raises an alert before users notice any impact. In monitoring and event management, this detection is an example of handling a(n):
options: Incident that must be escalated to major incident procedure
Problem record requiring root-cause analysis
Change request for more disk space
Event, which may be informational, a warning, or an exception
explain: Monitoring and event management observes services and components, detecting events — state changes of significance, classed as informational, warning, or exception. The 95% disk reading is a warning event; it is not yet an incident, problem, or change.

q: A provider and customer agree on measurable targets for incident resolution times and system availability, then review performance against those targets each quarter. This activity belongs to:
options: Change enablement
Monitoring and event management
Service level management
Service catalogue management
explain: Service level management sets clear, measurable, business-based targets (in SLAs) and monitors and reviews them to ensure services meet expectations. Monitoring detects technical events, the catalogue lists services, change enablement authorizes changes — agreeing and reviewing targets is SLM.

q: Before approving a server upgrade, the change authority asks which services would be affected if the server went down. The team can only guess, because no record links servers to the services they support. The practice that should maintain these links is:
options: Service configuration management
Incident management
Problem management
Monitoring and event management
explain: Service configuration management maintains accurate information about configuration items and their relationships, which change assessment depends on. Incident and problem management restore service and find causes; monitoring detects events — none maintains the CI-to-service dependency map.

q: The team installs a new version of the ordering application on the production servers but keeps it hidden behind a feature flag; customers will get access next week after staff training. In ITIL terms, the team has performed:
options: A release, because the software is on production servers
A change, because authorization is still pending
An incident, because customers cannot use it yet
Deployment without release
explain: Deployment management moves components into production environments; release management makes them available for use. The software is deployed (installed) but not released (no user access) — distinguishing the two prevents confusing 'installed' with 'live for customers'.

q: A team has finished planning how it will reach its improvement target and now begins executing that plan. In the continual improvement model, these two consecutive steps are:
options: 'Take action' followed by 'did we get there?'
'What is the vision?' followed by 'where are we now?'
'How do we get there?' followed by 'take action'
'Where do we want to be?' followed by 'how do we keep the momentum?'
explain: The continual improvement model runs: what is the vision, where are we now, where do we want to be, how do we get there, take action, did we get there, how do we keep momentum. Planning the route ('how do we get there?') is directly followed by executing it ('take action').

q: A provider holds quarterly business reviews with a strategic customer, aligning the service roadmap with the customer's changing business plans. This ongoing strategic alignment is the focus of:
options: Supplier management
Relationship management
Service level management
Service desk
explain: Relationship management establishes and nurtures links with stakeholders at strategic and tactical levels — exactly what joint roadmap alignment is. Supplier management faces vendors, SLM manages agreements and targets, the desk handles daily contacts.

q: A backup vendor's contract includes response-time commitments, but the vendor misses them three months running. The provider invokes penalty clauses and agrees a joint improvement plan with the vendor. This is:
options: Incident management, because the vendor caused incidents
Problem management, because the root cause is the vendor
Change enablement, because the contract is changing
Supplier management, because it manages supplier performance against contracts
explain: Supplier management ensures suppliers and their performance are managed appropriately, including contracts, performance, and value. The vendor's failures may cause incidents, but managing the vendor relationship and contract remedies is supplier management's purpose.

q: A licence audit reveals the company pays for 300 software licences but only 180 are installed, while 40 laptops cannot be located. The practice that should have prevented this waste is:
options: IT asset management
Service configuration management
Problem management
Capacity and performance management
explain: IT asset management plans and manages the full lifecycle of IT assets to maximize value and control costs and risks — including licence reconciliation and asset tracking. Configuration management tracks CIs for service delivery, not financial optimization of the asset base.

q: A provider introduces chargeback: each department receives a monthly bill showing exactly what its IT service consumption cost. The practice behind budgeting, accounting, and charging for services is:
options: Service portfolio management
Service financial management
Service level management
Strategy management
explain: Service financial management covers budgeting, accounting, and charging for services — chargeback is its charging mechanism. Portfolio management decides service investments, SLM manages agreements, strategy sets direction; the money mechanics are financial management.

q: A service meets its 99.5% availability target, yet users complain it is always down during their 9 AM peak. The provider's reporting is 'watermelon' — green on the outside, red inside. The lesson for availability management is that availability must be:
options: Measured only by the infrastructure team
Reported less frequently to avoid complaints
Measured and reported from the business and user perspective, not just the component level
Replaced by incident counts as the key metric
explain: Availability management must ensure services meet agreed needs — measured in business terms, including when users actually need the service. Component-level uptime that misses the peak hour is watermelon reporting; the fix is business-aligned measurement, not less reporting or different owners.

q: Ransomware encrypts the company's file servers. A dedicated team is formed with executive sponsorship, frequent communication updates, and all other work deprioritized. This response is a:
options: Major incident, because of its significant business impact and need for dedicated resources
Problem, because the root cause must be found
Standard change, because recovery follows a plan
Service request, because users need their files back
explain: A major incident has significant business impact and needs a separate procedure with dedicated resources and communication. Finding the root cause (problem) comes later; recovery is not a routine request or pre-authorized standard change.

q: Analysts review six months of incident trend data and discover a pattern of authentication failures that has never been reported as a single issue. Creating a problem record from this analysis is an example of:
options: Reactive problem management, because incidents already occurred
Incident management, because the data comes from incidents
Change enablement, because a fix will be needed
Proactive problem identification, because trends are analyzed before major impact
explain: Proactive problem management identifies problems by analyzing trends and data before incidents cause significant impact. Although incidents occurred, the problem was found through trend analysis rather than reacting to a specific incident — the hallmark of the proactive approach.

q: A database upgrade will take the ordering system offline for two hours on Saturday night. It needs assessment, authorization, and scheduling. In change enablement, this is a:
options: Standard change, because downtime is scheduled
Emergency change, because the system goes offline
Normal change, because it needs assessment and authorization
Change model, because it follows a procedure
explain: Normal changes are scheduled, assessed, and authorized (typically by a change authority such as the CAB). Planned downtime does not make it standard (not pre-authorized routine) or emergency (not urgent); a change model is the procedure it follows, not the change type.

q: A provider hires service desk analysts primarily for communication skills, empathy, and business understanding — not just technical certifications. This is because the service desk practice requires:
options: The cheapest available staffing model
Excellent customer service skills and business understanding alongside technical ability
Analysts who never escalate to specialists
Staff who only handle incidents, never requests
explain: The service desk is the human face of the provider: it needs excellent customer service, empathy, and understanding of the wider business, with technical skill supporting that. Hiring on communication and business sense reflects the practice's purpose; cost-cutting, no-escalation, or incidents-only models misunderstand it.

q: A new service fails at weekends because the supplier's support contract only covers Monday to Friday, a gap nobody checked during design. Which of the four dimensions of service management was neglected?
options: Partners and suppliers
Organizations and people
Information and technology
Value streams and processes
explain: The partners and suppliers dimension covers the organization's relationships with other organizations involved in service delivery. The weekend support gap is a supplier-contract issue; the people, technology, and process dimensions were not the source of this failure.

q: A customer reports that the ordering portal is down. The service desk logs the issue, diagnoses it, and works to restore the portal. In the service value chain, this work primarily uses the activity:
options: Engage, because the desk talks to the customer
Plan, because resources must be planned
Deliver and support, because it ensures services are delivered and supported per specifications
Improve, because the portal needs improvement
explain: Deliver and support ensures services are delivered and supported according to agreed specifications — the core of incident restoration. Engage covers understanding stakeholder needs and ongoing relationships; the desk's restoration work itself is deliver and support.

q: A provider interviews customers about their expansion plans for next year so it can shape its service roadmap accordingly. In the service value chain, this is primarily the activity:
options: Plan, because it concerns next year
Design and transition, because the roadmap will change services
Obtain/build, because new services must be built
Engage, because it provides a good understanding of stakeholder needs
explain: Engage provides a good understanding of stakeholder needs, transparency, and ongoing engagement. Interviewing customers about their plans is stakeholder engagement; plan focuses on a shared understanding of vision and status, not on gathering needs.

q: An organization decides to build a new customer portal with its own development team rather than buying a product. In the service value chain, creating the portal's components in-house is the activity:
options: Design and transition
Obtain/build
Deliver and support
Engage
explain: Obtain/build ensures service components are available when and where needed — whether built in-house or procured. Design and transition ensures new services meet expectations before going live; building the components themselves is obtain/build.

q: Before a new payroll service goes live, the team runs end-to-end tests proving it calculates pay correctly, handles peak load, and meets security requirements. In the service value chain, this verification is part of:
options: Engage, because users are involved in testing
Obtain/build, because the service was built
Improve, because testing finds improvements
Design and transition, because it ensures the service meets expectations before going live
explain: Design and transition ensures products and services continually meet stakeholder expectations for quality, costs, and time to market — including verification before launch. Building was obtain/build; engaging users is separate; the pre-live quality gate is design and transition.

q: A consultant's slide describes the service value system as 'guiding principles, governance, the service value chain, practices, continual improvement, the four dimensions — plus the service catalogue'. A colleague objects that one item does not belong. The item that is NOT a component of the SVS is:
options: The service catalogue
Guiding principles
Governance
Continual improvement
explain: The SVS components are the guiding principles, governance, the service value chain, practices, continual improvement, and the four dimensions. A service catalogue is a practice-level artefact, not an SVS component; the other three all are.

q: The board sets a policy that any change above a defined risk threshold needs executive approval, and it reviews compliance with that policy each quarter. This directing and monitoring of the organization is:
options: Management, because it involves daily operations
The service value chain in action
Governance, because governance evaluates, directs, and monitors
A management practice
explain: Governance is the means by which an organization is directed and controlled — it evaluates, directs, and monitors. Setting risk policy and reviewing compliance is directing and monitoring; management would be executing within those policies.

q: After implementing a faster onboarding process, the team compares the new onboarding times against the target it set at the start. In the continual improvement model, this check is the step:
options: 'What is the vision?'
'Did we get there?'
'Where are we now?'
'How do we keep the momentum?'
explain: After taking action, the model asks 'did we get there?' — comparing results against the original objectives. 'Where are we now?' was the earlier baseline assessment; 'keep the momentum' comes after confirming the target was reached.

q: To fulfil a 'new starter' request, the organization always combines the same value chain activities in the same way: engage the hiring manager, obtain a laptop, build the accounts, and deliver the ready workstation. This repeatable combination is called a:
options: Value stream
Management practice
Governance framework
Service offering
explain: A value stream is the specific combination of value chain activities the organization undertakes to deliver a product or service. The repeatable activity sequence for onboarding is a value stream; a practice is a capability set, governance directs the organization, and the offering is what is sold.

q: New data-protection legislation forces a provider to change how long it retains customer backups. In ITIL 4, this legislation is an example of:
options: An internal policy decision
A guiding principle
An external factor (such as PESTLE) that can affect the service value system
A service value chain activity
explain: External factors — political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental (PESTLE) — can affect how the SVS operates. Legislation is a legal external factor, not an internal policy, a principle, or a value chain activity.

q: Incident management, problem management, and change enablement all belong to which group of management practices?
options: General management practices
Service management practices
Technical management practices
Strategic management practices
explain: ITIL 4 groups its 34 practices into general, service, and technical management practices. Incident, problem, and change enablement are service management practices; 'strategic management practices' is not an ITIL grouping.

q: A startup notices that small clinics struggle with appointment scheduling and designs a service specifically for them. In the service value system, this unmet need is an example of:
options: Demand, because clinics will request the service
A practice, because scheduling is a capability
Governance, because it directs the startup
Opportunity, because it is a possibility to add value for a stakeholder
explain: Opportunity represents options or possibilities to add value for stakeholders — the trigger that starts value creation. Demand is the need for existing services; here the service does not exist yet, so the unmet need is an opportunity, not demand.

q: A new service fails because staff were never trained on it and quietly keep using the old workaround. Which of the four dimensions of service management was neglected?
options: Organizations and people
Information and technology
Partners and suppliers
Value streams and processes
explain: The organizations and people dimension covers roles, responsibilities, culture, and competence — including training and adoption. The failure is human, not technical or supplier-related; untrained staff rejecting the service is a people-dimension gap.

q: Each month, a provider analyzes service performance data to decide whether targets were met and where the service should be improved next. In the service value chain, this analysis is primarily the activity:
options: Engage, because stakeholders see the results
Improve, because it ensures continual improvement of services and practices
Deliver and support, because it supports the service
Plan, because it looks at the month ahead
explain: Improve ensures continual improvement of products, services, and practices across all value chain activities and the four dimensions. Analyzing performance to drive improvement is improve; deliver and support is about day-to-day delivery, plan is about shared vision and direction.

q: The ITIL service value system describes how all of an organization's components and activities work together to:
options: Maximize the number of management practices adopted
Eliminate all risk from service delivery
Enforce a fixed sequence of value chain activities
Enable value co-creation through the management of products and services
explain: The SVS represents how components and activities work together to facilitate value creation through service relationships. It does not mandate adopting every practice, cannot eliminate all risk, and the value chain is explicitly not a fixed sequence.

q: A service desk's effectiveness depends on its ticketing tool, its knowledge base articles, and the quality of information analysts can access. Which of the four dimensions do these elements belong to?
options: Organizations and people
Value streams and processes
Information and technology
Partners and suppliers
explain: The information and technology dimension covers the information, knowledge, and technologies needed to manage services. Tools and knowledge assets sit here; people covers roles and skills, processes cover workflows, partners cover external organizations.

q: A team keeps a single visible register of every improvement idea, its owner, and its status — from suggestion through implementation. In ITIL 4, maintaining this register is part of:
options: Change enablement, because improvements are changes
The continual improvement practice, which uses an improvement register
Problem management, because ideas come from problems
Service level management, because improvements affect targets
explain: The continual improvement practice maintains a continual improvement register of ideas from all sources, tracking them through to action. Improvements may later need changes, but the register itself belongs to continual improvement, not to problem or service level management.

q: A provider continuously gathers customer feedback during service operation and feeds it into planning for the next service iteration. This shows that the value chain activity 'engage':
options: Runs throughout the value chain, not just at the start
Is the only activity that involves customers
Replaces the need for the improve activity
Happens only after deliver and support
explain: The value chain is not a fixed sequence — activities combine and interact as value streams require, and engage runs throughout. Feedback during operation feeding planning shows engage operating alongside deliver and improve; it neither replaces improve nor waits until the end.

q: Each quarter, management reports service performance to the governing board, which evaluates whether the IT strategy stays on course and adjusts direction. The board's role here is:
options: Management, because it reviews performance data
A value chain activity, because it uses information
Governance, because it evaluates, directs, and monitors
A technical management practice
explain: Governance evaluates, directs, and monitors the organization — the board assessing strategy and adjusting direction is governance in action. Reviewing data alone is not management; executing within the set direction would be management's role.

q: Two value streams for the same service use different combinations of value chain activities — one leans on obtain/build, the other on engage and deliver. This is:
options: A violation of the service value chain model
Evidence that one stream is incorrectly designed
Proof that the four dimensions are misaligned
Expected, because the value chain is an operating model, not a fixed sequence
explain: The service value chain is a flexible operating model: activities combine and interact differently in each value stream as needed. Different combinations for different streams are normal and expected, not a violation or a design error.

q: An IT team proposes replacing its ITSM tool: the new tool costs 40% more per year but would cut the time users spend submitting requests in half. Applying 'focus on value', the team should:
options: Weigh the gains for users against the costs for the provider, considering all stakeholders, before deciding
Approve the purchase, because user benefits always outweigh provider costs
Keep the old tool, because any cost increase automatically destroys value
Decide on purchase price alone, because value is measured only in money
explain: Focus on value means assessing perceived benefits, utility, and warranty against costs and risks for every stakeholder - users, customers, and the provider organization. Neither 'users always win' nor 'cost rules' is correct: value must be balanced across the whole service relationship, and money is only one part of the value equation.

q: A company is rolling out formal knowledge management and discovers two support teams already maintain excellent troubleshooting wikis that analysts rely on daily. Following 'start where you are', the BEST approach is to:
options: Discard the wikis and build a new knowledge base from scratch for consistency
Reuse and build on the existing wikis, improving them where needed, rather than starting over
Copy a competitor's knowledge base design instead, since it is proven elsewhere
Force every team onto a single wiki immediately without reviewing what exists
explain: Start where you are means reusing what already works - the existing wikis are proven assets, so the team should observe, build on, and improve them. Discarding working assets or copying another organization wholesale ignores the value already present and risks destroying something effective.

q: An organization wants to move from annual releases to continuous delivery. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the FIRST sensible step is to:
options: Switch every service to continuous delivery on the same day to avoid mixed ways of working
Spend eighteen months designing the perfect pipeline, then launch it company-wide
Move one low-risk service to smaller, more frequent releases, learn from the experience, and expand from there
Run a pilot, ignore the feedback it produces, and roll out the original plan anyway
explain: Progress iteratively with feedback means organizing work into smaller, manageable sections that can be completed in time, with feedback sought before, during, and after each iteration. Big-bang switches and long planning phases without feedback deny the organization the learning that makes each iteration safer and better.

q: The infrastructure team and the application team each make changes to a shared service without the other knowing, causing repeated conflicting outages. Applying 'collaborate and promote visibility', the BEST response is to:
options: Assign blame to whichever team caused the latest outage so the other learns
Centralize all change authority in one manager so nobody else can act
Add three more approval layers so every change is checked by both teams
Create a shared view of planned work and involve both teams in decisions that affect the service
explain: Collaborate and promote visibility means including the right stakeholders and making work visible, because insufficient visibility leads to poor decisions. Blame, centralization, and extra approval layers hide the real problem - the teams cannot see or coordinate each other's work.

q: Procurement buys the cheapest storage available, saving 20% upfront - but the performance team then spends months fighting slow response times and support costs rise. Applying 'think and work holistically', the lesson is to:
options: Let each department optimize its own budget, since that is each manager's job
Always buy the most expensive option, because cheap components always fail
Ban procurement from buying storage without the CIO's personal approval
Consider how each component affects the whole service, since optimizing one part in isolation can damage the overall outcome
explain: Think and work holistically means considering how the components of services work together as an integrated system - no service or practice stands alone. Local optimization (cheapest storage) damaged the whole; buying the most expensive option or adding personal approvals are just different forms of non-holistic thinking.

q: The problem management process requires a twelve-page root-cause template for every known error - including trivial ones that took minutes to fix. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Simplify the template and scale the effort to the error's significance, eliminating steps that add no value
Keep the full template for everything, because thoroughness always improves quality
Add a second review of every template to make sure nothing was missed
Replace the template with an even longer one that covers every possible scenario
explain: Keep it simple and practical means using the minimum number of steps necessary and eliminating any step that produces no useful outcome - always think first about value. Thoroughness for its own sake, extra reviews, and longer templates add work without adding value.

q: A team wants to automate incident categorization with AI, but the current categories are inconsistent and the routing rules were never reviewed. Applying 'optimize and automate', the team should FIRST:
options: Automate immediately, since automation will fix the inconsistent categories by itself
