Standardize the categories and review the routing rules, then automate the optimized process
Abandon automation entirely, because the current process is too messy to ever automate
Automate only to reduce headcount, since that is the main purpose of automation
explain: Optimize and automate requires simplifying and optimizing the work BEFORE automating it - automating a broken process just produces bad results faster. The principle's purpose is to make automation genuinely useful, not to cut staff, and a messy process is a reason to optimize first, not to give up.

q: A provider considers bundling free on-site setup visits with every laptop order. Each visit costs the provider $150, but a survey shows most customers set up laptops themselves in minutes and rate the visit as unnecessary. Applying 'focus on value', the provider should:
options: Offer the visits anyway, because free extras always delight customers
Offer them only to the one customer who asked, regardless of the cost
Drop the idea, because it adds provider cost without improving any stakeholder's outcome
Offer them because competitors include setup visits in their bundles
explain: Focus on value judges every proposal by the value it creates for stakeholders - a costly extra nobody wants adds no value despite being free to the customer. 'Free delights', acting on one request, and copying competitors all substitute assumptions for an assessment of real stakeholder outcomes.

q: After a major outage, the network team publicly blames the database team in the incident review, and cooperation between the teams collapses. Applying 'collaborate and promote visibility', the BEST corrective action is to:
options: Identify which individuals caused the outage so they can be disciplined
Hold future reviews separately within each team to avoid confrontation
Publish the blame findings widely so everyone is motivated to avoid mistakes
Run blameless reviews focused on what happened and how the teams can improve together
explain: Collaboration requires trust and shared understanding, which blame destroys - the principle calls for working together across boundaries with openness. Discipline, separate reviews, and public blame all protect silos instead of building the cross-team cooperation that prevents repeat incidents.

q: A new CIO inherits a change process everyone calls slow, yet its risk checks have reliably caught dangerous changes for years. Following 'start where you are', her FIRST move should be to:
options: Scrap the entire process on day one, because a hated process cannot be worth keeping
Keep everything exactly as it is, because the risk checks prove it all works
Keep the reliable risk checks and redesign only the slow approval steps
Replace it with a vendor's best-practice model adopted without modification
explain: Start where you are means assessing what exists, keeping what works well, and improving what does not - the risk checks are a proven asset, the approval steps are the weakness. Scrapping everything destroys working controls, keeping everything preserves the waste, and wholesale adoption ignores the organization's actual situation.

q: A team plans to launch a new self-service catalogue to all 10,000 employees at once, then survey satisfaction after a year. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the BETTER plan is to:
options: Release the catalogue to one department first, gather feedback quickly, and adjust before wider rollout
Launch to everyone at once, because a single launch is simpler to manage
Delay the launch until every possible feature is built, to avoid rework
Survey users a year after launch, since early feedback is unreliable
explain: Progress iteratively with feedback means delivering in small sections and seeking feedback before, throughout, and after each iteration - early feedback from a small group makes the wider rollout safer. Big-bang launches, perfection-before-release, and year-late surveys all deny the team the learning that iterations provide.

q: Service desk analysts must choose from 200 incident categories; misclassification is soaring and reports are useless. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the BEST fix is to:
options: Train analysts harder on the 200 categories until they memorize them
Reduce the scheme to the categories actually used in reporting and decisions
Add more categories so every incident can be classified with perfect precision
Buy an AI tool to auto-categorize, leaving the 200 categories in place
explain: Keep it simple and practical means using the minimum necessary and eliminating what adds no value - 200 categories nobody can navigate add work without producing useful outcomes. More training, more categories, and AI on top of a bloated scheme all preserve the underlying complexity instead of removing it.

q: Automated deployment pipelines now release code in minutes, but the service desk is drowning: releases arrive with no runbooks, no training, and no user communication. Applying 'think and work holistically', the team should:
options: Slow deployments back down to the old pace so the desk can cope
Tell the service desk to cope, since deployment speed is what matters
Include support readiness - runbooks, training, communication - in the release workflow so automation benefits the whole service
Automate the service desk's work too, without changing the release workflow
explain: Think and work holistically means considering the whole system: faster deployments are only valuable if the surrounding service - support, documentation, communication - keeps up. Slowing down, telling the desk to cope, or automating around the gap all treat deployment as an isolated activity rather than part of an integrated service.

q: A team automated server provisioning, but the automated workflow still includes three approval steps that nobody can explain or justify. Applying 'optimize and automate', the team should:
options: Keep the approvals in the automation to be safe, since removing them is risky
Add two more approval steps to the automation for extra control
Blame the automation tool for being unable to handle the complexity
Remove the unjustified steps first, then automate the streamlined workflow
explain: Optimize and automate requires simplifying and optimizing before automating - steps nobody can justify produce no useful outcome and should be eliminated, not preserved in code. Keeping them 'to be safe', adding more, or blaming the tool all avoid the real work of questioning whether each step earns its place.

q: Executives make portfolio decisions using month-old dashboards, while the service teams hold real-time data they never share upward. Applying 'collaborate and promote visibility', the BEST action is to:
options: Schedule more status meetings so executives can ask teams for the data
Let one executive decide alone to avoid slowing decisions down
Keep the real-time data within the teams to avoid uncomfortable questions
Make current data visible to decision-makers and involve the teams that hold it in the decisions
explain: Collaborate and promote visibility means making work and information visible to the right stakeholders and including them in decisions - insufficient visibility leads to poor decisions. More meetings, solo decisions, and hiding data all preserve the gap between those who know and those who decide.

q: One large customer asks the provider to add 24/7 phone support. Before committing, applying 'focus on value' means the provider should:
options: Check whether the wider customer base values it and weigh the cost to the provider before committing
Build it immediately for that customer, because one request is enough justification
Reject it outright, because new support channels are always too expensive
Build it because competitors offer it, regardless of what customers actually need
explain: Focus on value considers all stakeholders - the requesting customer, the wider customer base, and the provider's own costs - since value is co-created across the service relationship. Acting on one request, blanket rejection, or copying competitors all substitute assumptions for an assessment of who gains value and at what cost.

q: A team adopting continual improvement has no formal process, but its monthly retrospectives reliably produce action items that get done. Following 'start where you are', the team should:
options: Discard the retrospectives as informal and design a formal process from zero
Use the existing retrospectives as the foundation, formalizing and strengthening them gradually
Hire consultants to install a completely new improvement framework immediately
Adopt another company's improvement model exactly as documented
explain: Start where you are means building on what already works - the retrospectives are a proven asset to observe, reuse, and improve. Discarding them, starting from zero, or copying another organization wholesale ignores existing capability and risks replacing something effective with something untested.

q: A company plans to bring its outsourced service desk back in-house with a single nine-month cutover. Applying 'progress iteratively with feedback', the BETTER approach is to:
options: Do the single big-bang cutover as planned, since splitting it adds coordination cost
Delay the move until every detail is perfect, however long that takes
Transition one support queue at a time, review performance and feedback, then continue
Keep the outsourcer forever, because any transition is too risky
explain: Progress iteratively with feedback means breaking large efforts into manageable sections with feedback at each stage - each queue transition teaches lessons that make the next one safer. Big-bang cutovers, perfection-before-action, and avoiding the change entirely all reject the learning that iterations provide.

q: Management wants to automate ticket triage mainly to cut analyst headcount. Applying 'optimize and automate' correctly, the goal of the automation should be to:
options: Eliminate as many analyst roles as possible, since that is the purpose of automation
Free analysts from repetitive triage so they can handle complex work that needs human judgment
Automate the triage exactly as it works today, including its known flaws
Avoid automation entirely, because it always harms service quality
explain: Optimize and automate aims to make work more effective by removing routine burden so people can focus where human judgment adds value - not to eliminate roles, and never to automate a flawed process unchanged. Headcount-cutting as the goal and automating flaws both miss the principle's intent of genuine improvement.

q: The change model for standard changes - pre-authorized, low-risk, well-understood - still routes every one through a five-person CAB review. Applying 'keep it simple and practical', the team should:
options: Remove the CAB step for pre-authorized standard changes, since it adds no value
Keep the CAB review for every change, because oversight can never hurt
Add more reviewers to the CAB to make the review even more thorough
Write better documentation explaining why the CAB step exists
explain: Keep it simple and practical means eliminating steps that produce no useful outcome - a standard change is already pre-authorized, so CAB review adds delay without adding control. More oversight, more reviewers, and better documentation of a valueless step all preserve waste instead of removing it.

q: A provider builds a technically excellent self-service portal, but customers barely use it and their outcomes do not improve. In ITIL 4 terms, the BEST explanation is:
options: Value is co-created through the customer's active engagement, so a service nobody uses cannot create value no matter how well it is built
The provider failed because value is delivered entirely by the provider alone
Customers are at fault for not appreciating a well-built service
Value was created at build time and customers simply have not noticed it yet
explain: Value is co-created through active collaboration between provider and consumer in the service relationship - the provider facilitates outcomes, but the customer must engage for value to emerge. The traps are provider-only value creation, blaming the customer, and treating value as something finished at build time.

q: A managed print vendor proposes a new contract. The facilities manager signs it and controls the budget, but she never uses a printer herself; office staff use the printers daily. In this service relationship the facilities manager is acting as the:
options: User, because she is involved in the service arrangement
Sponsor, because she authorizes the budget for service consumption
Customer, because she signed the vendor's contract
Provider, because she manages the office's printing needs
explain: The sponsor authorizes the budget for service consumption - signing and funding, without defining requirements or using the service. The customer defines requirements and takes responsibility for outcomes of consumption; the user actually uses the services; the provider delivers them.

q: A backup service restores files perfectly every time, but each restore takes twelve hours although the contract promises two. In ITIL 4 terms:
options: The service lacks utility, because restores are too slow to count as functionality
The service has neither utility nor warranty, so it cannot be called a service
The service has utility but lacks adequate warranty
Slow restores are a cost of the service, not a warranty failure
explain: Utility is the functionality offered (restores work - fit for purpose); warranty is the assurance it will perform as agreed (speed, availability - fit for use). Confusing the two - calling slow performance a utility failure, or dismissing it as merely a cost - misses that customers need both.

q: A project delivers a new self-service password tool on time and on budget, but service desk call volumes do not fall because nobody told users the tool exists. In ITIL 4 terms:
options: The outcome was achieved, because the tool was delivered as specified
Outputs and outcomes are the same thing, so delivery equals success
The project failed because the tool was delivered late
The output was delivered, but the desired outcome was not achieved because adoption was neglected
explain: An output is a tangible deliverable (the tool); an outcome is the result for a stakeholder enabled by outputs (fewer calls) - and outcomes need the consumer's participation, here adoption. Equating output with outcome, or blaming schedule, misses that value lives in the outcome, not the deliverable.

q: Moving to managed email removes the customer's server-maintenance costs, but the customer must now follow the provider's mailbox-provisioning procedures and train staff on them. In ITIL value analysis:
options: The service removes some costs for the customer while imposing others, and both sides must be weighed
All customer costs are removed by any managed service, by definition
Any imposed cost proves the service is a bad deal for the customer
Costs only matter to the provider, so the customer's new effort is irrelevant
explain: Every service relationship involves costs removed from the consumer AND costs imposed on the consumer - value assessment weighs both. The traps are assuming services remove all costs, treating any imposed cost as failure, or ignoring the consumer's side of the value equation entirely.

q: Migrating to the cloud removes the customer's hardware-failure risk, but introduces a new dependency: if the cloud provider has an outage, the customer's services stop. In ITIL 4, this shows that:
options: Services eliminate all risk for the consumer, so this migration was a mistake
Services remove or reduce some risks for the consumer while potentially imposing or leaving others
Any new risk means the service has failed and should be abandoned
Risk is solely the provider's concern once a service is consumed
explain: Services are a means of managing risk: the consumer no longer manages specific risks (hardware failure) but may face new ones (provider dependency) - both belong in the value assessment. The traps are expecting zero risk, treating any residual risk as failure, or assigning all risk to one party.

q: A provider's 'new starter package' includes a laptop the customer keeps, access to the corporate VPN, and a technician visit to set everything up. In ITIL 4, this service offering combines:
options: Goods, outcomes, and value
Resources, warranty, and costs
Goods, access to resources, and service actions
Utility, risks, and outputs
explain: A service offering can include goods (the laptop, transferring ownership), access to resources (the VPN), and service actions (the technician's setup work). Outcomes, value, utility, and costs describe what the offering produces or requires - not the three forms the offering itself can take.

q: An internal platform team provides managed CI/CD pipelines to product teams, who use them to deliver applications to business users. In ITIL 4, this shows that:
options: An organization is either a provider or a consumer, and the role never changes
Internal teams cannot be providers, because provision requires an external customer
Service relationships only work in a straight line from vendor to end user
One organization can be a provider and a consumer in different service relationships at the same time
explain: Organizations routinely play both roles: the platform team provides to product teams while consuming infrastructure itself, and product teams consume while providing to the business. Fixed single roles, 'internal teams can't provide', and straight-line-only chains all deny how real service relationships nest and overlap.

q: A provider's dashboards show every SLA target met, yet the customer says the service is worthless because month-end closing is still painful. In ITIL 4, the BEST conclusion is:
options: The provider's metrics prove value was delivered, so the customer is wrong
Value is determined solely by whether the contract targets were hit
The customer is always right, so the metrics should be discarded
Value is perceived by the consumer based on outcomes, so provider metrics alone cannot prove it
explain: Value is defined by the consumer's perception of the outcomes achieved - green provider metrics that miss what the customer actually needs are the classic watermelon-reporting trap. Provider metrics don't override perception, contracts don't define value by themselves, and the answer is not to discard measurement but to measure what matters to the consumer.

q: A hospital requires its patient-records system to be available during clinic hours, handle the morning login surge, recover from a failure within one hour, and keep audit logs tamper-proof. In ITIL 4, these requirements are:
options: Warranty requirements - they assure how the service performs rather than what it does
Utility requirements, because they describe the system's features
Outputs the provider must deliver at go-live
Risk statements, because each describes something that could go wrong
explain: Warranty is the assurance that a service will meet agreed requirements - availability, capacity, continuity, and security are its classic aspects (fit for use). Utility is the functionality itself (fit for purpose); outputs and risk statements are different concepts - these are promises about performance.

q: A provider runs its platform 24/7, monitors it, and maintains spare capacity; the customer must supply clean data each week and assign staff to act on reports. In ITIL 4, this shows that:
options: The provider does everything, so the customer has no responsibilities
Service provision and service consumption each require resources, and each party must manage its own
Only the provider's resources count, because the customer merely receives
Consumption needs no resources, since using a service is effortless
explain: Service provision (managing resources to deliver) and service consumption (managing resources needed to use the service) are both active roles requiring resources. The traps are provider-does-everything thinking, counting only provider resources, and pretending consumption is free of effort or cost.

q: A retail chain's operations director specifies exactly what a new point-of-sale service must do, funds it, and will be accountable for the sales results it enables. In this service relationship she is the:
options: User, because the service supports her operations
Sponsor, because she funds the service
Customer, because she defines the requirements and takes responsibility for the outcomes of consumption
Provider, because she is accountable for results
explain: The customer defines the requirements for a service and takes responsibility for the outcomes of service consumption. The user uses the service, the sponsor authorizes the budget, and the provider delivers - funding alone is sponsorship, and accountability for business results is the customer's defining trait.

q: Hundreds of call-centre agents use the CRM every day but had no say in its selection and do not control its budget. In the service relationship, the agents are acting as:
options: Customers, because they are the reason the CRM was bought
Sponsors, because their work justifies the CRM's cost
Providers, because they deliver service to callers through the CRM
Users, because they use the service without defining its requirements or funding it
explain: Users are the people who use services day to day - distinct from customers (who define requirements and own consumption outcomes) and sponsors (who authorize budgets). Being the reason for a purchase or delivering service through the tool does not make someone the customer, sponsor, or provider.

q: A logistics company's desired result is 'deliveries completed on the promised day without manual tracking calls'. In ITIL 4 terms, this desired result is:
options: An outcome - a result for a stakeholder, enabled by one or more outputs
An output, because it describes what the provider must produce
Utility, because it describes functionality the service must have
Warranty, because it promises a level of performance
explain: An outcome is a result for a stakeholder enabled by outputs - here, the provider's outputs (tracking systems, notifications) enable the customer's result. Calling it an output confuses the deliverable with the result; utility and warranty describe the service's fitness, not the stakeholder's result.

q: Two customers buy the same monitoring service. One calls it invaluable; the other cancels, calling it overpriced. In ITIL 4, the BEST explanation is:
options: The provider failed the second customer, because a good service satisfies everyone
Value is perceived by each stakeholder, so the same service can represent different value to different consumers
The first customer is mistaken, because value is objective and identical for all
The service has no real value, since opinions about it differ
explain: Value is subjective - defined by the consumer's perception of outcomes, costs, and risks - so identical services legitimately hold different value for different stakeholders. Expecting universal satisfaction, treating value as objective, or dismissing the service because perceptions differ all deny the consumer's central role in defining value.

q: A provider's 'branch office kit' includes routers that become the customer's property, access to the provider's cloud management console, and an engineer day for installation. In ITIL 4, this service offering combines:
options: Goods, outcomes, and value
Resources, warranty, and costs
The routers as goods, the console as access to resources, and the installation as a service action
Utility, risks, and outputs
explain: A service offering can include goods (ownership transfers - the routers), access to resources (the console), and service actions (the engineer's installation work). Outcomes, value, utility, and costs describe what the offering produces or requires - not the three forms the offering itself can take.

q: A managed security service depends on the provider's threat-intelligence feeds, its SIEM platform, and its analysts' investigative skills. In ITIL 4, these feeds, platforms, and skills are:
options: Outputs, because they are what the provider produces for the customer
Costs, because they are what the provider spends money on
Outcomes, because they produce results for customers
Resources that the provider configures and manages to deliver its services
explain: Resources include the provider's people, technology, information, and other assets configured to deliver services - feeds, platforms, and expertise alike. They are not outputs (deliverables), not merely costs (spending), and not outcomes (stakeholder results) - they are what the provider manages in service provision.

q: A retailer outsources its e-commerce platform: it no longer maintains servers, but it must rebuild its product catalogue in the provider's format and train merchandisers on the new tools. In ITIL value analysis, the catalogue rebuild and training are:
options: Costs imposed on the consumer to consume the service, which reduce the service's net value
Costs borne by the provider, since providers pay for customer adoption
Not real costs, because they involve no payment to the vendor
Irrelevant to value, because value only counts the subscription price
explain: Costs imposed on the consumer - effort, rebuilding, training - are part of the value equation and offset the service's benefits. They are not the provider's costs, they are real costs despite involving no vendor payment, and value counts all costs and risks, not just the price tag.

q: An email service is fast, secure, and full-featured, but it is unavailable every weekday morning between 9 and 10. In ITIL 4 terms:
options: It lacks utility, because an email service must always be available
It offers utility but fails warranty, because availability is an assurance not a feature
It has no value at all, since any outage destroys all value
Warranty is irrelevant here, because the features all work correctly
explain: Utility (fit for purpose - the features work) is present; warranty (fit for use - available when agreed) is broken, since availability is a classic warranty aspect. Calling this a utility failure confuses the two, total-value-destruction overstates one gap, and dismissing warranty ignores half of what makes a service valuable.

q: A provider delivers a collaboration platform and one department redesigns its meeting culture around it, doubling its productivity. Another department changes nothing about how it works and sees no benefit. In ITIL 4, the BEST conclusion is:
options: The provider failed the second department, because a good platform works for everyone
The platform was defective, since results differed between departments
Value is co-created: the provider enables outcomes, but the consumer must act for value to emerge
Outcomes are the provider's sole responsibility once the platform is delivered
explain: Value is co-created through the consumer's active participation - the same outputs produced value where the consumer engaged and none where it did not. Blaming the provider for the difference, calling the platform defective, or assigning outcomes solely to the provider all deny that consumption is an active role with its own duties.

q: A user cannot access the VPN. The service desk restores access in ten minutes using a documented workaround, without discovering why the VPN failed. In ITIL 4 terms:
options: The incident is resolved; a problem record is only needed if the underlying cause warrants investigation
The problem is resolved, because the user can work again
The known error is closed, because a workaround was applied
The workaround is a permanent fix, so no further action is required
explain: Incident management restores normal service operation quickly - the incident is resolved even though the cause is unknown. Problem management investigates underlying causes to prevent recurrence, and that is a separate decision; a workaround never closes a problem or a known error, and it is not a permanent fix.

q: The same database deadlock halts order processing every month. Each time, the service desk restarts the service and closes the ticket. With the pattern now obvious, the CORRECT next step is for:
options: Incident management to keep restarting faster, since restoration is its purpose
Problem management to investigate the underlying cause so the deadlock stops recurring
The service desk to stop logging the incidents, since they are all the same
Change enablement to authorize the restarts as emergency changes instead
explain: Problem management exists to reduce the likelihood and impact of incidents by identifying actual and potential causes - a monthly recurrence is exactly its trigger. Faster restarts, suppressed logging, and relabeling restarts as changes all leave the cause in place, guaranteeing the next outage.

q: Investigation finds that a faulty storage driver causes the monthly backup failures, a workaround is documented, and the permanent fix is scheduled for next quarter. In ITIL 4, this situation is now a:
options: Closed incident, because the failures are understood
Open problem only, because the fix is not yet applied
Known error - the underlying cause is identified and a workaround exists
Service request, because the fix has been requested
explain: A known error is a problem for which the underlying cause has been identified and a workaround documented - both conditions are met here. It is more than a closed incident (the cause persists), more specific than an open problem (cause known, workaround exists), and certainly not a service request.

q: A critical vulnerability is being actively exploited and a patch must be deployed tonight, with no time for the normal CAB cycle. Organizational policy pre-defines an accelerated assessment path and names an emergency authority. This is:
options: A standard change, because patching is routine work
Proof that no change process is needed in a real emergency
A normal change handled faster, with the CAB informed afterwards
An emergency change - it still follows a defined model, just on an accelerated path
explain: Emergency changes are still changes: they follow a pre-defined emergency model with its own assessment steps and authority - speed never means skipping the process. Calling it standard ignores the urgency and risk, skipping process invites uncontrolled damage, and treating it as a normal change misstates the model being used.

q: Two incidents arrive together: the CFO reports a slow email client, and the order-processing system is down for 300 customers. Applying ITIL priority correctly, the service desk should prioritize:
options: The order-processing incident, because priority is set by impact and urgency, not the reporter's seniority
The CFO's incident, because senior executives always outrank other users
Whichever ticket was logged first, because first-in-first-out is the fairest rule
The incident reported most loudly, because urgency means whoever shouts
explain: Priority is determined by impact (breadth of business affected) and urgency (how quickly resolution is needed) - 300 blocked customers outweigh one slow mailbox regardless of titles. Seniority-based, FIFO, and loudest-voice priority all substitute the wrong criteria and would leave the business bleeding.

q: A service desk analyst cannot diagnose a complex storage incident and transfers it to the specialist storage team because of their expertise. This is an example of:
options: Hierarchical escalation, because the incident moved to a different team
Functional escalation - the transfer is based on the skills and knowledge needed
A major incident procedure, because specialists are now involved
Problem escalation, because the cause is not yet known
explain: Functional escalation moves an incident based on the expertise required to resolve it. Hierarchical escalation moves it up authority levels for decisions or resources; involving specialists does not make it a major incident; and 'problem escalation' is not the ITIL term for this handoff.

q: A faulty storage controller takes down the national rail booking system on a holiday weekend. A dedicated team with executive authority coordinates the recovery, with hourly updates to passengers and the business. This is most likely a:
options: Standard incident, because the service desk is involved in recovery
Problem record, because the faulty controller must be investigated
Major incident - significant business impact demanding dedicated resources and coordination
Routine service request, because recovery steps are pre-defined
explain: A major incident has significant business impact and triggers special procedures: dedicated teams, executive authority, and frequent communication. It is not a standard incident (impact is far beyond routine), not merely a problem record (restoration comes first), and not a service request (nothing about this is a normal pre-defined request).

q: A new starter asks for the standard software bundle to be installed on her laptop on her first day. Nothing is broken or degraded, and this bundle is installed routinely for every joiner. The service desk should handle this as:
options: An incident, because the user cannot do her work without the software
A problem, because the software should have been pre-installed
A change, because the laptop's configuration is being altered
A service request - a pre-defined request that forms a normal part of service delivery
explain: Service requests are pre-defined user requests that initiate as a normal part of service delivery - routine standard-bundle installs are the textbook example. It is not an incident (no interruption or degradation), not a problem (no underlying cause to investigate), and routine fulfillment is not a change.

q: A university's SLA promises 99.5% Wi-Fi availability to students. The internal infrastructure team commits to supporting targets in an internal agreement, while the external ISP signs a contract with its own response targets. In ITIL 4, the internal team's agreement is an:
options: OLA - an internal agreement underpinning the SLA - while the ISP's contract is an underpinning contract
SLA, because both the team and the ISP support the same Wi-Fi service
OLA for both, because any agreement supporting a service is an OLA
Underpinning contract for both, because both support the SLA
explain: An OLA (operational level agreement) is between internal parties supporting the SLA; an underpinning contract (UC) is with an external supplier. Calling internal commitments SLAs confuses customer-facing targets with internal ones, and OLAs never apply to external vendors.

q: Each morning the monitoring platform logs 'all probes responding normally' and the NOC takes no action. In monitoring and event management, this is an:
options: Exception event, because every probe result should be reviewed
Informational event - it confirms normal operation and needs no action
Warning event, because the probes are critical and deserve attention
Incident, because every event must become a ticket
explain: Informational events simply confirm that something expected happened - no action or decision is required. Exceptions signal breaches needing action, warnings signal approaching thresholds, and not every event is an incident; treating routine confirmations as exceptions would drown the team in noise.

q: Monitoring detects that both the primary and backup links to the data centre have failed, and immediately pages the on-call network engineer. In monitoring and event management, this detection represents:
options: An informational event, because the monitoring system is just reporting status
A warning event, because the links might recover on their own
An exception event - a failure requiring immediate action
Not an event at all, because only the engineer's response matters
explain: Exception events indicate that something exceptional has occurred - a failure or potential breach - and require action, here the automatic page. Informational events need no action, warnings signal approaching (not reached) thresholds, and dismissing the event ignores that detection is what triggered the response.

q: Staff in the London office phone individual engineers they know personally instead of the service desk. Tickets go untracked, and two engineers unknowingly fix the same issue twice. The BEST remedy is to:
options: Let staff contact anyone they like, since direct access is faster
Disband the service desk, because staff have voted with their phones
Hire more engineers so duplicated effort hurts less
Re-establish the service desk as the single point of contact so work is coordinated and tracked
explain: The service desk's purpose includes capturing demand for incidents and requests and acting as the coordination point - bypassing it destroys visibility and duplicates effort. Letting chaos continue, disbanding the desk, or adding engineers all preserve the untracked, uncoordinated work that caused the pain.

q: Every month the CAB spends two hours approving routine certificate renewals and password-policy updates that have never once failed. The BEST application of change enablement here is to:
options: Abolish the CAB, because change control only slows things down
Review these routine items even more carefully, since the agenda proves changes are risky
Hold longer CAB meetings so the routine items get proper attention too
Handle them as standard changes with pre-authorized models, so the CAB focuses on changes that need judgment
explain: Change enablement balances effectiveness with speed: standard changes (low-risk, pre-authorized, well-understood) should not consume CAB time meant for normal changes needing risk assessment. Abolishing control, reviewing harder, or meeting longer all keep the bottleneck while missing the structural fix.

q: At 1 AM a failed storage array starts corrupting customer data. The CAB cannot convene, but the emergency change policy names the infrastructure duty manager as the emergency authority. The CORRECT action is for:
options: The duty manager to authorize the fix under the emergency change model
The team to wait for the next scheduled CAB, since only the CAB can authorize changes
Any available engineer to authorize it, because emergencies override all authority rules
The team to act without authorization, since emergencies mean no process applies
explain: The emergency change model pre-defines both the accelerated assessment steps and who holds emergency authority - the named duty manager acts within the process, not outside it. Waiting for the CAB wastes the model's purpose, 'anyone can authorize' ignores the designated authority, and skipping authorization entirely is uncontrolled change.

q: Problem management can staff only one investigation: recurring login failures blocking 2,000 shop-floor workers, or an intermittent typo in an internal admin report. With limited capacity, problem management should prioritize:
options: Whichever problem was logged first, because queues should be worked in order
The login failures, based on business impact and urgency
The typo, because it will be quicker to solve
The problem reported by the most senior manager, regardless of impact
explain: Problem prioritization, like incident prioritization, weighs impact and urgency - 2,000 blocked workers outweigh a cosmetic typo. FIFO, easiest-first, and seniority-based ordering all substitute the wrong criteria and would leave the damaging problem festering.

q: For eighteen months, operators have restarted the reporting service every Monday morning instead of fixing the memory leak behind the crashes. Problem management should:
options: Close the problem record, because the restart routine has become standard practice
Reclassify the restarts as standard changes and forget the underlying leak
Review whether the workaround remains acceptable or whether the permanent fix should now be scheduled
Ignore it, because workarounds that old are no longer problem management's concern
explain: Problem management owns known errors until the underlying cause is resolved or formally accepted - a workaround aging into routine still carries the risk and cost of the unresolved error. Closing, reclassifying, or ignoring it abandons the error-control responsibility to keep pushing toward a real resolution.

q: A provider reports 100% SLA achievement, yet customers remain unhappy: the targets were set without reference to month-end processing peaks that matter most to the business. The root failure of service level management here is that:
options: Too few metrics were reported, so more dashboards are needed
The targets were too easy, so they should simply be made stricter
SLA reporting is pointless when customers complain
Targets were not agreed with the customer to reflect real business needs
explain: Service level management must set, agree, and monitor targets that reflect what the business actually needs - unilaterally set targets that miss peak periods produce watermelon reporting: green metrics, red experience. More metrics, stricter targets, or abandoning SLM all dodge the real failure to agree meaningful targets with the customer.

q: During a major outage, three analysts log the same event as 'printer issue', 'slow application', and 'network down', so the incident manager cannot see the true scope for an hour. This shows that:
options: Accurate, consistent logging and categorization matter, because misclassified incidents get the wrong response
Logging is bureaucratic overhead that slows down real technical work
The category field is cosmetic and has no effect on resolution
Speed matters more than accuracy, so analysts should log as little as possible
explain: Incident management depends on logging and categorization to route work correctly and reveal true scope - inconsistent categories hid the outage's scale for an hour. Dismissing logging as bureaucracy, calling categorization cosmetic, or prizing speed over accuracy all guarantee repeated misdirection.

q: The service desk has one spare projector for Friday: both the board meeting and a graduate training session request it. For service request management, the CORRECT basis for deciding is:
options: The board meeting always wins, because seniority determines priority
The agreed prioritization policy - for example, business need or target dates - not the requester's rank
Random selection, because all requests are equal
First-come-first-served, with no exceptions ever
explain: Service requests are prioritized according to agreed policy - often based on business need, impact, or fulfillment targets - not the seniority of the requester. Seniority-based, random, and rigid FIFO approaches all ignore that the organization should define fair, transparent prioritization rules in advance.

q: The facilities team plans a power shutdown for Saturday while the database team plans a major upgrade in the same window. The value of the change schedule here is that:
options: Both proceed, because the schedule is only informational
Both are cancelled automatically when a clash is detected
The change authority can spot the conflict in the schedule and coordinate the timing
Whichever team booked first automatically wins the window
explain: The change schedule gives the change authority visibility of all planned changes so conflicts, collisions, and risks can be managed proactively. Treating it as read-only, auto-cancelling, or first-booked-wins all waste the coordination purpose the schedule exists to serve.

q: A new HR portal is deployed to the production servers, but HR staff have not been trained and the help articles are unwritten. The release manager withholds the launch announcement until training and documentation are ready. This shows that release management is concerned with:
options: Making the release usable for customers, not just technically deployed
Deploying code as fast as possible regardless of readiness
Training, which is the customer's responsibility, not the provider's
Avoiding releases entirely, since every release carries risk
explain: Release management makes new and changed services available for use - which includes training, documentation, and communications, not just the technical deployment. Speed-at-all-costs, pushing training onto customers, and avoiding releases all confuse release (available for use) with mere deployment.

q: The team copies the new booking engine onto the live servers, where it sits idle; travellers will be switched over to it after the holiday peak. In ITIL 4:
options: The release is complete, because the code is on the production servers
Deployment has moved the components to live, but release - making the version available for use - has not happened yet
The deployment failed, because travellers cannot use the new engine
The idle copy itself counts as the release
explain: Deployment management moves new or changed components to live environments; release management makes them available for use - the engine is deployed but not released. Equating the two, calling it a failure, or treating the idle copy as the release all blur this deliberate separation.

q: Decommissioned servers are still racked and powered, the company keeps paying maintenance on them, and nobody knows which ones hold customer data. The practice that addresses this across the full asset lifecycle is:
options: Service configuration management, because the servers are in the CMDB
Procurement, because the problem started at purchase time
IT asset management - maximizing value, controlling costs, and managing risks of assets through their lifecycle
Financial management, because this is purely a spending problem
explain: IT asset management plans and manages the full lifecycle of IT assets to maximize value, control costs, and manage risks - covering use, maintenance, and disposal. Configuration management tracks relationships for service delivery, procurement only buys, and finance alone misses the operational and risk aspects.

q: Before decommissioning an old database server, the team queries the CMDB to find which applications still connect to it. This use of configuration information to assess the impact of a planned removal is enabled by:
options: IT asset management, because the server is an asset
Monitoring and event management, because it watches the server
Change enablement alone, because impact assessment is its job
Service configuration management - CIs and their relationships support impact analysis
explain: Service configuration management ensures accurate information about configuration items and their relationships is available when needed - exactly what impact analysis consumes. Asset management tracks value and cost, monitoring watches live status, and change enablement uses the data but does not maintain it.

q: The video-conferencing service never goes offline, but every all-hands meeting with 500 participants collapses under the load. For availability management, the CORRECT view is:
options: Availability includes the service performing its agreed function when required, not merely 'not down'
Availability is fine, because the service never actually stopped
This is purely a capacity problem, so availability management has no role
Users are wrong to complain, because uptime is the only availability measure
explain: Availability is the ability of a service to perform its agreed function when required - a meeting service that collapses at the required scale is not truly available. 'Never stopped' thinking, punting everything to capacity management, and uptime-only measurement all reduce availability to a server ping rather than usable service.

q: The reporting service crawls every month-end although CPU sits at 30%: every department runs full-history exports at the same time. Capacity and performance management should:
options: Buy more servers, because slow performance always means insufficient capacity
Address the demand side - for example, staggering the exports - since capacity balances supply with demand
Hand the problem to availability management, because slow reports are an outage
Ignore it, because low CPU proves there is no capacity problem
explain: Capacity and performance management ensures services meet agreed performance by managing both supply AND demand - simultaneous full-history exports are a demand-side problem that extra servers would not fix. Buying hardware blindly, relabeling it as availability, or ignoring it because utilization looks fine all miss the demand side of the equation.

q: A ransomware attack destroys the primary site. The provider fails over to the secondary site and restores critical services within the agreed four hours, using a plan it rehearses twice a year. This is the work of:
options: Availability management, because the services became available again
Incident management, because the attack caused incidents
Service continuity management - ensuring services can be recovered within agreed times after a disaster
Risk management, because the attack was a risk that materialized
explain: Service continuity management ensures that service availability and performance can be maintained at sufficient levels following a disaster, with tested recovery plans. Availability manages day-to-day uptime, incident management restores normal operation after interruptions, and risk management identifies risks - none of them owns the disaster-recovery capability.

q: The new-starter checklist grants every joiner access to the payroll system 'just in case' - including interns and short-term contractors. The practice that addresses this excessive access is:
options: Availability management, because payroll data must stay available to staff
Knowledge management, because access lists are organizational knowledge
Workforce management, because this is a staffing issue
Information security management - confidentiality requires restricting access to authorized staff
explain: Information security management protects confidentiality, integrity, and availability - and confidentiality means access limited to those who need it, not granted 'just in case'. Availability is about the service working, knowledge management is about sharing usable knowledge, and staffing is not the issue; the issue is uncontrolled access to sensitive data.

q: The only person who understands how the legacy billing batch works is retiring next month, and nothing about it is written down. The practice that addresses capturing and sharing this knowledge before it walks out the door is:
options: Workforce and talent management, because the answer is better hiring
Documentation, which is wasteful overhead that slows experts down
Incident management, because the knowledge is used when batches fail
Knowledge management - ensuring the right knowledge is available to the right people
explain: Knowledge management improves efficiency by ensuring knowledge - including tacit expertise - is captured, shared, and usable where needed. Hiring alone doesn't preserve knowledge, dismissing documentation guarantees the loss repeats, and incident management consumes knowledge without preserving it.

q: Leadership cannot tell from the monthly pack of 40 system metrics whether customers are actually getting value. The team replaces them with five outcome indicators tied to business goals, and decisions improve. For measurement and reporting, the lesson is:
options: Reports should provide information that supports decisions, not just raw data and metrics
More metrics are always better, so the 40 should have been kept alongside the five
Reports exist only for compliance, so leadership's confusion does not matter
Leadership should have learned to interpret the 40 system metrics
explain: Measurement and reporting should support good decision-making - data becomes information only when it is organized for a purpose, and the outcome indicators served decisions while the system metrics did not. More metrics, compliance-only thinking, and blaming the readers all treat reporting as data-dumping rather than decision support.

q: The service desk team collects 25 improvement suggestions from analysts but has only one free afternoon a month to act on them. Under the continual improvement practice, the team should:
options: Work the suggestions first-come-first-served, because that is fairest
Prioritize suggestions by alignment with business goals and expected value
Fund the suggestions from the loudest analysts to keep the peace
Attempt all 25 at once so nobody feels ignored
explain: Continual improvement prioritizes improvement opportunities by their contribution to business objectives and expected value - resources are finite, so alignment decides. FIFO, loudest-analyst, and do-everything approaches all ignore that improvement exists to serve strategy, not to be fair or popular.

q: A new expense system launches, but employees keep filing paper claims: managers never explained why the change matters and never reinforced the new way of working. The practice addressing the people side - sponsorship, communication, and reinforcement - is:
options: Deployment management, because the system was deployed
Training, which alone will fix any resistance
Organizational change management - managing the human aspects so changes succeed and stick
Mandating usage more strictly, because resistance means the mandate was weak
explain: Organizational change management ensures changes are smoothly and successfully implemented so lasting benefits are achieved - addressing sponsorship, communication, and reinforcement. Deployment covers the technical move, training alone doesn't create sponsorship, and stronger mandates without buy-in breed workarounds.

q: The provider's catalogue still lists a fax service nobody has ordered in years, while a mobile app that customers keep requesting sits unfunded in the pipeline. The practice for managing this mix of live, planned, and dying services is:
options: Strategy management, because these are strategic choices
Financial management, because these are spending decisions
Project management, because each service involves projects
Portfolio management - deciding the right mix of services across pipeline, catalogue, and retired states
explain: Portfolio management ensures the organization has the right mix of services to meet outcomes across the pipeline (proposed), catalogue (live), and retired services. Strategy sets direction, finance manages money, and projects deliver - but the invest/grow/retire mix decision is portfolio management's domain.

q: To decide whether the backup service should continue, the provider calculates its full cost - hardware, licences, and staff time - and compares it with the value the service delivers. This analysis of funding, accounting, and value for money is the work of:
options: Service financial management - managing the organization's budgets, accounting, and charging requirements
Simple bookkeeping, which needs no management practice behind it
Procurement, because it involves what was paid for the service
Financial planning, which is the same thing under a different name
explain: Service financial management supports the organization's strategies by managing budgets, accounting, and charging for services - understanding true service cost is its foundation. Calling it bookkeeping, procurement, or generic financial planning misses its service-specific purpose: informing decisions about services with real cost and value data.

q: Executives decide the company will compete on reliability rather than price, and will direct investment accordingly over the next three years. In ITIL 4, this formulation of goals and the means to achieve them is:
options: Portfolio management, because it involves choosing services
Strategy management - defining the organization's direction and how to get there
The plan activity of the value chain, which covers all planning
Governance, because executives are doing the governing
explain: Strategy management formulates the organization's goals and adopts the courses of action and resource allocation to achieve them - competing on reliability with aligned investment. Portfolio manages the service mix within that strategy, plan is a value chain activity not the practice, and governance evaluates/directs/monitors rather than formulating strategy.

q: The provider's network hardware vendor keeps missing delivery dates, delaying customer installations, but each contract renewal is signed without any review of the vendor's performance. The practice that should formalize this is:
options: Procurement, because the relationship started with a purchase
The partners and suppliers dimension, which is a perspective rather than a practice
Supplier management - managing supplier relationships, contracts, and performance
Relationship management, because all relationships are the same
explain: Supplier management ensures suppliers and their performance are managed appropriately to support quality services - contracts, performance tracking, and enforcement. Procurement only buys, the dimension is a lens not a practice, and relationship management covers broader stakeholder relationships rather than supplier performance.

q: Before migrating the customer database, a team identifies that the migration could corrupt records, assesses the likelihood and impact, and rehearses the migration twice in a staging environment. This is:
options: Change enablement only, because a migration is a change
Testing, which is a technical activity rather than a practice
Risk avoidance, because the only safe option is to cancel the migration
Risk management - identifying, assessing, and responding to risks
explain: Risk management is about understanding and dealing with risks - identification, assessment, and response (here, rehearsal as mitigation). Change enablement authorizes the change but doesn't own risk analysis, testing is one response technique not the practice, and cancelling everything confuses management with avoidance.

q: A team designing a patient check-in kiosk works with clinic staff to define acceptable wait times, accessibility needs, and how failures should be handled - before building anything. This is:
options: Service design - designing services that are fit for purpose and fit for use
Building first and designing later, which is faster
Documentation, because the agreement is just paperwork
Technical architecture only, since design means infrastructure
explain: Service design ensures services meet agreed utility (fit for purpose) and warranty (fit for use) requirements before they are built. Build-first, paperwork-dismissal, and infrastructure-only views all skip the deliberate design of the whole service against agreed requirements.

q: The account manager runs quarterly business reviews with the customer's CIO, aligning the service roadmap with the customer's changing business plans and strengthening cooperation at senior level. This investment in stakeholder relationships is:
options: Service level management, because roadmaps are about meeting targets
Relationship management - establishing and nurturing links with stakeholders at strategic and tactical levels
Incident management, because alignment prevents incidents
Public relations, which is not an ITIL practice
explain: Relationship management establishes and nurtures the links between the organization and its stakeholders - exactly what the quarterly reviews build. SLM manages targets not trust, incident management restores services not relationships, and dismissing it as PR misses that stakeholder cooperation is a managed practice.

q: All database expertise sits with one contractor whose contract ends in six months, so the provider starts training two employees as successors. Ensuring the organization has the right people with the right skills is:
options: Knowledge management only, because skills are just knowledge
HR's problem, not something ITIL practices address
Workforce and talent management - ensuring the organization has the right people with the right skills and knowledge
Hiring contractors, which is the only realistic fix
explain: Workforce and talent management ensures the organization has the right people with the right skills, knowledge, and roles to support its objectives - including succession for critical skills. Knowledge management preserves information not capability, 'HR's problem' denies the practice exists, and contractors-only is one tactic not the practice.

q: A trainer's slide describes the ITIL service value system as 'the value chain plus the practices'. This description is:
options: Incomplete - the SVS also includes the guiding principles, governance, and continual improvement
Correct - those two elements are the complete service value system
Incomplete only because governance is missing; the rest is complete
Correct, because the guiding principles are optional philosophy rather than SVS components
explain: The SVS has five components: guiding principles, governance, service value chain, practices, and continual improvement - the principles guide the whole system and are not optional. Omitting them, or treating governance as the only gap, leaves an incomplete model of how value is created.

q: Hundreds of employees ask for a self-service way to reset their VPN tokens after the helpdesk queue for resets grows sharply. In ITIL 4, this widespread desire for a product or service entering the SVS is:
options: An opportunity, because the provider sees a possibility to add value
Demand - a need or desire for products and services from consumers
Value, because satisfying it will create value
An output of the service value system
explain: Demand represents the need or desire for products and services - here, consumers actively wanting the reset capability. Opportunity is a possibility to add value or improve the organization; value is the SVS output, not its input; and inputs to the SVS are opportunity and demand, not outputs.

q: A new payroll service goes live, but the external payroll processor's maintenance windows were never checked during design - so the service is unavailable every Sunday. Within the four dimensions, the neglected one is:
options: Information and technology, because the service design was flawed
Organizations and people, because the design team made an error
Partners and suppliers - the external provider's constraints were not considered
Value streams and processes, because the maintenance process was wrong
explain: The partners and suppliers dimension covers the organization's relationships with other organizations involved in service delivery - the processor's maintenance windows were a constraint that design ignored. The failure was not the technology, the people's competence, or the process design, but the unexamined supplier relationship.

q: The team runs end-to-end tests proving the new ordering service handles peak load, then confirms support staff are trained and runbooks exist before go-live. This pre-live verification belongs mainly to the value chain activity:
options: Plan, because the tests were scheduled during planning
Engage, because stakeholders were informed
Obtain/build, because the service was constructed
Design and transition - ensuring services meet expectations and can be moved to live operation
explain: Design and transition ensures that services are designed to meet stakeholder expectations for quality, costs, and time to market, and can be transitioned to operation with trained support. Plan creates shared understanding of direction, engage handles stakeholder interaction, and obtain/build ensures components are available - none owns the pre-live verification.

q: The board approves the IT strategy, requires quarterly assurance that risk controls are working, and adjusts direction when they are not. This illustrates:
options: Management, because assurance work is done by managers
That governance and management are the same thing
That the board should leave service management entirely to executives
Governance - the governing body evaluates, directs, and monitors, and remains accountable
explain: Governance is the means by which an organization is directed and controlled: the governing body evaluates, directs, and monitors, and is accountable - delegation does not transfer accountability. Calling it management confuses doing with directing, and excluding the board denies governance its proper place in the SVS.

q: An improvement team jumps straight from assessing its current resolution times to taking action, without agreeing what it wants to achieve. The risk, in continual improvement model terms, is that:
options: They skipped 'where do we want to be?' - without agreed targets, they cannot tell whether the actions worked
They skipped the vision step, which is the only step that matters
The model is optional, so skipping steps carries no risk
They should have skipped the current-state assessment instead
explain: The continual improvement model requires defining 'where do we want to be?' (measurable targets) before acting - without targets, the 'did we get there?' assessment is impossible. The vision matters but is not the only step, the model is the SVS's improvement engine not an optional extra, and skipping assessment would be worse, not better.

q: A provider handles incidents through one value stream - fast, standardized, heavily automated - and introduces new services through a completely different one. Within the SVS, this is:
options: A violation, because an organization must use a single value stream for everything
Expected - value streams are tailored combinations of value chain activities designed for specific scenarios
A sign the four dimensions are misaligned
Evidence that the value chain is being used as a fixed sequence
explain: Value streams are the specific combinations of value chain activities an organization uses for particular scenarios - different scenarios legitimately need different streams. Demanding one stream, crying misalignment, or treating the chain as a fixed sequence all misunderstand the value chain as a flexible operating model.

q: A sudden currency devaluation doubles the cost of the provider's imported hardware, forcing a complete replan of the infrastructure refresh. In ITIL 4, this devaluation is:
options: An internal factor, because it affects internal budgets
An opportunity created by the service value system
An external factor - economic - that the SVS must respond to
Demand, because the provider must demand cheaper hardware
explain: External factors such as economic shifts (the economic part of PESTLE) sit outside the organization but shape what the SVS must deliver. They are not internal, not opportunities, and not demand - they are constraints and drivers the value system must absorb.

q: Incident analysts work from three different spreadsheets with conflicting on-call contact lists, so escalations repeatedly go to the wrong people. Within the four dimensions, the failing one is:
options: Organizations and people, because the analysts lack skills
Partners and suppliers, because the spreadsheets came from vendors
Value streams and processes, because escalation is a process
Information and technology - the information needed for the work is unreliable
explain: The information and technology dimension covers the information and knowledge needed to manage services - here the contact information itself is untrustworthy. The analysts' skills are not the issue, no vendor is the cause, and no process redesign fixes bad data.

q: A service manager shadows warehouse staff for a week to understand how they actually use the inventory system before proposing any changes. In the service value chain, this is mainly the activity:
options: Engage - understanding stakeholder needs and building relationships to shape direction
Plan, because a proposal will follow the shadowing
Deliver and support, because warehouse staff are being served
Improve, because the changes will improve the system
explain: Engage provides a good understanding of stakeholder needs and ensures transparency and good relationships - shadowing users to learn their reality is textbook engage. Plan creates shared understanding of vision and direction from such input, deliver and support handles ongoing service, and improve acts on lessons - the understanding itself is engage.

q: The executive team agrees the company will become the region's most reliable cloud provider. Service management translates this into a three-year plan with milestones, targets, and resource needs. This translation of vision into direction is mainly the value chain activity:
options: Engage, because executives were consulted
Plan - creating a shared understanding of the vision, current status, and improvement direction
Design and transition, because the plan is being designed
Obtain/build, because resources will be needed
explain: Plan ensures a shared understanding of the vision, current status, and improvement direction across the organization - turning the executives' vision into a concrete plan. Engage is stakeholder interaction, design and transition covers service design, and obtain/build secures components - the translation of vision into direction is plan.

q: An internal team builds a custom authentication module that the new service will depend on. In the service value chain, building this component is mainly the activity:
options: Design and transition, because the module was designed
Deliver and support, because the service will use it
Obtain/build - ensuring service components are available when and where they are needed
Engage, because the team engaged with the requirement
explain: Obtain/build ensures that service components are available when and where they are needed, whether built in-house, bought, or sourced - building the module is exactly this. Design and transition integrates and verifies it, deliver and support operates the live service, and engage is about stakeholders, not construction.

q: Each morning the operations team checks overnight alerts, restores any degraded services, and answers the user questions that came in from the night shift. These ongoing operational activities fall mainly under:
options: Engage, because users are being communicated with
Design and transition, because the services were recently designed
Improve, because operations always improve things
Deliver and support - ensuring services are delivered and supported according to agreed specifications
explain: Deliver and support ensures that services are delivered and supported according to agreed specifications and stakeholders' expectations - the ongoing operational home. Engage covers stakeholder interaction around the service, design and transition ends at go-live, and improve is about enhancement, not daily operation.

q: After each release, the team reviews what slowed it down and removes one bottleneck before the next release. In value chain terms, this steady adjustment is the activity:
options: Improve - ensuring continual improvement of services, practices, and value chain activities
Plan, because each review produces a decision
Design and transition, because the release process was redesigned
Governance, because the team was directed to change
explain: Improve ensures continual improvement of services, practices, and the organization's value chain activities - removing one bottleneck per cycle is textbook improve. Plan sets direction, design and transition handles service transitions, and governance evaluates and directs at the organizational level rather than improving a practice.

q: A trainer asks the class: opportunity and demand flow into the service value system - what flows out of it?
options: Services, because the SVS produces services for customers
Value - value co-created for stakeholders from the inputs
Products, because products are what organizations sell
Outcomes, which are the same as value
explain: The SVS describes how all organizational components work together to enable value co-creation - value is its defined output. Services and products are means within the system, and while outcomes matter to stakeholders, the SVS output as defined is value itself.

q: The new on-call rota looks perfect on paper, but nobody told the night-shift engineers, who keep escalating to the old contacts. Within the four dimensions, the root issue sits in:
options: Information and technology, because the rota tool should have notified them
Partners and suppliers, because the night shift is a separate team
Organizations and people - roles, responsibilities, and communication were neglected
Value streams and processes, because the rota process is at fault
explain: The organizations and people dimension covers roles, responsibilities, communication, and organizational structure - the stated cause of the breakdown. The tool is fine, no external supplier is involved, and the rota design is not the problem; the human and organizational side is.

q: A team documents its change process in fine detail, but every change still stalls at handoffs because nobody mapped how work flows end to end. Within the four dimensions, the gap is in:
options: Organizations and people, because staff are not following the document
Information and technology, because better tools would fix the handoffs
Partners and suppliers, because handoffs always involve vendors
Value streams and processes - activities were never organized into an effective end-to-end value stream
explain: The value streams and processes dimension is about how activities are organized into value streams and how well processes work end to end - documented steps that stall at handoffs show the stream was never designed. The people follow what exists, tools can't fix a missing stream design, and handoffs here are internal, not supplier-related.

q: After cutting resolution times by 30%, the team publishes a short case study, trains new joiners in the new method, and reviews the metrics every quarter. In the continual improvement model, this is:
options: How do we keep the momentum going? - sustaining the improvement so gains are not lost
Take action, because the team is doing something
Did we get there? - because resolution times were cut
What is the vision? - because the case study spreads the vision
explain: Keeping the momentum going is the model's final step: embedding improvements so they stick and launching the next cycle - training joiners and periodic metric reviews are classic sustainment. Take action was the earlier execution, did-we-get-there was the assessment against targets, and vision was the starting point.

q: The CIO funds new value chain tooling and practices but tells teams to skip the guiding principles as 'soft stuff'. Within the SVS, this is:
options: Acceptable, because principles are optional once practices are in place
A mistake - the guiding principles guide every component of the SVS and shape all decisions
Acceptable for operations, since principles only apply to improvement work
A mistake only if the provider also skips governance
explain: The guiding principles are a core SVS component that guides the organization in all circumstances - they shape how the value chain, practices, governance, and improvement are applied. Treating them as optional philosophy, limiting them to improvement, or conditioning their relevance on governance all deny their system-wide role.

q: A hospital applies the service value system to its patient-discharge process. This is:
options: Inappropriate, because the SVS only applies to IT organizations
Inappropriate, because patient discharge is not a service
Appropriate - the SVS describes how organizational components work together to enable value co-creation, whatever the industry
Appropriate only with formal permission from the ITIL publisher
explain: The SVS is a generic model of how all components and activities of an organization work together to facilitate value creation - ITIL 4 explicitly applies beyond IT. Restricting it to IT, denying discharge is a service, or requiring publisher permission all misunderstand its universal, flexible nature.
